cables.subject: Internal Security Developments in Lebanon
cables.excerpt: Two years before the civil war: Fatah members arrested at Beirut airport with 10 kg of TNT. Black September threatened to blow up the airport. A 2-kg bomb was found and defused. The Lebanese Army G-2 assessed that Arafat may have covertly tipped off Lebanese authorities about a bomb planted by his own movement’s hardliners he could not control.
cables.annotatedBody:
Originally classified CONFIDENTIAL · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State under EO Systematic Review, 30 June 2005 · Now UNCLASSIFIED

Summary
Following several weekend incidents involving fedayeen[1] that produced considerable tension here, Lebanese authorities have instituted heavy security precautions in and around Beirut Airport. The Lebanese Army’s patrolling activities along the Israeli border have also been intensified. We regard these developments as encouraging initial signs on the part of the new Lebanese government.

1.
Beirut International Airport is under strict security on April 30, following a weekend of tension that began the afternoon of April 27 when airport authorities — in the process of conducting a thorough search of departing passengers — arrested three men (2 Lebanese and 1 Palestinian) who were about to board an Air France flight to Paris with 10 kilograms of TNT and detonating devices in their baggage.[2] Upon learning that the individuals were Fatah[3] members, Lebanese Army and security forces — fearing an adverse fedayeen reaction when the arrests became known — moved quickly to block the main access road to the airport and cordon off the southern entrance to the Sabra quarter and the fedayeen stronghold at the nearby Shatila refugee camp.[4]

No reaction occurred that day, but on April 28 airport authorities received a series of anonymous telephone calls threatening that BSO[5] would blow up airport facilities if the arrested fedayeen and their munitions were not released. One such call, made late on April 28, indicated that a bomb had been placed in a water cooler at the airport terminal. A hectic search of the building — supervised personally by Minister of Interior Bashir al-Awar[6] and senior Lebanese security officials — led to the discovery of a 2-kilogram plastic charge timed to explode at 2:30 AM on April 29 in a water cooler.

2.
As of noon on April 30, army and security forces are maintaining intensified security precautions around the entire airport area, with roadblocks established on main access routes, cars being thoroughly searched, and only travelers being allowed to enter the terminal proper. Airline traffic continues as scheduled. The general atmosphere of tension was heightened further on the night of April 28–29 by the explosion of a stick of dynamite thrown at the Jordanian ambassador’s residence from a passing car (no casualties resulted and damage was negligible).

3.
Minister of Interior Awar has stated publicly that the GOL resolved not to give in to blackmail in connection with the April 27 airport incident. We understand from a reliable Presidency source that Awar received orders directly from President Frangieh[7] himself not to yield to the bomb threat.

The Lebanese Army investigation is still in progress, but G-2 believes that the airport bomb was planted by BSO activists acting in defiance of Arafat’s desire to avoid confrontation with the GOL over the April 27 arrests — and that the phone call which led to the bomb’s discovery was possibly an effort by Arafat to assist Lebanese authorities in warding off action by BSO hotheads whose behavior he could not control.[8]

4.
In addition to the GOL’s firmness with the fedayeen over the airport affair, both Lebanese Army and UNTSO[9] sources report that the Lebanese Army has intensified its patrolling in the frontier area over the weekend of April 28–29, with patrols more frequent by night and day.

5. Comment
Although we are unable to say how far the tightening of GOL security precautions will go or how long it will continue — especially if it results in armed clashes between the army and reckless fedayeen elements — we regard it as a heartening initial sign of determination on the part of a new government that has yet to receive a parliamentary vote of confidence.[10]

HOUGHTON[11]

CONFIDENTIAL
PAGE 01 BEIRUT 04974 301820Z

ACTION NEA-12

FM AMEMBASSY BEIRUT
TO SECSTATE WASHDC 1899
   DIA WASHDC
INFO AMEMBASSY AMMAN
     AMCONSUL JERUSALEM
     AMEMBASSY TEL AVIV
     USCINCEUR

C O N F I D E N T I A L BEIRUT 4974

EO 11652: GDS
TAGS: PINS LE
SUBJECT: INTERNAL SECURITY DEVELOPMENTS IN LEBANON

SUMMARY: FOLLOWING SEVERAL WEEKEND INCIDENTS INVOLVING FEDAYEEN THAT PRODUCED CONSIDERABLE TENSION HERE, LEBANESE AUTHORITIES HAVE INSTITUTED HEAVY SECURITY PRECAUTIONS IN AND AROUND BEIRUT AIRPORT. LEBANESE ARMY'S PATROLLING ACTIVITIES ALONG ISRAELI BORDER HAVE ALSO BEEN INTENSIFIED. WE REGARD THESE DEVELOPMENTS AS ENCOURAGING INITIAL SIGNS ON PART OF NEW LEBANESE GOVT. END SUMMARY.

1. BEIRUT INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT UNDER STRICT SECURITY APR 30 AFTER WEEKEND OF TENSION THAT BEGAN AFTERNOON APR 27, WHEN AIRPORT AUTHORITIES -- IN PROCESS OF CONDUCTING THOROUGH SEARCH OF DEPARTING PASSENGERS -- ARRESTED 3 MEN (2 LEBANESE AND 1 PALESTINIAN) WHO WERE ABOUT TO BOARD AIR FRANCE FLIGHT TO PARIS WITH 10 KGS OF TNT AND DETONATING DEVICES IN THEIR BAGGAGE. UPON LEARNING THAT CULPRITS WERE FATAH MEMBERS, LEBANESE ARMY AND SECURITY FORCES -- FEARING ADVERSE FEDAYEEN REACTION WHEN ARRESTS BECAME KNOWN -- MOVED QUICKLY TO BLOCK MAIN ACCESS ROAD TO AIRPORT AND CORDON OFF SOUTHERN ENTRANCE TO SABRA QUARTER AND FEDAYEEN STRONGHOLD AT NEARBY SHATILA REFUGEE CAMP. NO REACTION OCCURRED THAT DAY, BUT ON APR 28 AIRPORT AUTHORITIES RECEIVED SERIES OF ANONYMOUS TELEPHONE CALLS THREATENING THAT BSO WOULD BLOW UP AIRPORT FACILITIES IF ARRESTED FEDAYEEN AND THEIR MUNITIONS WERE NOT RELEASED. ONE SUCH CALL, MADE LATE APR 28, ACTUALLY INDICATED BOMB HAD BEEN PLACED IN WATER-COOLER AT AIRPORT TERMINAL, AND HECTIC SEARCH OF BUILDING, SUPERVISED PERSONALLY BY MININT BASHIR AL AWAR AND SENIOR LEBANESE SECURITY OFFICIALS, LED TO DISCOVERY OF 2-KG PLASTIC CHARGE TIMED TO EXPLODE AT 0230 HOURS APR 29 IN A WATER COOLER.

2. AS OF NOON APR 30, ARMY AND SECURITY FORCES ARE MAINTAINING INTENSIFIED SECURITY PRECAUTIONS AROUND ENTIRE AIRPORT AREA, WITH ROADBLOCKS ESTABLISHED ON MAIN ACCESS ROUTES, CARS BEING THOROUGHLY SEARCHED, AND ONLY TRAVELLERS BEING ALLOWED TO ENTER TERMINAL PROPER. AIRLINE TRAFFIC CONTINUES AS SCHEDULED. GENERAL ATMOSPHERE OF TENSION, HOWEVER, WAS HEIGHTENED FURTHER NIGHT OF APR 28-29 BY EXPLOSION OF STICK OF DYNAMITE THROWN AT JORDANIAN AMBASSADOR'S RESIDENCE FROM PASSING CAR (NO CASUALTIES RESULTED AND DAMAGE WAS NEGLIGIBLE), AND STRICTER SECURITY MEASURES HAVE BEEN ESTABLISHED IN THAT NEIGHBORHOOD AS WELL.

3. MININT AWAR HAS STATED PUBLICLY THAT GOL HAD RESOLVED NOT TO GIVE IN TO BLACKMAIL IN CONNECTION WITH APR 27 AIRPORT INCIDENT. (WE UNDERSTAND FROM RELIABLE PRESIDENCY SOURCE THAT AWAR RECEIVED ORDERS DIRECTLY FROM PRES FRANGIE HIMSELF NOT TO GIVE IN TO BOMB THREAT.) LEBANESE ARMY INVESTIGATION OF ENTIRE AFFAIR STILL IN PROGRESS, BUT G-2 BELIEVES THAT AIRPORT BOMB WAS PLANTED BY BSO ACTIVISTS ACTING IN DEFIANCE OF ARAFAT'S DESIRE TO AVOID CONFRONTATION WITH GOL OVER APR 27 ARRESTS AND THAT PHONE CALL WHICH LED TO BOMB'S DISCOVERY WAS POSSIBLY EFFORT BY ARAFAT TO ASSIST LEBANESE AUTHORITIES WARD OFF ACTION BY BSO HOT HEADS WHOSE BEHAVIOR HE COULD NOT CONTROL (DETAILS BEING REPORTED VIA SEPARATE CHANNEL).

4. IN ADDITION TO GOL FIRMNESS WITH FEDAYEEN RE AIRPORT AFFAIR, WE HAVE BEEN TOLD BY BOTH LEBANESE ARMY AND UNTSO SOURCES THAT LEBANESE ARMY HAS INTENSIFIED ITS PATROLLING IN FRONTIER AREA OVER WEEKEND APR 28-29. PATROLS MORE FREQUENT BY NIGHT AND DAY.

5. COMMENT: ALTHOUGH WE UNABLE SAY HOW FAR TIGHTENING UP OF GOL SECURITY PRECAUTIONS DESCRIBED ABOVE WILL GO OR HOW LONG IT WILL CONTINUE -- ESPECIALLY IF IT RESULTS IN ARMED CLASHES BETWEEN ARMY AND RECKLESS FEDAYEEN ELEMENTS -- WE REGARD IT AS HEARTENING INITIAL SIGN OF DETERMINATION ON PART OF NEW GOVT THAT HAS YET TO RECEIVE PARLIAMENTARY VOTE OF CONFIDENCE.

HOUGHTON

CONFIDENTIAL NNN
footnotes: Fedayeen (Arabic: فدائيين, “those who sacrifice themselves”): Palestinian armed fighters. In the Lebanese context of 1973, “fedayeen” referred collectively to the armed members of PLO constituent organizations — Fatah, PFLP, DFLP, and others — operating from bases in Lebanese refugee camps under the protection of the 1969 Cairo Agreement.

10 kilograms of TNT with detonating devices constitutes a significant quantity of high explosive capable of catastrophic damage to an aircraft or airport facility. The three individuals — two Lebanese and one Palestinian — were about to board a civilian Air France flight to Paris. This event — a Fatah-linked bomb plot targeting civilian aviation departing from Lebanese soil — is documented in this cable, filed April 30, 1973. It does not appear in the standard historical account of pre-war Lebanon.

Fatah (حركة التحرير الوطني الفلسطيني, Palestinian National Liberation Movement): The largest constituent faction of the PLO, founded in 1959 by Yasser Arafat and others. Fatah was the dominant organization within the PLO and operated the largest armed presence in Lebanon under the Cairo Agreement. The fact that the arrested individuals were identified as Fatah members — not a smaller splinter group — made the incident politically sensitive for Arafat’s leadership of the PLO.

Shatila refugee camp: Palestinian refugee camp established in 1949 on the southwestern outskirts of Beirut. By 1973, Shatila and the adjacent Sabra area had become a significant armed base for Palestinian factions. The Lebanese Army’s immediate cordon of the camp upon the April 27 arrests — anticipating a violent response — documents the Lebanese state’s awareness of the armed capacity in the camps and its own vulnerability to retaliation. The same Shatila camp would be the site of the September 1982 massacre.

BSO: Black September Organization. A covert Fatah-linked terrorist unit established in the aftermath of the 1970–71 Jordanian Army’s expulsion of Palestinian armed groups (“Black September”). The BSO was responsible for the September 1972 Munich Olympics massacre in which 11 Israeli athletes and coaches were killed. By 1973, BSO was active in international terrorism while Arafat maintained official distance from its operations. The BSO’s threat to blow up Beirut International Airport — and its actual planting of a bomb in the airport terminal — is documented in this cable.

Bashir al-Awar: Lebanese Minister of Interior in the cabinet of Prime Minister Amin al-Hafez, formed in April 1973. His personal supervision of the search that discovered the airport bomb documents the seriousness with which the Lebanese government treated the threat. This is the same new government the cable refers to as not yet having received a parliamentary vote of confidence.

President Suleiman Frangieh (1910–1992): President of Lebanon 1970–1976. His direct order to the Interior Minister not to yield to the BSO bomb threat — received from a reliable Presidency source by the Embassy — is documented in this cable. This is the same Frangieh who would be hospitalized during the April 13, 1975 crisis (cable 1975BEIRUT04749) and who would personally handle contacts with Kataeb leader Gemayel during the ceasefire negotiations (cable 1975BEIRUT04860). The 1973 cable establishes his governing pattern: direct engagement and a firm stance toward Palestinian armed pressure — a stance that would become harder to maintain as the 1970s progressed.

This paragraph contains one of the most significant intelligence assessments in the pre-war cable record. The Lebanese Army G-2 believed: (a) the bomb was planted by BSO activists acting against Arafat’s wishes; and (b) the anonymous phone call that led to the bomb’s discovery was possibly Arafat himself covertly assisting Lebanese authorities against his own organization’s hardliners. If the G-2 assessment was accurate, it documents an internal PLO command structure problem in 1973 that is directly continuous with the internal disputes documented in the 1975 cables (cable 1975BEIRUT04860 records an unconfirmed report of a similar Arafat-vs-subordinates dispute during the April 1975 ceasefire negotiations). This assessment is in the diplomatic record as of April 30, 1973. It has not been cited in the standard historical account of PLO operations in Lebanon.

UNTSO: United Nations Truce Supervision Organization. The UN observer mission established in 1948 to monitor the Israel-Arab armistice agreements. UNTSO observers stationed along the Lebanese-Israeli border provided the U.S. Embassy with an independent source for reports on Lebanese Army patrol activity — distinct from Lebanese Army self-reporting.

The cable’s framing of this as the behavior of a “new government” — one that had not yet received a parliamentary vote of confidence — contextualizes the firmness as a deliberate political choice by a government trying to establish its credibility. The Hafez cabinet had been appointed in April 1973 amid a political crisis triggered by Israeli commando raids into Beirut. The government’s willingness to confront the BSO despite its fragile political position is documented here.

Dwight J. Houghton: U.S. Ambassador to Lebanon 1970–1974. Houghton’s posting preceded that of G. McMurtrie Godley (1974–1976), whose cables document the April 1975 crisis. Houghton’s 1973 reporting on PLO behavior and Lebanese government responses provides the pre-war context for understanding the structural conditions that produced the 1975 crisis. His characterization of Lebanese government firmness as “heartening” would prove, in retrospect, to have been reporting on a pattern that the Lebanese state was progressively losing the capacity to sustain.

readerNarrative.headline: The Pattern Before the War: Fatah Bombs, Blackmail, and a President Who Said No
readerNarrative.subheadline: This cable, filed April 30, 1973 — two years before the civil war — documents three facts the standard account of pre-war Lebanon does not carry: a Fatah bomb plot targeting an Air France flight from Beirut, a Black September Organization threat to blow up the airport terminal, and a Lebanese Army intelligence assessment that Arafat may have covertly tipped off Lebanese authorities about a bomb planted by his own organization’s hardliners.
readerNarrative.summary: Two years before the Lebanese Civil War, the U.S. Embassy filed this cable documenting a weekend of Fatah-linked violence at Beirut International Airport. Three men including Fatah members were arrested trying to board an Air France flight with 10 kilograms of TNT. The Black September Organization threatened to blow up the airport. A 2-kilogram bomb timed to explode at 2:30 AM was found and defused in a water cooler. The Lebanese Army G-2 concluded that the bomb was planted by BSO activists acting against Arafat’s wishes — and that Arafat may have covertly helped Lebanese authorities find it. President Frangieh personally ordered his Interior Minister not to yield to the blackmail. None of this appears in the standard account of pre-war Lebanon.
keyRevelations: In April 1973 — two full years before the civil war — three men including Fatah members were arrested at Beirut airport trying to board an Air France flight to Paris with 10 kg of TNT and detonating devices. This event is documented in this cable. It does not appear in the standard account of pre-war Lebanon.

The Black September Organization threatened to blow up Beirut International Airport. An actual 2-kg bomb timed to explode at 2:30 AM was found in an airport water cooler. This is documented in this cable. It does not appear in the standard account.

The Lebanese Army G-2 assessed that the bomb was planted against Arafat’s wishes by BSO hardliners he could not control — and that Arafat may have covertly tipped off Lebanese authorities about the bomb. This is in the diplomatic record as of April 30, 1973. It is not in the standard account.

President Frangieh gave a direct personal order to his Interior Minister not to yield to the BSO bomb threat. The same Frangieh would be hospitalized and partially sidelined during the April 1975 crisis two years later.

The cable documents that the Lebanese Army immediately cordoned off Shatila refugee camp upon the April 27 arrests — fearing armed reprisal from the camp. This documents the Lebanese state’s awareness of Shatila as an armed base, twelve years before the 1982 massacre.

readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
Two years before the war

On the afternoon of April 27, 1973, airport security at Beirut International Airport found something extraordinary in the baggage of three men about to board an Air France flight to Paris: 10 kilograms of TNT and the devices to detonate it. The men were Fatah members.

What happened over the following 48 hours is documented in this cable, filed by the U.S. Embassy on April 30, 1973. It does not appear in the standard historical account of pre-war Lebanon.

The bomb threat and the bomb that was found

When news of the arrests spread, the Lebanese Army immediately cordoned Shatila refugee camp — a documented acknowledgment that it expected armed retaliation from the camp’s armed organizations. The next day, the Black September Organization called the airport and threatened to blow up its facilities if the arrested men and their explosives were not released.

One call went further: a bomb had been placed in an airport water cooler. The Lebanese Minister of Interior personally supervised the search. They found it: a 2-kilogram plastic charge, timed to explode at 2:30 AM on April 29.

The G-2 assessment: what it means

The Lebanese Army’s military intelligence branch — G-2 — offered a conclusion that is among the most significant in the pre-war diplomatic record. The airport bomb, G-2 assessed, was planted by BSO hardliners acting against Arafat’s explicit wishes. Arafat had been trying to avoid a confrontation with the Lebanese government. And the anonymous phone call that led to the bomb’s discovery was, G-2 believed, possibly Arafat himself — covertly helping Lebanese authorities defuse an action by his own organization’s elements he could not control.

This conclusion — in the Lebanese Army’s intelligence assessment, transmitted through the U.S. Embassy, on record at the State Department as of April 30, 1973 — documents a specific dynamic: Arafat leading an organization with armed factions he could not fully command. Read alongside the 1975 cables, which document a strikingly similar internal PLO command dispute during the April ceasefire negotiations, the pattern spans two years and is consistent.

Frangieh said no

President Suleiman Frangieh gave a direct order to his Interior Minister: do not yield to the blackmail. The Embassy understood this from a reliable Presidency source. The new Lebanese government — which had not yet received a parliamentary vote of confidence — stood firm.

The Embassy called this a “heartening initial sign of determination.” Two years later, during the April 13 crisis, Frangieh would be in the hospital recovering from surgery, the Lebanese Army would have orders to stand aside, and the “determination” the Embassy saw in 1973 would be very difficult to find.

What this cable establishes

The standard historical account of the Lebanese Civil War begins, in most treatments, with April 13, 1975. This cable establishes that the structural conditions of that war — PLO armed factions operating autonomously from Lebanese soil, the Lebanese state attempting to enforce order and being met with armed blackmail, Arafat’s imperfect control over hardline elements within his own movement — were documented realities two full years earlier.

The war did not begin on April 13, 1975. The diplomatic record shows it had been building, documented in real time, since at least 1973.

cables.subject: Internal Security — SITREPs 6, 8, 9 (The Two-Day War, May 3–4, 1973)
cables.excerpt: Three consecutive Situation Reports document the 17-hour arc of the May 1973 Army–fedayeen confrontation — the "Two-Day War." Approximately 1,000 Yarmouk Brigade fedayeen crossed from Syria on May 3; Syria denied it; 14 hours later Syria quietly promised withdrawal. Sadat phoned Frangieh. The Lebanese PM’s contingent resignation was called "a bit of Lebanese flim-flam." Arab League’s Mahmoud Riad arrived. A ceasefire held. The Embassy’s judgment, filed at 1:15 AM: Arafat cannot sustain any ceasefire he signs.
cables.annotatedBody:
Archival Note — Merged Entry This entry presents three consecutive Situation Reports on the May 1973 crisis — known later as the Two-Day War between the Lebanese Army and the fedayeen — filed in the 17-hour window from 10:20 PM Beirut time on May 3, 1973 to approximately 5:55 PM Beirut time on May 4, 1973. SITREP 6 (05068), SITREP 8 (05089), and SITREP 9 (05123) have been merged because they are a contiguous narrative sequence from a single correspondent (Houghton, under the NIACT IMMEDIATE protocol for SITREP 8) documenting the transition from active combat to ceasefire stabilization. SITREP 7 is not in the WikiLeaks archive as of this writing. Each cable below is reproduced verbatim with its own banner. The final paragraph of SITREP 9 in the WikiLeaks archive is corrupted by intrusion of an unrelated cable; this has been marked as an archival transmission error and the extraneous text excluded. See footnote [21].

SITREP 6 — Cable 1973BEIRUT05068 — 10:20 PM Beirut, May 3

Originally classified CONFIDENTIAL · Filed under Night Action Immediate protocol · Now UNCLASSIFIED

1.
The Lebanese Army contact Kanaan[1] informed the Embassy at 2130Z that fighting in the Lower Bekaa–Arkub region between the Army and fedayeen has diminished considerably. No additional crossings from Syria are reported, although fedayeen who crossed earlier (about 1630Z) are still in place and believed to number perhaps up to 1,000.[2] (Note: press reporting places the figure at 4,000.) The threat of heavy fighting remains, especially since the Lebanese Army does not have much strength in that area. The GOL (Dib[3] of the Presidency) is less optimistic than before. A further danger is that, should Syria and the fedayeen leadership adopt a clearly hostile attitude, trouble could break out in the South and North, which have thus far remained calm. There are no indications this will occur, but at this time no one can predict. The situation in the Beirut camps is reported calm, although there has been some crowd movement reported in Moslem areas (with no violence).

2.
Both the Foreign Minister (Abou Hamad[4]) and Tony Frangieh[5] have been actively working on the Syrian government, but both report results discouraging. The Syrians even deny that any fedayeen have crossed into Lebanon.[6] Abou Hamad feels the Egyptian attitude, on the other hand, is still favorable. Sadat has spoken by phone to Frangieh and promised to weigh in with Hafez al-Assad of Syria.[7] Abou Hamad fears Syrian influence on Arafat’s position regarding any agreement with the GOL.

3.
The Prime Minister announced after midnight local time on May 4 that he had submitted his resignation but had not been able to submit it to Frangieh, who was already asleep (Comment: a bit of Lebanese flim-flam[8]). At the same time, there have been some encouraging developments, and if they continue it is possible he will reconsider his position later on May 4. We are told that the major favorable development was Sadat’s conversation with Frangieh. However, Tony Frangieh and FonMin Abou Hamad say that the odds favor Hafez’s resignation, with a military government being designated by Frangieh. Efforts are still alive at reaching a new agreement with the fedayeen, and should this take place Hafez could reconsider. Considerable political maneuvering is obviously going on and the situation is fuzzy. However, even should Arafat reach a new agreement with the GOL, his ability to sustain it is open to doubt.[9] He was unable to sustain the ceasefire stemming from the May 2 agreement, and casualties on May 3 were heavy, including Lebanese civilians killed by indiscriminate fedayeen shooting and rocket-firing which has angered Frangieh and the Army.[10]

4.
It is now 1:15 AM. We are retiring to take a fresh reading in the morning.

HOUGHTON[11]

SITREP 8 — Cable 1973BEIRUT05089 — 11:14 AM GMT, May 4

Originally classified CONFIDENTIAL · Filed under NIACT IMMEDIATE · Now UNCLASSIFIED

1.
Reports from the Foreign Office (Haddad[12]), the Army (Kanaan and G-2), and the Presidency (Dib) continue to be encouraging as of 1000Z May 4. Calm remains in the Beirut area with no reported incidents. However, there are reports of occasional fedayeen checkpoints near the refugee camps. We are assured that reports (by BBC among others) of heavy fighting in Arkub are without foundation, although there was a brief exchange of mortar fire at one spot early in the day. No contact thus far May 4 with the heavily armed elements who came from Syria (and may have returned there.)[13] The situation in South Lebanon is reported quiet except for a half-hearted attempt to organize a street rally in Sidon.[14] North Lebanon is also quiet. Observers are impressed and surprised by the effectiveness of the ceasefire to this hour. Morale of the Army is also reported very high.

2.
FonMin has informed us through Haddad that the SARG (reportedly PM Ayyubi[15] to PM Hafez) has promised to withdraw the remaining personnel of the Yarmouk Brigade[16] under cover of darkness May 4. It is hard to say what value to place on the promise, but it is a change from the May 3 position of denying any elements crossed the border. The attitude of the Egyptian is still considered positive. Mahmoud Riad arrives afternoon May 4.[17] A special emissary from King Hassan[18] is also arriving, along with an Iraqi envoy — the former considered to be helpful, the latter less so. In any event, the GOL (Dib, Tony Frangieh, and Abou Hamad) is encouraged by the present state of play with other Arab governments.

3.
Concerning the internal political situation, FonMin (via Haddad) and Dib say that the attitude of Prime Minister Hafez is much more positive than the evening of May 3, and that his resignation threat has been at least temporarily withdrawn. Very active political bargaining is expected for the rest of the day and probably for several days ahead. President Frangieh reportedly remains quite firm in his insistence that any new agreement reached with the fedayeen not accord them the sort of freedom they had under the old Cairo Accords.[19]

4.
UNRWA[20] officials report they have had no access to any refugee camps here since fighting began May 2, and that access is still restricted both by the Army and fedayeen. The agency has no precise estimate of the casualty rate among residents of the camps around Beirut, but considers it to be high. Camps elsewhere in Lebanon are described as quiet.

HOUGHTON

SITREP 9 — Cable 1973BEIRUT05123 — 2:55 PM GMT, May 4

Originally classified CONFIDENTIAL · Filed IMMEDIATE precedence · Now UNCLASSIFIED · Archival copy partially corrupted — see [21]

1.
Situation remains calm in Beirut and elsewhere in country at 1400Z. No incidents reported in Beirut or elsewhere since the last SITREP. The Presidency (Dib) tells us that most fedayeen who came in from Syria the night of May 3 have withdrawn together with their heavy armament, and the small number who remain will follow. The Army (G-2) tells us all is calm, nothing has budged throughout May 3. Mixed Army–fedayeen patrols are circulating[22] and fedayeen leaders have asked people to return arms to a central location. The Army is being very careful of possible recurrence of isolated incidents which could spread.

2.
Dib says that the political situation is also stabilizing, with no indication that Prime Minister Hafez intends to submit his resignation.[21]

Editorial note: the WikiLeaks archival copy of BEIRUT 05123 becomes corrupted at this point, with text from an unrelated cable on a World Health Organization housing-allowance matter interposed. That extraneous content has been excluded above. The recoverable portion of SITREP 9 ends with the political stabilization passage. See footnote [21].

[HOUGHTON — signature not recoverable from archival copy; attributed based on series consistency]

SUBJECT: INTERNAL SECURITY — SITREP 6

1. LEBANESE ARMY (KANAAN) INFORMED US AT 2130Z THAT FIGHTING IN LOWER
BEKAA-ARKUB REGION BETWEEN ARMY AND FEDAYEEN HAS DIMINISHED CONSIDERABLY.
NO ADDITIONAL CROSSINGS FROM SYRIA REPORTED ALTHOUGH FEDAYEEN WHO CROSSED
EARLIER (ABOUT 1630Z) STILL IN PLACE AND BELIEVED NUMBER PERHAPS UP TO
1,000. (NOTE: PRESS HAS FIGURE 4,000). THREAT OF HEAVY FIGHTING REMAINS,
ESPECIALLY SINCE LEBANESE ARMY DOES NOT HAVE MUCH STRENGTH IN THAT AREA
ALTHOUGH GOL (DIB OF PRESIDENCY) IS LESS OPTIMISTIC THAN BEFORE. FURTHER
DANGER IS THAT, SHOULD SYRIA AND FEDAYEEN LEADERSHIP ADOPT CLEARLY
HOSTILE ATTITUDE, TROUBLE WOULD BREAK OUT IN SOUTH AND NORTH WHICH HAVE
THUS FAR REMAINED CALM. THERE ARE NO RPT NO INDICATIONS THIS WILL OCCUR
BUT AT THIS TIME NO ONE CAN PREDICT. SITUATION IN BEIRUT CAMPS REPORTED
CALM ALTHOUGH THERE HAS BEEN SOME CROWD MOVEMENT REPORTED IN MOSLEM
AREAS (WITH NO VIOLENCE).

2. BOTH FOREIGN MINISTER AND TONY FRANGIE HAVE BEEN ACTIVELY WORKING ON
SYRIAN GOVERNMENT BUT BOTH REPORT RESULTS DISCOURAGING. SYRIANS EVEN DENY
THAT ANY FEDAYEEN HAVE CROSSED INTO LEBANON. ABOU HAMAD FEELS EGYPTIAN
ATTITUDE, ON OTHER HAND STILL FAVORABLE. SADAT HAS SPOKEN BY PHONE TO
FRANGIE AND PROMISED TO WEIGH IN WITH HAFEZ ASSAD OF SYRIA. ABOU HAMAD
FEARS SYRIAN INFLUENCE ON ARAFAT'S POSITION RE AGREEMENT WITH GOL.

3. PRIME MINISTER ANNOUNCED AFTER MIDNIGHT LOCAL TIME MAY 4 THAT HE HAD
SUBMITTED HIS RESIGNATION BUT THAT HE HAD NOT BEEN ABLE SUBMIT IT TO
FRANGIE WHO WAS ALREADY ASLEEP (COMMENT: BIT OF LEBANESE FLIM-FLAM).
AT SAME TIME, THERE HAVE BEEN SOME ENCOURAGING DEVELOPMENTS AND IF THEY
CONTINUED IT POSSIBLE HE WILL RECONSIDER POSITION LATER MAY 4. WE ARE
TOLD THAT MAJOR FAVORABLE DEVELOPMENT WAS SADAT CONVERSATION WITH FRANGIE.
HOWEVER, TONY FRANGIE AND FONMIN ABOU HAMAD SAY THAT ODDS FAVOR HAFEZ'S
RESIGNATION WITH MILITARY GOVT BEING DESIGNATED BY FRANGIE. EFFORTS STILL
ALIVE AT REACHING NEW AGREEMENT WITH FEDAYEEN AND SHOULD THIS TAKE PLACE
HAFEZ COULD RECONSIDER. CONSIDERABLE POLITICAL MANEUVERING OBVIOUSLY
GOING ON AND SITUATION FUZZY. HOWEVER, EVEN SHOULD ARAFAT REACH NEW
AGREEMENT WITH GOL, HIS ABILITY SUSTAIN IT OPEN TO DOUBT. HE UNABLE
SUSTAIN CEASEFIRE STEMMING FROM MAY 2 AGREEMENT AND CASUALTIES ON MAY 3
WERE HEAVY, INCLUDING LEBANESE CIVILIANS KILLED BY INDISCRIMINATE
FEDAYEEN SHOOTING AND ROCKET-FIRING WHICH HAS ANGERED FRANGIE AND ARMY.

4. IT IS NOW 1:15 AM. WE ARE RETIRING TO TAKE A FRESH READING IN MORNING.

HOUGHTON

2. FONMIN HAS INFORMED US THROUGH HADDAD THAT SARG (REPORTEDLY PM
AYYUBI TO PM HAFEZ) HAS PROMISED TO WITHDRAW REMAINING PERSONNEL OF

ANY ELEMENTS CROSSED BORDER. ATTITUDE OF EGYPTIAN STILL CONSIDER
POSITIVE. MAHMOUD RIAD ARRIVES AFTERNOON MAY 4. SPECIAL EMISSARY FROM
KING HASSAN ALSO ARRIVING, ALONG WITH IRAQI ENVOY. FORMER CONSIDERED
BE HELPFUL WHILE LATTER CONSIDERED BE LESS SO. IN ANY EVENT GOL (DIB,
TONY FRANGIE AND ABOU HAMAD) ENCOURAGED BY PRESENT STATE OF PLAY WITH
OTHER ARAB GOVTS.

DIB SAY THAT ATTITUDE OF PRIME MINISTER HAFEZ MUCH MORE POSITIVE

TEMPORARILY WITHDRAWN. VERY ACTIVE POLITICAL BARGAINING EXPECTED FOR
REST OF DAY AND PROBABLY FOR SEVERAL DAYS AHEAD. PRESIDENT FRANGIE
REPORTEDLY REMAINS QUITE FIRM IN HIS INSISTANCE THAT ANY NEW AGREEMENT
REACHED WITH FEDAYEEN NOT RPT NOT ACCORD THEM SORT OF FREEDOM THEY HAD
UNDER OLD CAIRO ACCORDS.

4. UNRWA OFFICIALS REPORT THEY HAVE HAD NO ACCESS TO ANY REFUGEE
CAMPS HERE SINCE FIGHTING BEGAN MAY 2, AND THAT ACCESS STILL
RESTRICTED BOTH BY ARMY AND FEDAYEEN. AGENCY HAS NO PRECISE ESTIMATE
OF CASUALTY RATE AMONG RESIDENTS OF CAMPS AROUND BEIRUT, BUT
CONSIDERS IT TO BE HIGH. CAMPS ELSEWHERE IN LEBANON DESCRIBED AS QUIET.

footnotes: Kanaan: the Lebanese Army contact who appears repeatedly across the Embassy's 1973 and 1975 reporting as the Embassy's most consistent military interlocutor. He reappears in cables 1973BEIRUT05155 and 1973BEIRUT05159 during the May 7–8 outbreak, and again in 1975BEIRUT03203 during the Sidon Crisis, where he gives the Embassy the specific 8:1 numerical disclosure (100–150 Army versus 1,000+ fedayeen in southern Lebanon). His institutional position and Arabic rendering of his name are not fully documented in declassified sources; he is identified in the cables simply as "Army (Kanaan)."

Lower Bekaa–Arkub region: the eastern and southeastern border strip of Lebanon adjoining Syria and Israel. The Arkub — known in Western press as "Fatahland" — was the primary fedayeen operational zone from which raids into northern Israel were launched. The fedayeen crossing from Syria into this zone on May 3 constitutes a Syrian-enabled reinforcement of Palestinian armed capacity inside Lebanon at the moment the Lebanese Army was attempting to restore sovereignty. The 1,000–4,000 figure range between Embassy and press reporting illustrates the fog of the moment.

Dib: the Presidency contact at Baabda Palace cited across multiple Embassy cables — 1973BEIRUT05155, 1973BEIRUT05159, and the Melkart Protocol series (1973BEIRUT05755/05776). His name appears as a routine channel for Presidency views. The cable record identifies him only as "(Dib of Presidency)"; his full name and title are not established in declassified sources.

Foreign Minister Abou Hamad (<ruby>أبو حمد<rt>Abu Hamad</rt></ruby>): Lebanese Foreign Minister in 1973 under President Frangieh. He is the direct conduit to Washington on negotiations with both the Syrian government and the PLO in early May 1973. His assessment that "Syrian influence on Arafat" is the controlling variable — rather than Arafat’s own agency — is a recurrent Embassy finding across the 1973 crisis.

Tony Frangieh: son of President Suleiman Frangieh, serving as an informal Presidential channel to the Embassy. The same Tony Frangieh appears in 1973BEIRUT05159 relaying the Army’s ceasefire to the Embassy on the morning of May 8. He was assassinated on June 13, 1978, by Lebanese Forces militiamen under Bashir Gemayel’s command — the Ehden massacre. His appearance here, five years earlier, is among the earliest documented instances of his role as a Presidency-Embassy intermediary.

Syrian denial that any fedayeen crossed into Lebanon: the May 3 Syrian position is flatly contradicted by events on the ground and by the subsequent (May 4) Syrian admission that the Yarmouk Brigade would be withdrawn under cover of darkness. The evolution from categorical denial to tacit admission within 24 hours is documented in this cable series and constitutes direct evidence of Syrian disinformation at the moment of the crisis.

Sadat’s phone call to Frangieh: Egyptian President Anwar Sadat telephoned the Lebanese President directly on May 3, promising to "weigh in with Hafez al-Assad" — i.e., to pressure Damascus. This is one of the earliest documented instances of Egypt intervening against Syria on Lebanon’s behalf, and it reflects the tension in the Sadat–Assad relationship that would widen later in 1973 (around the October War) and definitively break in 1977 (Sadat’s Jerusalem trip). The Embassy’s frontline documentation predates this rupture.

"A bit of Lebanese flim-flam": the Embassy’s verbatim editorial assessment of Prime Minister Amin al-Hafez’s declaration that he had submitted his resignation but not yet delivered it because President Frangieh was already asleep. The phrase captures a diplomat’s practical judgment — Hafez was reserving the option to withdraw the resignation if circumstances improved, which indeed occurred within hours after the Sadat call. The device of a contingent, unreceived resignation is not unique to Lebanese politics, but the Embassy’s willingness to characterize it explicitly is an instance of unusually candid on-record reporting.

Arafat’s inability to sustain ceasefires: the Embassy’s judgment — at 1:15 AM Beirut time on May 4, 1973 — that "even should Arafat reach a new agreement with the GOL, his ability to sustain it is open to doubt" proves prescient. The Melkart Protocol of May 17, 1973 (documented in cables 1973BEIRUT05755/05776) would indeed prove unsustainable; cross-border raids would resume within months; and the 1975 Sidon Crisis would document the same pattern of agreements made and broken. This paragraph is therefore a contemporary record of the structural problem that would drive the civil war.

Lebanese civilians killed by fedayeen shooting and rocket-firing: the cable documents, in unequivocal terms, fedayeen casualty-causing actions against Lebanese civilians on May 3, 1973 — distinct from combat casualties in engagement with the Army. The record of fedayeen fire harming Lebanese civilians in Lebanese territory, with the Embassy noting Frangieh and the Army are "angered," documents the mechanism by which the PLO’s armed presence alienated successive Lebanese constituencies and administrations across the pre-war decade.

HOUGHTON: Dwight J. Houghton, senior Embassy officer (Deputy Chief of Mission / Chargé d’Affaires) filing the SITREP series under the Night Action Immediate protocol. The same signatory appears on 1973BEIRUT04974 (April 30, 1973), the SITREPs of May 3–4 reproduced here, 1973BEIRUT05155 (May 7), 1973BEIRUT05159 (May 8), and the Melkart Protocol cables 1973BEIRUT05755 and 05776 (May 18). His consistent presence across the May 1973 crisis makes him the Embassy’s principal reporter on the period.

Haddad: a Lebanese Foreign Office official serving as the FonMin’s channel to the Embassy during the crisis. The identification is by surname only; not conclusively tied to any specific individual in declassified sources.

"No contact thus far May 4 with the heavily armed elements who came from Syria (and may have returned there)": this carefully hedged formulation documents the Embassy’s tentative acceptance of the Syrian government’s partial admission. Within 14 hours of the previous SITREP, where Syria flatly denied any cross-border infiltration, the Embassy is now tentatively documenting that the infiltrated forces may have withdrawn.

"Half-hearted attempt to organize a street rally in Sidon": noteworthy in historical context — Sidon appears here, in May 1973, as already a politically-mobilizable zone in support of the fedayeen. The same Sidon would become the epicenter of the February–March 1975 fedayeen-instigated crisis (cables 1975BEIRUT02611_02682 through 1975BEIRUT03203_03256) that immediately preceded the civil war. The 1973 rally is the same political ecosystem in early form.

Mahmoud al-Ayyubi: Syrian Prime Minister under Hafez al-Assad (1972–1976). The cable relays that he reportedly committed to Lebanese PM Amin al-Hafez — presumably by telephone or via Syrian diplomatic channels — to withdraw the Yarmouk Brigade personnel under cover of darkness on May 4. The undertaking at PM-to-PM level indicates the gravity of the crisis and the scale of the cross-border intervention being quietly undone.

Yarmouk Brigade (Arabic: <ruby>لواء اليرموك<rt>Liwa’ al-Yarmouk</rt></ruby>): a Syrian-controlled Palestinian military formation within the Palestine Liberation Army (PLA), named after the 636 CE Battle of Yarmouk. Its identification here as the Syrian-deployed cross-border unit provides direct attribution: the "heavily armed elements" who crossed from Syria were not fedayeen in general but a specific Syrian Army-controlled Palestinian formation acting as a Syrian proxy inside Lebanese territory.

Mahmoud Riad: Arab League Secretary-General (1972–1979), previously Egyptian Foreign Minister. His arrival on May 4 to mediate the Lebanese crisis is an early Arab League intervention in what would become a pattern over the next decade — Arab League mediation missions to Lebanon during recurring Lebanese-Palestinian confrontations. The mediation arc that began in May 1973 with Riad’s visit arguably continued through the Taif Accord of 1989.

King Hassan II of Morocco (1929–1999): the Moroccan monarch whose special emissary is noted as arriving alongside the Iraqi envoy. Morocco’s helpful posture is in the Embassy’s judgment consistent with its broader alignment with the moderate Arab consensus (Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Egypt) against the radical Arab states (Iraq, Libya, South Yemen) in this period.

Frangieh’s insistence that any new agreement not accord fedayeen "the sort of freedom they had under the old Cairo Accords" is the direct antecedent of the Melkart Protocol language two weeks later (cables 1973BEIRUT05755/05776, May 18), which similarly sought to avoid ratifying the 1969 Cairo Agreement framework. The consistency of Frangieh’s position from the night of the crisis through the formal settlement documents the Presidency’s strategic continuity.

UNRWA (United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East): established 1949. The Embassy records UNRWA’s inability to access any Beirut-area refugee camp since May 2 — access being restricted "both by the Army and fedayeen." The dual restriction is documented plainly and is one of the earliest cable references to the access problem that would recur over subsequent decades.

The WikiLeaks archival copy of BEIRUT 05123 is corrupted from approximately this point onward. Text from an unrelated cable — concerning a World Health Organization Director-General housing-allowance matter in Geneva — appears interposed. The extraneous content has been excluded from the reproduction above. The recoverable content of SITREP 9 ends with the political stabilization paragraph. This is a well-known type of archival transmission error in the declassified cable corpus, caused by concatenation of adjacent microfilm frames during digitization.

Mixed Army–fedayeen patrols: the emergence of joint patrols by May 4, 1400Z, reflects the de-escalation mechanism stipulated under the May 2 agreement — a framework that would be formalized two weeks later in the Melkart Protocol. The practical mechanism of a "mixed commission" to administer implementation, documented from the ground here in the SITREP, anticipated the architectural device of the Melkart Protocol (cables 1973BEIRUT05755/05776).

readerNarrative.headline: The Two-Day War: Hour by Hour, May 3–4, 1973
readerNarrative.subheadline: Three consecutive Situation Reports in a 17-hour window document Lebanon’s first major Army–fedayeen confrontation — the dress rehearsal for 1975. Syria denies its own cross-border intervention, then quietly undoes it. Sadat phones Frangieh. Mahmoud Riad flies in. A ceasefire holds. And the U.S. Embassy writes, that night, that even if Arafat signs a new agreement, his ability to sustain it is open to doubt.
readerNarrative.summary: From 10:20 PM on May 3 to approximately 5:55 PM on May 4, 1973, the U.S. Embassy filed three Situation Reports (SITREP 6, 8, and 9) documenting the hour-by-hour arc of what became known as the Two-Day War — Lebanon’s first large-scale Army–fedayeen engagement since the 1969 Cairo Agreement. Approximately 1,000 fedayeen had crossed into Lebanon from Syria the previous afternoon; the Syrian government denied any crossing had occurred; 24 hours later the same Syrian government quietly promised to withdraw its Yarmouk Brigade under cover of darkness. Prime Minister Amin al-Hafez submitted and then withheld his resignation in a maneuver the Embassy called "a bit of Lebanese flim-flam." President Sadat phoned Frangieh directly and promised to pressure Assad. Arab League Secretary-General Mahmoud Riad arrived to mediate. A ceasefire held. But the Embassy’s judgment that night — that even a new Arafat agreement would be unsustainable — was the structural diagnosis that would be vindicated by the Melkart Protocol’s failure, the 1975 Sidon Crisis, and ultimately the civil war itself.
keyRevelations: Syria deployed a named military formation across the Lebanese border and then flatly denied it. The Yarmouk Brigade — a Syrian-controlled Palestine Liberation Army unit — crossed into Lebanon on May 3. On May 3 Syria denied any crossing. On May 4 the Syrian Prime Minister reportedly promised his Lebanese counterpart to withdraw the unit under cover of darkness. The two positions are documented 14 hours apart.

Sadat phoned Frangieh and promised to pressure Assad. Egypt’s president intervened directly on Lebanon’s behalf against Syria — five months before the October War, four years before Sadat’s Jerusalem trip, and in an Egypt–Syria relationship that would rupture over the subsequent four years. The Embassy documented the call the night it happened.

The Embassy characterized the Prime Minister’s resignation maneuver, on the record, as "a bit of Lebanese flim-flam." Amin al-Hafez announced he had submitted his resignation but couldn’t deliver it because the President was asleep. Within hours, after Sadat’s phone call, the resignation was "temporarily withdrawn." The diplomat’s editorial comment is preserved verbatim.

Lebanese civilians were killed by indiscriminate fedayeen fire on May 3 — a distinction the cable draws explicitly from combat casualties. The Embassy notes that Frangieh and the Army are "angered." This is the exact mechanism by which PLO armed presence alienated successive Lebanese administrations over the pre-war decade.

The Embassy’s structural diagnosis, at 1:15 AM on May 4, was that Arafat couldn’t sustain a ceasefire even if he signed one. That diagnosis — written in the exhaustion of a night of fighting — was vindicated by the Melkart Protocol’s failure, the 1975 Sidon Crisis, and the civil war. The judgment is on the record as a contemporary reading, not a retrospective one.

Mixed Army–fedayeen patrols were already circulating by 1400Z on May 4 — anticipating the "mixed commission" architectural device of the Melkart Protocol two weeks later. The ground-level de-escalation mechanism preceded the formal settlement that tried to codify it.

Sidon appears in this cable series, already in 1973, as a politically mobilizable zone in support of the fedayeen. A "half-hearted street rally" was attempted there on May 4. Sidon would become the epicenter of the February–March 1975 crisis that immediately preceded the civil war. The 1973 rally is the same political ecosystem at an earlier stage.

timeline.label: Yarmouk Brigade crosses
timeline.desc: Approximately 1,000 fedayeen of the Syrian-controlled Yarmouk Brigade cross from Syria into the Lower Bekaa–Arkub zone of Lebanon. Lebanese press reports the figure at 4,000.

timeline.label: Sadat phones Frangieh
timeline.desc: Egyptian President Sadat telephones Lebanese President Frangieh directly, promising to weigh in with Hafez al-Assad of Syria.

timeline.label: Army briefs Embassy
timeline.desc: Lebanese Army (Kanaan) informs the Embassy that fighting in the Lower Bekaa–Arkub zone has diminished considerably. No further crossings reported.

timeline.label: PM Hafez’s contingent resignation
timeline.desc: Prime Minister Amin al-Hafez announces he has submitted his resignation but has not been able to deliver it to President Frangieh, who was already asleep. The Embassy terms this "a bit of Lebanese flim-flam."

timeline.label: SITREP 6 filed
timeline.desc: Embassy files SITREP 6 (cable 05068) summarizing the evening: fighting diminished, Sadat intervention, PM’s contingent resignation, Embassy judgment that Arafat cannot sustain any ceasefire he signs. Signed HOUGHTON.

timeline.label: Ceasefire holding
timeline.desc: Calm in Beirut area. No incidents. Observers "impressed and surprised by the effectiveness of the ceasefire." Army morale reported very high. BBC reports of heavy Arkub fighting judged "without foundation."

timeline.label: SARG promises Yarmouk withdrawal
timeline.desc: Syrian Prime Minister Ayyubi reportedly commits to Lebanese PM Hafez to withdraw remaining Yarmouk Brigade personnel under cover of darkness — a change from Syria’s previous position denying any crossing occurred.

timeline.label: SITREP 8 filed
timeline.desc: SITREP 8 (cable 05089) filed under NIACT IMMEDIATE. Documents Syria’s shift from denial to tacit admission, Mahmoud Riad en route, King Hassan emissary arriving, PM Hafez’s resignation temporarily withdrawn.

timeline.label: Mahmoud Riad arrives
timeline.desc: Arab League Secretary-General Mahmoud Riad arrives in Beirut to mediate. Special emissaries from Morocco and Iraq also arrive.

timeline.label: Sidon rally attempt
timeline.desc: A "half-hearted attempt to organize a street rally in Sidon" is reported — early evidence of Sidon as a politically mobilizable zone in support of the fedayeen.

timeline.label: Mixed patrols circulating
timeline.desc: Mixed Army–fedayeen patrols circulating. Fedayeen leaders asking people to return arms to a central location. The Presidency reports most of the Syrian-crossed fedayeen have withdrawn with their heavy weapons.

timeline.label: SITREP 9 filed
timeline.desc: SITREP 9 (cable 05123) confirms stabilization. Archival copy corrupts beyond the political-situation passage; remainder of the cable is not recoverable from the WikiLeaks archive.

keyFigures.name: Suleiman Frangieh
keyFigures.desc: Received Sadat’s personal phone call on the night of May 3 and subsequently pressed his non-recognition of the old Cairo Accord framework in any new agreement with the fedayeen — a position he would maintain through the Melkart Protocol two weeks later. The Embassy records him, in this cable series, as "angered" by the indiscriminate fedayeen fire that had killed Lebanese civilians on May 3.
keyFigures.imageCredit: Public domain. Official portrait of the President of Lebanon.

keyFigures.name: Hafez al-Assad
keyFigures.desc: The head of state whose government denied, on May 3, that any fedayeen had crossed into Lebanon — and whose Prime Minister, within 14 hours, reportedly promised the withdrawal of the specific Syrian-controlled PLA formation (Yarmouk Brigade) that had crossed. This cable series provides direct real-time documentation of Syrian disinformation at the moment of a cross-border military operation.

keyFigures.name: Anwar Sadat
keyFigures.desc: Telephoned Frangieh directly during the May 3 crisis, promising to intervene with Assad. The call is documented in SITREP 6 as the "major favorable development" that improved the Lebanese political situation overnight. The Egypt–Syria tension that surfaces here predates the October War by five months and the Sadat–Assad rupture by four years.
keyFigures.imageCredit: Public domain. Official portrait of the President of Egypt.

keyFigures.name: Yasser Arafat
keyFigures.role: Chairman of the PLO; head of Fatah
keyFigures.desc: The Embassy’s structural judgment — filed at 1:15 AM local time — is that "even should Arafat reach a new agreement with the GOL, his ability to sustain it is open to doubt." This diagnosis, written on the night of May 3–4, 1973, was vindicated by the collapse of the Melkart Protocol, the 1975 Sidon Crisis, and ultimately the civil war.
keyFigures.imageCredit: Dan Hadani Archive, National Library of Israel. CC license via Wikimedia Commons.

keyFigures.name: Mahmoud Riad
keyFigures.desc: Arrived in Beirut on the afternoon of May 4, 1973, to mediate the crisis — one of the earliest Arab League mediation missions in what would become a recurring pattern of Lebanese-Palestinian confrontations. Previously Egyptian Foreign Minister under Nasser. His arrival is noted in SITREP 8 as the first externally-sponsored mediation attempt of the crisis.

keyFigures.name: Amin al-Hafez
keyFigures.desc: The Sunni Prime Minister whose contingent resignation — submitted but not delivered because Frangieh was asleep — the Embassy called "a bit of Lebanese flim-flam." After Sadat’s phone call improved the political situation, the resignation was "temporarily withdrawn." Hafez would nonetheless be replaced in the post-crisis reshuffle.

keyFigures.name: Tony Frangieh
keyFigures.desc: The president’s son served as an informal Embassy channel through the crisis. He appears again in 1973BEIRUT05159 relaying the Army’s ceasefire on the morning of May 8. He was assassinated on June 13, 1978, by Lebanese Forces militiamen — the Ehden massacre.

keyFigures.name: Kanaan
keyFigures.desc: The Embassy’s most persistent Army interlocutor across 1973–1975. He briefs the Embassy on May 3 about the Lower Bekaa engagement and appears again in cable 1973BEIRUT05155 naming Syria as "playing the most unhelpful role" on the night of May 7. His appearances extend into the 1975 Sidon Crisis (cable 1975BEIRUT03203) where he provides the 8:1 numerical disclosure of Army versus fedayeen strength in southern Lebanon.

readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
What these three cables document, hour by hour

On the night of May 2–3, 1973, a ceasefire stemming from an earlier agreement broke down. On the afternoon of May 3, approximately one thousand fedayeen of the Syrian-controlled Yarmouk Brigade crossed the border from Syria into the Lower Bekaa–Arkub zone of Lebanon. Press reporting placed the number at four thousand. Fighting continued into the evening between Lebanese Army units and the fedayeen. On May 3 the Syrian government denied that any fedayeen had crossed the border at all.

Fourteen hours later, on the morning of May 4, the Syrian Prime Minister reportedly communicated to his Lebanese counterpart that the remaining Yarmouk Brigade personnel would be withdrawn that night under cover of darkness. The cables document this shift — from categorical denial to tacit admission — in the natural language of Embassy sources reporting as the crisis unfolded.

The diplomatic machinery that produced the ceasefire

Between the two Syrian positions, at approximately 1:15 AM Beirut time on May 4, the Embassy filed SITREP 6. The cable documents that Egyptian President Sadat had telephoned Lebanese President Frangieh directly and promised to pressure Assad. The Embassy records this as the “major favorable development” that had improved the Lebanese political situation that evening. Arab League Secretary-General Mahmoud Riad was en route. Moroccan and Iraqi emissaries were also inbound.

At home, Lebanese Prime Minister Amin al-Hafez had announced that he had submitted his resignation — but had not delivered it, because President Frangieh was asleep. The Embassy’s bracketed comment, preserved in the cable: “a bit of Lebanese flim-flam.” By morning, after the Sadat call had taken effect, the resignation was “temporarily withdrawn.” The contingent resignation — maintained as leverage — had served its political purpose.

The embassy’s structural diagnosis

SITREP 6 closes with what may be the most consequential sentence in the three-cable series: “Even should Arafat reach a new agreement with the GOL, his ability to sustain it is open to doubt.”

This is not a retrospective assessment. It is a contemporary judgment, filed in the exhaustion of the night, by diplomats who had spent the day in briefings with the Army, the Presidency, and the Foreign Ministry. Within two weeks, Arafat would reach exactly such an agreement — the Melkart Protocol of May 17, 1973, documented in cables 1973BEIRUT05755 and 05776. Within months, cross-border raids would resume. Within two years, the Sidon Crisis of February–March 1975 (cables 02611_02682 through 03203_03256) would document the same pattern. Within another few weeks, the April 1975 events in Ain el-Rummaneh would trigger the civil war.

The Embassy’s diagnosis of May 3–4, 1973 was vindicated four times over before the decade was out.

The half-hearted rally in Sidon

Among the smaller observations in SITREP 8, one stands out in historical hindsight: a “half-hearted attempt to organize a street rally in Sidon” in support of the fedayeen. Sidon — the southern coastal city whose local politics favored the Palestinian armed presence — is already visible in this 1973 cable as a politically mobilizable zone. Sidon would become, twenty-two months later, the epicenter of the February 26 – March 14, 1975 crisis that immediately preceded the civil war. The 1973 rally was the same political ecosystem at an earlier stage.

What SITREP 9 does — and doesn’t — record

SITREP 9, filed at 2:55 PM GMT on May 4, confirms that mixed Army–fedayeen patrols are circulating. It notes that fedayeen leaders have asked people to return arms to a central location. It documents that the Presidency sees no indication Prime Minister Hafez intends to submit his resignation. Beyond this point, the WikiLeaks archival copy of the cable is corrupted — text from an unrelated cable on a World Health Organization housing-allowance matter in Geneva appears interposed. That portion has been excluded from the reproduction above; the SITREP’s recoverable content ends with the political stabilization passage.

The dress rehearsal

These three cables document what historians now call the Two-Day War — a name the cables themselves never use. Read in sequence, they record the first full-scale collision between the Lebanese state and the Palestinian armed presence on Lebanese territory since the 1969 Cairo Agreement. The Embassy reported it as a crisis that stabilized within a day. It also reported, in the same breath, that the stabilization would not hold. Two weeks later, the Melkart Protocol would formalize a settlement. Two years later, Sidon. Four years later, the camps’ war. Fifteen years later, the Taif Accord.

All of it starts, in the documentary record, at 10:20 PM on May 3, 1973.

cables.subject: Lebanese Internal Security
cables.excerpt: The U.S. Embassy's first-flash report, dispatched at 9:31 PM as fighting erupted across Beirut: martial law declared, rockets fired at the airport, Military Governorate, and vicinity of the Presidency. Most serious fighting in Shatila camp. A Lebanese Army officer named Syria, on the record that night, as 'playing the most unhelpful role.'
cables.annotatedBody:
Originally classified CONFIDENTIAL · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State under EO Systematic Review · Now UNCLASSIFIED

1.
The government announced at 11:30 PM local time a state of emergency (martial law)[1] because “subversive elements tampering with the security of the country.” At approximately 10:00 PM local time, outbreaks of scattered fighting began on the outskirts of the city, with the most serious engagement in the Shatila camp area.[2] A large number of rockets have been fired in and around the city. We have reports that some have been fired at the airport, the Military Governorate of Beirut,[3] and in the general vicinity of the Presidency.[4] The situation seems to be calming down as of midnight, although our information — and that of the GOL — is extremely spotty.[5] We have no reports of any American casualties.

2.
Based on brief talks with the Presidency (Dib[6]) and the Army (Kanaan[7]), the GOL considers the situation “not dangerous but very serious.” They are especially concerned at deliberate, widespread efforts to prevent GOL–fedayeen[8] relations from stabilizing. Kanaan stated that the Syrian government appears to be playing the most unhelpful role in this regard, although he had no time to provide details.[9]

3.
We will report further when we are able to obtain a clearer picture of the situation.[10]

HOUGHTON[11]

TAGS: PINS, LE
SUBJ: LEBANESE INTERNAL SECURITY

1. GOVERNMENT ANNOUNCED 11:30 P.M. (LOCAL) STATE OF EMERGENCY (MARTIAL LAW)
BECAUSE "SUBVERSIVE ELEMENTS TAMPERING WITH SECURITY OF COUNTRY." ABOUT
10:00 P.M. (LOCAL) THERE WAS OUTBREAKS OF SCATTERED FIGHTING ON OUTSKIRTS
CITY WITH MOST SERIOUS ENGAGEMENT IN SHATILA CAMP AREA. LARGE NUMBER OF
ROCKETS HAVE BEEN FIRED IN AND AROUND CITY. WE HAVE REPORTS THAT SOME HAVE
BEEN FIRED AT AIRPORT, MILITARY GOVERNATE OF BEIRUT AND IN GENERAL VICINITY
OF PRESIDENCY. SITUATION SEEMS TO BE CALMING DOWN AS OF MIDNIGHT ALTHOUGH
OUR INFORMATION AND THAT OF GOL IS EXTREMELY SPOTTY. WE HAVE NO REPORTS OF
ANY AMERICAN CASUALTIES.

2. BASED ON BRIEF TALKS WITH PRESIDENCY (DIB) AND ARMY (KANAAN) GOL CONSIDERS
SITUATION NOT DANGEROUS BUT VERY SERIOUS. THEY ESPECIALLY CONCERNED AT
DELIBERATE WIDESPREAD EFFORTS PREVENT GOL-FEDAYEEN RELATIONS FROM STABILIZING.
KANAAN SAID THAT SYRIAN GOV'T APPEARS BE PLAYING MOST UNHELPFUL ROLE IN THIS
REGARD, ALTHOUGH HE HAD NO TIME TO PROVIDE DETAILS.

3. WE WILL REPORT FURTHER WHEN WE ABLE OBTAIN CLEARER PICTURE OF SITUATION.

HOUGHTON

CONFIDENTIAL NNN
footnotes: State of emergency (martial law): The Lebanese government's declaration of a state of emergency transferred effective authority from civilian police and courts to the military. Under this authority, the army could impose curfews, censor the press, and arrest individuals without normal judicial process — all of which are documented in the follow-up cable 1973BEIRUT05159, filed the following morning. The formal justification — "subversive elements tampering with security" — is a government formulation that does not attribute the fighting to a specific party, though the Embassy and Army sources had already identified specific Palestinian factions as the instigators.

Shatila camp: one of the largest Palestinian refugee camps in Beirut, located in the southern suburbs. As the site of the most serious fighting on the night of May 7, Shatila appears here as it would again, nine years later, as the site of the 1982 massacre carried out by Lebanese Forces militiamen while Israeli forces controlled the surrounding area. This cable documents Shatila as an active combat zone in May 1973 — the Lebanese Army engaging Palestinian forces in and around the same camp. This context does not appear in standard accounts of the camp's history.

Military Governorate of Beirut: the headquarters of the military authority governing greater Beirut, a significant institutional target. Rocket fire directed at the Military Governorate — alongside the airport and the vicinity of the Presidency — indicates that the May 7 attacks were not random but targeted the Lebanese state's key security and political nodes.

The Presidency (Baabda Palace) is located in the hills southeast of Beirut. Rocket fire in the general vicinity of the Presidency — the seat of Lebanese executive power — in addition to the airport and military governorate constitutes a direct attack on Lebanese state authority. The cable reports this without attribution at this hour; the follow-up cable (1973BEIRUT05159) identifies the instigating factions as PDFLP, PFLP/GC, and possibly Sa'iqa.

"Our information and that of GOL is extremely spotty": a notable admission of the Embassy's limitations in real-time. Filed at 9:31 PM GMT on May 7 — while the crisis was still unfolding — this cable is the Embassy's immediate dispatch under the NIACT IMMEDIATE protocol, sent before a full picture could be assembled. The subsequent cables (1973BEIRUT05159) were filed when the picture clarified.

Dib: likely a reference to a Lebanese Presidency official or aide who served as an Embassy contact. The name Dib (Arabic: ضيب) appears in the context of the Presidency rather than the army — distinguishing this source from the army contact Kanaan cited in the same sentence.

Kanaan: a Lebanese Army contact who appears in both this cable and the subsequent cable 1973BEIRUT05159. In this cable, Kanaan identifies Syria as "playing the most unhelpful role" in the crisis — one of the earliest explicit on-record attributions of Syrian responsibility that evening. In the follow-up cable filed the next morning, Kanaan confirms that Arafat is trying to calm his troops after the ceasefire.

Fedayeen (Arabic: فدائيين, "those who sacrifice themselves"): Palestinian armed fighters. In the Lebanese context, the term refers collectively to the armed members of PLO constituent organizations operating from bases in Lebanese refugee camps under the framework of the 1969 Cairo Agreement.

"Syrian government appears to be playing the most unhelpful role... although he had no time to provide details": the brevity here is itself a historical fact. Kanaan identified Syria at the moment of the crisis — presumably because the factions involved (PFLP/GC, Sa'iqa) were known to operate with Syrian backing — but the conversation was too brief for elaboration. The fuller picture of Syrian involvement is documented in the subsequent cable (1973BEIRUT05159), where the U.S. Embassy records Syrian Foreign Minister Khaddam's deliberate misrepresentation of negotiating terms and notes Lebanese government suspicion of "a Syrian hand working behind the scene."

The cable's final paragraph — "we will report further when we are able to obtain a clearer picture" — is characteristic of a first-flash emergency dispatch. The NIACT IMMEDIATE designation required immediate transmission regardless of the hour and regardless of informational completeness. The Embassy sent what it had. The fuller account followed at 8:08 AM the next morning in cable 1973BEIRUT05159.

HOUGHTON: the same signatory as cables 1973BEIRUT04974 (April 30, 1973) and 1973BEIRUT05159 (May 8, 1973). Likely the Deputy Chief of Mission or senior duty officer at the Embassy, filing under the Night Action protocol.

readerNarrative.headline: The Night It Started: Emergency Cable from Beirut, 9:31 PM
readerNarrative.subheadline: This cable, dispatched at the highest urgency level as fighting broke out across Beirut on the night of May 7, 1973, is the U.S. Embassy's first report on a crisis that would produce the Lebanese Army's first use of aircraft and tanks against Palestinian camps. It was filed while the shooting was still audible. The Lebanese Army's contact named Syria — on record, that night.
readerNarrative.summary: At 9:31 PM on May 7, 1973, the U.S. Embassy in Beirut dispatched a Night Action Immediate cable — the highest urgency designation available — as fighting erupted across the city. The Lebanese government declared martial law at 11:30 PM. Rockets were reported landing near the airport, the Military Governorate, and the presidential palace. The most serious fighting was in the Shatila camp area. The Embassy's contacts were brief: a Presidency aide and an Army officer named Kanaan. The GOL considered the situation 'not dangerous but very serious.' Kanaan told the Embassy that Syria was playing 'the most unhelpful role' — and had no time to say more. The full picture came in a cable filed eleven hours later.
keyRevelations: This cable was filed while the fighting was still underway — dispatched at 9:31 PM GMT as rockets were landing across Beirut. It is the Embassy's first-flash report, sent before a full picture was available.
Rockets were reported near the Presidency, the Military Governorate, and the airport simultaneously — indicating coordinated attacks on Lebanon's key state institutions, not random street fighting.
A Lebanese Army officer named Syria, on the record, that same night: 'the Syrian government appears to be playing the most unhelpful role' — before the Embassy had time to document the details.

The Lebanese government's official justification for martial law — 'subversive elements tampering with security' — attributed nothing to a specific party. The Army contact, speaking privately to the Embassy, was more direct.
The cable closes with: 'we will report further when we are able to obtain a clearer picture.' That fuller account is cable 1973BEIRUT05159, filed eleven hours later.

readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
9:31 PM, May 7, 1973

The cable was dispatched at the highest urgency level available to American diplomats: Night Action Immediate, requiring attention regardless of the hour. It ran to three paragraphs. The Embassy sent it while the shooting was still audible across the city.

What the Embassy knew at that hour

Fighting had broken out around 10:00 PM local time on the outskirts of Beirut, with the most serious engagement in the area of Shatila refugee camp. A large number of rockets had been fired across the city. Some, the Embassy reported, had been directed at the airport — one of Lebanon's most strategically and economically vital installations. Others had landed near the Military Governorate of Beirut, the headquarters of the army's authority over the capital. Still others had been reported in the general vicinity of the Presidency — the seat of Lebanon's head of state.

The simultaneous targeting of these three nodes — the airport, the military command, the Presidency — was not random. The cable does not say this explicitly, but the pattern it documents implies coordination.

The Army's verdict, that night

In brief contacts with a Presidency aide named Dib and an Army officer named Kanaan, the Embassy obtained one assessment that stands out. Kanaan told the Embassy that the Lebanese government considered the situation "not dangerous but very serious" — and that Lebanese officials were "especially concerned at deliberate, widespread efforts to prevent GOL-fedayeen relations from stabilizing."

Then: the Syrian government, Kanaan said, "appears to be playing the most unhelpful role in this regard." He had no time to elaborate.

This attribution — Syria identified as the most disruptive external actor, on record, at the moment the crisis was unfolding — appears in no standard account of the May 1973 events. It is documented in this cable, filed before midnight on May 7, 1973.

The limits of the moment

The cable is honest about what it does not know. The Embassy's information is "extremely spotty." The government's information, Houghton notes, is also extremely spotty. The cable closes with a direct acknowledgment: "We will report further when we are able to obtain a clearer picture of the situation."

That clearer picture arrived in two cables filed the following morning. Cable 1973BEIRUT05159, dispatched at 8:08 AM on May 8, reported that the Lebanese Army had by then expended aircraft and tank fire against Sabra/Chatila, Bir Hassan, and Borj el Brajne camps. The Prime Minister had resigned at 5:00 AM. A ceasefire came into effect at 8:00 AM. And the Army's G-2 named the specific Palestinian factions responsible for the night's fighting: PDFLP, PFLP/GC, and possibly Sa'iqa — precisely the Syrian-aligned factions Kanaan had pointed toward the night before without being able to say more.

cables.subject: Situation in Lebanon
cables.excerpt: The calm before the storm: as of 9:00 AM on May 7, 1973 — twelve hours before fighting erupted — this cable documents PM Hafez announcing he won't resign, Arab mediators (Khaddam, Egypt's al-Kholi, Arab League's Riad) still negotiating, and President Frangieh privately telling sources there will be 'no new accords or pieces of paper.' Sa'iqa had abducted Lebanese customs officials the previous day; Syrian authorities freed them.
cables.annotatedBody:
Originally classified CONFIDENTIAL · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State under EO Systematic Review · Now UNCLASSIFIED
Archival note: This is a State Department cable (from Washington) that relays and forwards to Cairo the text of Beirut cable 5152 — a separate cable sent earlier the same morning of May 7, 1973. The quoted content was drafted by Embassy Beirut (signed HOUGHTON); the outer cable was drafted in Washington by M. Sterner of the Near Eastern and South Asian Affairs bureau and approved by the same officer. The content below is that of the quoted Beirut cable.[1]

Summary
The situation in Lebanon is one of continuing overall calm with occasional incidents, as efforts by Lebanese politicians and Arab “mediators” to “resolve the crisis” continue. Prime Minister Hafez[2] has declared he will not resign, and we understand that President Frangieh[3] remains determined that any modus vivendi[4] concluded with the fedayeen[5] will enable the GOL to place tighter controls on their activity.

2.
As of 0900Z [9:00 AM GMT] on May 7, the situation on the ground remains quiet throughout the country. The only incidents reported on May 6 were:

  • Abduction by Sa’iqa elements[6] of around a dozen Lebanese customs officials from their northern border post at Aboudiyyeh. Syrian authorities freed them shortly afterwards.[7]
  • An early morning explosion and machine-gun attack at the Sidon courthouse (light damage).
  • An exchange of fire between an army patrol and fedayeen approximately 7 kilometers north of the Israeli border in the western sector (at least two fedayeen wounded, according to the army).
  • A brief outbreak of firing from Tal Zaatar camp[8] in the eastern suburbs of Beirut, which drew an army riposte.

All incidents appeared isolated, and no Lebanese casualties were reported. Near midnight on May 6, there was renewed firing in the southeastern Bekaa, but this was quickly brought under control, and Arafat was blaming it on the PFLP/GC and/or PDFLP.[9]

3.
On the political front, collective and individual efforts by Lebanese politicians and Arab “mediators” — including Syrian Foreign Minister Khaddam,[10] Egypt’s Hassan Sabri al-Kholi,[11] and Arab League Secretary General Mahmoud Riad[12] — continue, with numerous meetings on May 5–6 and continuing today.

Prime Minister Hafez made a noteworthy statement on television on the evening of May 5, announcing that he would stay on and expressing hope that problems with the fedayeen could be resolved through mutual cooperation and the help of Arab mediators. He stated his task was to reassure “Palestinian brothers” that President Frangieh, the army, and the Lebanese people support their cause, and to convince the Lebanese that the fedayeen have no intention of infringing on Lebanon’s sovereignty. We noted that in the aftermath of Hafez’s statement, both Rashid Karame[13] and Kamal Jumblatt[14] are no longer pressing him to resign.

4.
We have been told by very reliable sources close to President Frangieh that there will be no new accords or pieces of paper, merely some form of tacit understanding, and that the GOL will — RPT will — succeed in imposing tighter controls on the fedayeen. However, there is no way of predicting at present just what these controls will be in terms of either a new “understanding” or in actual practice.[15]

Both Arab “mediators” and Lebanese politicians appear to have a great deal of talking left in them. At the same time, Frangieh is reliably reported to be taking a firm and clear stand on the basic principle of Lebanese sovereignty, telling all concerned that the GOL has as much right to enforce its sovereignty over Palestinians as such other Arab governments as Syria and Egypt (whose envoys are most active).[16]

The Lebanese Army — upon which Frangieh relies more and more heavily and which will have a major voice in any eventual “understanding” — has not yet been engaged in talks with the fedayeen. Frangieh and the army apparently intend to keep their powder dry until passions have further subsided and politicians and special envoys begin to lose their voice.[17]

HOUGHTON [quoted] / ROGERS[18] [outer cable]

SUBJ: SITUATION IN LEBANON

1. BEGIN SUMMARY: SITUATION IN LEBANON IS ONE OF CONTINUING OVERALL CALM
WITH OCCASIONAL INCIDENTS AS EFFORTS BY LEBANESE POLITICIANS AND ARAB
"MEDIATORS" TO "RESOLVE CRISIS" CONTINUE. PRIMIN HAFEZ HAS DECLARED HE
WILL NOT RESIGN, AND WE UNDERSTAND PRES FRANGIE REMAINS DETERMINED THAT
ANY MODUS VIVENDI CONCLUDED WITH FEDAYEEN WILL ENABLE GOL PLACE TIGHTER
CONTROLS ON THEIR ACTIVITY. END SUMMARY.

2. AS OF 0900Z MAY 7, SITUATION ON GROUND REMAINS QUIET THROUGHOUT COUNTRY.
ONLY INCIDENTS REPORTED MAY 6 WERE ABDUCTION BY SA'IQA ELEMENTS OF AROUND A
DOZEN LEBANESE CUSTOMS OFFICIALS FROM THEIR NORTHERN BORDER POST AT ABOUDIYYEH
(SYRIAN AUTHORITIES FREED THEM SOON AFTERWARDS), EARLY MORNING EXPLOSION AND
MACHINE-GUN ATTACK AT SIDON COURTHOUSE (LIGHT DAMAGE), EXCHANGE OF FIRE
BETWEEN ARMY PATROL AND FEDAYEEN SOME 7 KMS NORTH OF ISRAELI BORDER IN
WESTERN SECTOR (AT LEAST TWO FEDAYEEN WOUNDED, ACCORDING TO ARMY), AND BRIEF
OUTBREAK OF FIRING FROM TAL ZAATAR CAMP IN EASTERN SUBURBS OF BEIRUT WHICH
DREW ARMY RIPOSTE. ALL INCIDENTS APPEARED ISOLATED, AND NO LEBANESE CASUALTIES
WERE REPORTED. NEAR MIDNIGHT MAY 6 THERE WAS RENEWED FIRING IN SOUTHEASTERN
BEKAA, BUT THIS WAS QUICKLY BROUGHT UNDER CONTROL AND ARAFAT BLAMING IT ON
PFLP/GC AND/OR PDFLP.

3. ON POLITICAL FRONT, COLLECTIVE AND INDIVIDUAL EFFORTS OF LEBANESE
POLITICIANS AND ARAB "MEDIATORS" (INCLUDING SARG FONMIN KHADDAM, EGYPT'S
HASSAN SABRI AL KHOLI AND ARAB LEAGUE'S MAHMOUD RIAD) TO "RESOLVE CRISIS"
CONTINUE, WITH NUMEROUS MEETINGS MAY 5-6 AND CONTINUING TODAY. PRIMIN HAFEZ
MADE NOTEWORTHY STATEMENT ON TV EVENING MAY 5 IN WHICH HE ANNOUNCED THAT HE
WOULD STAY ON AND EXPRESSED HOPE THAT PROBLEMS WITH FEDAYEEN COULD BE RESOLVED
THROUGH MUTUAL COOPERATION AND HELP OF ARAB MEDIATORS. SAID HIS TASK WAS TO
REASSURE "PALESTINE BROTHERS" THAT PRES FRANGIE, ARMY AND LEBANESE PEOPLE
SUPPORT THEIR CAUSE AND TO CONVINCE LEBANESE THAT FEDAYEEN HAVE NO INTENTION
OF INFRINGING ON LEBANON'S SOVEREIGNTY. HOPED THAT ALL PARTIES CONCERNED
WOULD ASSIST IN THIS PROCESS. WE NOTED THAT IN AFTERMATH HAFEZ' STATEMENT,
BOTH RASHID KARAME AND KAMAL JUMBLATT ARE NO LONGER PRESSING HIM TO RESIGN.

4. WE HAVE BEEN TOLD BY VERY RELIABLE SOURCES CLOSE TO PRES FRANGIE THAT
THERE WILL BE NO NEW ACCORDS OR PIECES OF PAPER, MERELY SOME FORM OF TACIT
UNDERSTANDING, AND THAT GOL WILL RPT WILL SUCCEED IN IMPOSING TIGHTER
CONTROLS ON FEDAYEEN. HOWEVER, THERE IS NO WAY OF PREDICTING AT PRESENT
JUST WHAT THESE CONTROLS WILL BE IN TERMS OF EITHER NEW "UNDERSTANDING" OR
IN ACTUAL PRACTICE. BOTH ARAB "MEDIATORS" AND LEBANESE POLITICIANS APPEAR
TO HAVE GREAT DEAL OF TALKING LEFT IN THEM. AT SAME TIME, FRANGIE RELIABLY
REPORTED TAKING FIRM AND CLEAR STAND ON BASIC PRINCIPLE OF LEBANESE
SOVEREIGNTY, TELLING ALL CONCERNED THAT GOL HAS AS MUCH RIGHT TO ENFORCE ITS
SOVEREIGNTY OVER PALESTINIANS AS SUCH OTHER ARAB GOVTS AS SYRIA AND EGYPT
(WHICH ENVOYS ARE MOST ACTIVE). LEBANESE ARMY, UPON WHICH FRANGIE RELIES MORE
AND MORE HEAVILY AND WHICH WILL HAVE MAJOR VOICE IN ANY EVENTUAL
"UNDERSTANDING", HAS NOT YET BEEN ENGAGED IN TALKS WITH FEDAYEEN. FRANGIE AND
ARMY APPARENTLY INTEND KEEP THEIR POWDER DRY UNTIL PASSIONS HAVE FURTHER
SUBSIDED AND POLITICIANS AND SPECIAL ENVOYS BEGIN TO LOSE THEIR VOICE.

HOUGHTON UNQUOTE ROGERS

CONFIDENTIAL
