Originally classified CONFIDENTIAL · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State · Now UNCLASSIFIED

Archival Note — Merged Entry

This is a merged archival entry combining two companion cables filed on consecutive days, March 3 and March 4, 1975, documenting the second round of the Sidon crisis. Cable 1975BEIRUT02837 (031720Z) reports the March 1–2 street fighting: the Army attempted to reopen the coastal road, was ambushed by 1,000+ fedayeen with RPGs and recoilless rifles, and was forced to withdraw again after 48 hours of urban combat. Cable 1975BEIRUT02894 (041604Z) is the next-day report: an Army truck has been ambushed from the medieval citadel itself, nine soldiers are dead, and an all-out Army clean-up operation in Sidon has been seriously discussed and then scotched. Together the two cables document the moment when the Lebanese state tried to reassert control over Sidon and failed.

Cable 1 of 2 — 1975BEIRUT02837 — 031720Z Mar 75

Subject: Renewal of Clashes in Sidon · CONFIDENTIAL · Ref: BEIRUT 2682

SUMMARY: Renewed clashes between Lebanese Army and “armed elements” in Sidon over the weekend have culminated in another truce.

1.
The uneasy truce reported reftel between the Lebanese Army and “armed elements” in Sidon was shattered at approximately 1700 local on March 1, when Army units reentered the town[1] to reopen the arterial north-south coastal road which had been closed by insurgents in the aftermath of the February 26 clashes. According to Army G-2, the Army forced the barricades when the 1700 local deadline for their dismantling passed without compliance. One detachment was ambushed and suffered casualties as it approached Sidon, and although the road was subsequently reopened, troops became involved in continuous fighting with insurgents (encroaching from the old city located between the road and the seacoast) until 1600 local on March 2 when a second truce was arranged.

2.
We understand from G-2 that the decision to impose and enforce the March 1 deadline was taken by Pres Frangie in consultation with Primin Solh and the Army high command.[2] Between the original February 27 truce and the March 1 action, the Army garrison in Sidon had become penned up in its barracks and routine resupply — not only of the Sidon garrison but of all Army units in South Lebanon — was impossible because the coast road was blocked by insurgents and the mountain routes to the Bekaa valley in eastern Lebanon were blocked by snow. Frangie’s decision to force the coastal road open was thus apparently made with full knowledge of Primin Solh, one of whose cabinet ministers (MinEcon Abbas Khalaf) was engaged in “negotiations” with insurgents throughout March 1 until the Army deadline expired and fighting resumed.[3]

3.
The result of the March 1–2 street fighting between the Army (equipped with tanks, armored cars and APCs) and an unknown number of insurgents (whose arsenal includes RPG and Katyusha rockets, recoilless rifles and 23mm Soviet heavy machine-guns) positioned on rooftops, windows and in alleyways of Sidon’s medieval quarter was 5 dead and 10 wounded on the Army side, plus several armored vehicles put out of commission by rocket fire. Insurgent and “civilian” casualties are more difficult to define, but the most reliable estimates place them at 10–15 dead and at least 40 wounded. Army G-2 identifies the insurgents as a combination of leftist Sidonian civilians and fedayeen (primarily PFLP).[4]

4.
At last report, Army units had again withdrawn from Sidon under terms of the truce arranged March 2, but their positions have been taken by Lebanese gendarmes. The coastal road was open on March 3, but traffic on it and elsewhere in Sidon was being directed by persons wearing civilian clothes.[5]

5.
The above developments have served to heighten anti-GOL agitation and a sense of outrage among Lebanese leftist and Sunni Muslim groups. (Sidonian population is predominantly Sunnite, and its leftist groups are thick as fleas with fedayeen, especially the latter’s most radical elements.) Even before fighting resumed March 1, Primin Solh had thrown Henri Lahoud, Governor of South Lebanon, to the wolves by announcing that he had been placed on 20 days “administrative leave”. As a result of the latest clashes, leftist and Sunni pressures on the Solh cabinet to resign have materialized, and one Sunni minister (Malik Salam, Min of Water and Electricity) has submitted his resignation[6] in protest against the GOL’s failure to dismiss Gen Ghanem for the Army’s “unilateral action” in reentering Sidon on March 1. (General Sunni complaint — which is false but which Primin Solh has done nothing to deny — is that the Army moved on its own initiative and without consulting the GOL.)[7] MinEconomy Abbas Khalaf reportedly also wants to resign, but his party boss Kamal Jumblatt has thus far been cooperating with Pres Frangie in trying to restore order and is preventing Khalaf from quitting.

6.
“Negotiations” between Sidon insurgents on one hand and a combined team of GOL ministers and PLO notables (Abu Za’im and Zuhayr Muhsen) on the other resumed on the evening of March 2, and the hope is that this will at least allow time for tempers to cool and enable the GOL-PLO team to persuade “armed elements” to vacate the rooftops and other strategic points which they continue to occupy in Sidon. In the meantime, the town remains controlled by insurgents; telephone communications with it are still cut; leftist, Sunni and other “oppositionist” agitation against the GOL continues; and Primin Solh remains insistent that no rpt no fedayeen have been involved in the entire affair.[8]

7. Comment
(A) Solh’s position is admittedly difficult, caught as he is between (a) his official responsibilities to enforce law and order and (b) his desire not to lose credibility with Lebanon’s Sunni community and leftist forces and to preserve the fiction of fedayeen non-involvement. The whole business points up once again how difficult it is for any Lebanese Sunni political leader to act with purpose and determination in dealing with troublesome situations resulting from the strong attachment on the part of his co-religionists to sectarian and non-Lebanese (i.e., extremist fedayeen) causes.[9] The next few days will tell whether the Solh government can survive the furor and tensions created by the Sidon clashes, and also whether the situation which produced those clashes can be resolved without further fighting.

(B) In the meantime, the fishermen whose complaint was the ostensible cause of this entire episode have been largely forgotten, except for purposes of continuing leftist agitation. (A mysterious bomb-blast which destroyed the Beirut office of Camille Chamoun’s fishing company on the night of February 28 has been attributed to fishermen, but there is little doubt that it was perpetrated by radical leftists.)[10] All this tends to reinforce our initial suspicion (para 3 Beirut 2611) that the Sidon clashes resulted from a deliberate attempt by fedayeen “rejectionist” elements and their local leftist allies to cause commotion on the eve of Secretary Kissinger’s return to the Middle East and to embroil fedayeen leadership with the Lebanese Army and GOL.[11] The fact that the latter objective has not been attained is probably the only plus to emerge out of this whole sad affair.

HOUGHTON

Cable 2 of 2 — 1975BEIRUT02894 — 041604Z Mar 75

Subject: More Clashes in Sidon · CONFIDENTIAL · Ref: BEIRUT 2837

1.
The Department will doubtless have noted from FBIS reports that another incident occurred in Sidon at 1815 local on March 3, when an Army truck transporting Lebanese soldiers to their units in South Lebanon was ambushed on the main coastal road by “armed elements” firing rockets and machine guns from positions in the town’s citadel.[12] Official casualty toll was one soldier killed and 29 rpt 29 wounded, which brings total Army-police casualties in Sidon to 9 dead and 43 wounded since fighting began on February 26.

2.
The above incident apparently provoked renewed exchanges of fire between Lebanese troops and Sidon insurgents during the evening hours of March 3. We understand that it also caused Army leadership to consider launching an all-out clean-up operation in Sidon on March 4, but this idea apparently was scotched and a cease-fire restored when PLO’s Abu Za’im succeeded in arresting the alleged instigator of the incident (identified as a Lebanese leftist thug) and turned him over to GOL authorities.[13] His accomplices are still being sought, but there seems to be no info regarding their whereabouts, nor has there been any explanation of how Abu Za’im managed to lay his hands on the alleged instigator so handily.[14]

3.
As of mid-day March 4, Sidon reportedly was again quiet but still under insurgent control, and “negotiations” were evidently still in progress between the GOL-PLO team and leftist Sidonian elements. Pressures reported reftel on the Solh cabinet to resign are still in evidence, but we expect no decisive developments on this front until after the cabinet meeting with Pres Frangie, reportedly scheduled for March 5.

4.
March 3 witnessed a mass funeral in Sidon of 8 persons killed in clashes reported over the past several days. Although the atmosphere was charged with tension, the funerals proceeded without incident.[15]

HOUGHTON

E.O. 11652: GDS
TAGS: PINS LE
SUBJECT: RENEWAL OF CLASHES IN SIDON
REF: BEIRUT 2682

SUMMARY: RENEWED CLASHES BETWEEN LEBANESE ARMY AND "ARMED ELEMENTS" IN
SIDON OVER WEEKEND HAVE CULMINATED IN ANOTHER TRUCE.

1. UNEASY TRUCE REPORTED REFTEL BETWEEN LEB ARMY AND "ARMED ELEMENTS" IN
SIDON WAS SHATTERED APPROX 1700 LOCAL MAR 1, WHEN ARMY UNITS REENTERED
TOWN TO REOPEN ARTERIAL NORTH-SOUTH COASTAL ROAD WHICH HAD BEEN CLOSED BY
INSURGENTS IN AFTERMATH OF FEB 26 CLASHES (BEIRUT 2611). ACCORDING ARMY
G-2, ARMY FORCED BARRICADES WHEN 1700 LOCAL DEADLINE FOR THEIR DISMANTLING
PASSED WITHOUT COMPLIANCE. ONE DETACHMENT WAS AMBUSHED AND SUFFERED
CASUALTIES AS IT APPROACHED SIDON, AND ALTHOUGH ROAD WAS SUBSEQUENTLY
REOPENED, TROOPS BECAME INVOLVED IN CONTINUOUS FIGHTING WITH INSURGENTS
(ENCROACHING FROM OLD CITY LOCATED BETWEEN ROAD AND SEACOAST) UNTIL 1600
LOCAL MAR 2 WHEN SECOND TRUCE WAS ARRANGED.

2. WE UNDERSTAND FROM G-2 THAT DECISION TO IMPOSE AND ENFORCE MAR 1
DEADLINE WAS TAKEN BY PRES FRANGIE IN CONSULTATION WITH PRIMIN SOLH AND
ARMY HIGH COMMAND. BETWEEN ORIGINAL FEB 27 TRUCE AND MAR 1 ACTION, ARMY
GARRISON IN SIDON HAD BECOME PENNED UP IN ITS BARRACKS AND ROUTINE
RESUPPLY -- NOT ONLY OF SIDON GARRISON BUT OF ALL ARMY UNITS IN SOUTH
LEBANON -- WAS IMPOSSIBLE BECAUSE COAST ROAD WAS BLOCKED BY INSURGENTS
AND MOUNTAIN ROUTES TO BEKAA VALLEY IN EASTERN LEBANON WERE BLOCKED BY
SNOW. FRANGIE'S DECISION TO FORCE COASTAL ROAD OPEN WAS THUS APPARENTLY
MADE WITH FULL KNOWLEDGE OF PRIMIN SOLH, ONE OF WHOSE CABINET MINISTERS
(MINECON ABBAS KHALAF) WAS ENGAGED IN "NEGOTIATIONS" WITH INSURGENTS
THROUGHOUT MAR 1 UNTIL ARMY DEADLINE EXPIRED AND FIGHTING RESUMED.

3. RESULT OF MAR 1-2 STREET FIGHTING BETWEEN ARMY (EQUIPPED WITH TANKS,
ARMORED CARS AND APCS) AND UNKNOWN NUMBER OF INSURGENTS (WHOSE ARSENAL
INCLUDES RPG AND KATYUSHA ROCKETS, RECOILLESS RIFLES AND 23MM SOVIET
HEAVY MACHINE-GUNS) POSITIONED ON ROOFTOPS, WINDOWS AND IN ALLEYWAYS OF
SIDON'S MEDIEVAL QUARTER WAS 5 DEAD AND 10 WOUNDED ON ARMY SIDE, PLUS
SEVERAL ARMORED VEHICLES PUT OUT OF COMMISSION BY ROCKET FIRE. INSURGENT
AND "CIVILIAN" CASUALTIES MORE DIFFICULT TO DEFINE, BUT MOST RELIABLE
ESTIMATES PLACE THEM AT 10-15 DEAD AND AT LEAST 40 WOUNDED. ARMY G-2
IDENTIFIES INSURGENTS AS COMBINATION OF LEFTIST SIDONIAN CIVILIANS AND
FEDAYEEN (PRIMARILY PFLP).

4. AT LAST REPORT, ARMY UNITS HAD AGAIN WITHDRAWN FROM SIDON UNDER TERMS
OF TRUCE ARRANGED MAR 2, BUT THEIR POSITIONS HAVE BEEN TAKEN BY LEBANESE
GENDARMES. COASTAL ROAD WAS OPEN ON MAR 3, BUT TRAFFIC ON IT AND
ELSEWHERE IN SIDON WAS BEING DIRECTED BY PERSONS WEARING CIVILIAN CLOTHES.

5. ABOVE DEVELOPMENTS HAVE SERVED TO HEIGHTEN ANTI-GOL AGITATION AND
SENSE OF OUTRAGE AMONG LEBANESE LEFTIST AND SUNNI MOSLEM GROUPS.
(SIDONIAN POPULATION IS PREDOMINANTLY SUNNITE, AND ITS LEFTIST GROUPS ARE
THICK AS FLEAS WITH FEDAYEEN, ESPECIALLY LATTER'S MOST RADICAL ELEMENTS.)
EVEN BEFORE FIGHTING RESUMED MAR 1, PRIMIN SOLH HAD THROWN HENRI LAHOUD,
GOVERNOR OF SOUTH LEBANON, TO WOLVES BY ANNOUNCING THAT HE HAD BEEN
PLACED ON 20 DAYS "ADMINISTRATIVE LEAVE". AS RESULT OF LATEST CLASHES,
LEFTIST AND SUNNI PRESSURES ON SOLH CABINET TO RESIGN HAVE MATERIALIZED,
AND ONE SUNNI MINISTER (MALIK SALAM, MIN OF WATER AND ELECTRICITY) HAS
SUBMITTED HIS RESIGNATION IN PROTEST AGAINST GOL'S FAILURE TO DISMISS GEN
GHANEM FOR ARMY'S "UNILATERAL ACTION" IN REENTERING SIDON ON MAR 1.
(GENERAL SUNNI COMPLAINT -- WHICH IS FALSE BUT WHICH PRIMIN SOLH HAS DONE
NOTHING TO DENY -- IS THAT ARMY MOVED ON ITS OWN INITIATIVE AND WITHOUT
CONSULTING GOL.) MINECONOMY ABBAS KHALAF REPORTEDLY ALSO WANTS TO RESIGN,
BUT HIS PARTY BOSS KAMAL JUMBLATT HAS THUS FAR BEEN COOPERATING WITH PRES
FRANGIE IN TRYING TO RESTORE ORDER AND IS PREVENTING KHALAF FROM QUITTING.

6. "NEGOTIATIONS" BETWEEN SIDON INSURGENTS ON ONE HAND AND COMBINED TEAM
OF GOL MINISTERS AND PLO NOTABLES (ABU ZA'IM AND ZUHAYR MUHSEN) ON THE
OTHER RESUMED ON EVENING OF MAR 2, AND HOPE IS THAT THIS WILL AT LEAST
ALLOW TIME FOR TEMPERS TO COOL AND ENABLE GOL-PLO TEAM TO PERSUADE "ARMED
ELEMENTS" TO VACATE ROOFTOPS AND OTHER STRATEGIC POINTS WHICH THEY
CONTINUE TO OCCUPY IN SIDON. IN MEANTIME, TOWN REMAINS CONTROLLED BY
INSURGENTS; TELEPHONE COMMUNICATIONS WITH IT ARE STILL CUT; LEFTIST,
SUNNI AND OTHER "OPPOSITIONIST" AGITATION AGAINST GOL CONTINUES; AND
PRIMIN SOLH REMAINS INSISTENT THAT NO RPT NO FEDAYEEN HAVE BEEN INVOLVED
IN THE ENTIRE AFFAIR.

7. COMMENT: (A) SOLH'S POSITION IS ADMITTEDLY DIFFICULT, CAUGHT AS HE IS
BETWEEN (A) HIS OFFICIAL RESPONSIBILITIES TO ENFORCE LAW AND ORDER AND
(B) HIS DESIRE NOT TO LOSE CREDIBILITY WITH LEBANON'S SUNNI COMMUNITY AND
LEFTIST FORCES AND TO PRESERVE FICTION OF FEDAYEEN NON-INVOLVEMENT. WHOLE
BUSINESS POINTS UP ONCE AGAIN HOW DIFFICULT IT IS FOR ANY LEBANESE SUNNI
POLITICAL LEADER TO ACT WITH PURPOSE AND DETERMINATION IN DEALING WITH
TROUBLESOME SITUATIONS RESULTING FROM STRONG ATTACHMENT ON PART OF HIS
CO-RELIGIONISTS TO SECTARIAN AND NON-LEBANESE (I.E., EXTREMIST FEDAYEEN)
CAUSES. NEXT FEW DAYS WILL TELL WHETHER SOLH GOVT CAN SURVIVE FUROR AND
TENSIONS CREATED BY SIDON CLASHES, AND ALSO WHETHER SITUATION WHICH
PRODUCED THOSE CLASHES CAN BE RESOLVED WITHOUT FURTHER FIGHTING.
(B) IN MEANTIME, FISHERMEN WHOSE COMPLAINT WAS OSTENSIBLE CAUSE OF THIS
ENTIRE EPISODE HAVE BEEN LARGELY FORGOTTEN, EXCEPT FOR PURPOSES OF
CONTINUING LEFTIST AGITATION. (MYSTERIOUS BOMB-BLAST WHICH DESTROYED
BEIRUT OFFICE OF CAMILLE CHAMOUN'S FISHING COMPANY NIGHT OF FEB 28 HAS
BEEN ATTRIBUTED TO FISHERMEN, BUT THERE IS LITTLE DOUBT THAT IT WAS
PERPETRATED BY RADICAL LEFTISTS.) ALL THIS TENDS TO REINFORCE OUR INITIAL
SUSPICION (PARA 3 BEIRUT 2611) THAT SIDON CLASHES RESULTED FROM
DELIBERATE ATTEMPT BY FEDAYEEN "REJECTIONIST" ELEMENTS AND THEIR LOCAL
LEFTIST ALLIES TO CAUSE COMMOTION ON EVE OF SECRETARY KISSINGER'S RETURN
TO ME AND TO EMBROIL FEDAYEEN LEADERSHIP WITH LEBANESE ARMY AND GOL. FACT
THAT LATTER OBJECTIVE HAS NOT BEEN ATTAINED IS PROBABLY THE ONLY PLUS TO
EMERGE OUT OF THIS WHOLE SAD AFFAIR.

HOUGHTON

     AMEMBASSY DAMASCUS, AMCONSUL JERUSALEM, AMEMBASSY JIDDA,

E.O. 11652: GDS
TAGS: PINS LE
SUBJECT: MORE CLASHES IN SIDON
REF: BEIRUT 2837

1. DEPT WILL DOUBTLESS HAVE NOTED FROM FBIS REPORTS THAT ANOTHER INCIDENT
OCCURRED IN SIDON AT 1815 LOCAL MAR 3, WHEN ARMY TRUCK TRANSPORTING
LEBANESE SOLDIERS TO THEIR UNITS IN SOUTH LEBANON WAS AMBUSHED ON MAIN
COASTAL ROAD BY "ARMED ELEMENTS" FIRING ROCKETS AND MACHINE GUNS FROM
POSITIONS IN TOWN'S CITADEL. OFFICIAL CASUALTY TOLL WAS ONE SOLDIER
KILLED AND 29 RPT 29 WOUNDED, WHICH BRINGS TOTAL ARMY-POLICE CASUALTIES
IN SIDON TO 9 DEAD AND 43 WOUNDED SINCE FIGHTING BEGAN ON FEB 26.

2. ABOVE INCIDENT APPARENTLY PROVOKED RENEWED EXCHANGES OF FIRE BETWEEN
LEBANESE TROOPS AND SIDON INSURGENTS DURING EVENING HOURS MAR 3. WE
UNDERSTAND THAT IT ALSO CAUSED ARMY LEADERSHIP TO CONSIDER LAUNCHING
ALL-OUT CLEAN-UP OPERATION IN SIDON MAR 4, BUT THIS IDEA APPARENTLY WAS
SCOTCHED AND CEASE FIRE RESTORED WHEN PLO'S ABU ZA'IM SUCCEEDED IN
ARRESTING ALLEGED INSTIGATOR OF INCIDENT (IDENTIFIED AS A LEBANESE
LEFTIST THUG) AND TURNED HIM OVER TO GOL AUTHORITIES. HIS ACCOMPLICES ARE
STILL BEING SOUGHT, BUT THERE SEEMS TO BE NO INFO REGARDING THEIR
WHEREABOUTS, NOR HAS THERE BEEN ANY EXPLANATION OF HOW ABU ZA'IM MANAGED
TO LAY HIS HANDS ON ALLEGED INSTIGATOR SO HANDILY.

3. AS OF MID-DAY MAR 4, SIDON REPORTEDLY WAS AGAIN QUIET BUT STILL UNDER
INSURGENT CONTROL, AND "NEGOTIATIONS" WERE EVIDENTLY STILL IN PROGRESS
BETWEEN GOL-PLO TEAM AND LEFTIST SIDONIAN ELEMENTS. PRESSURES REPORTED
REFTEL ON SOLH CABINET TO RESIGN ARE STILL IN EVIDENCE, BUT WE EXPECT NO
DECISIVE DEVELOPMENTS ON THIS FRONT UNTIL AFTER CABINET MEETING WITH PRES
FRANGIE, REPORTEDLY SCHEDULED FOR MAR 5.

4. MAR 3 WITNESSED MASS FUNERAL IN SIDON OF 8 PERSONS KILLED IN CLASHES
REPORTED OVER PAST SEVERAL DAYS. ALTHOUGH ATMOSPHERE WAS CHARGED WITH
TENSION, FUNERALS PROCEEDED WITHOUT INCIDENT.

HOUGHTON
footnotes: The Army re-entry of March 1: The most consequential Army action of the entire crisis. On February 27 the Army had withdrawn to the outskirts of Sidon in the expectation that the PLO would restore order inside the town. Over the next 48 hours the PLO did not do so: fedayeen-manned barricades remained in place, the coastal road stayed closed, the Army garrison in Sidon’s barracks was cut off from resupply, and through the same road closure all Lebanese Army units in the entire south of the country were unable to receive ammunition, food, or rotation. Mountain passes to the Bekaa were blocked by unusually heavy February snow. The March 1 deadline was not aggressive policing; it was a logistical imperative. That even this necessary re-entry produced 48 hours of street fighting and forced another Army withdrawal demonstrated that the Lebanese state could no longer impose its will in Sidon by any means short of a massive escalation it was not politically capable of ordering.

Frangieh-Solh concurrence: This paragraph is the Embassy’s direct rebuttal of the Sunni political narrative that would dominate the rest of the crisis. Sunni leaders charged that the Army had acted unilaterally, bypassing the civilian (Sunni) Prime Minister. The Embassy’s Army G-2 source — citing the Army chain of command itself — confirms that the decision to enforce the deadline was taken by President Frangieh in direct consultation with Prime Minister Solh. Solh knew the action was coming; his own Minister of Economy Khalaf was conducting parallel negotiations with the insurgents right up to the moment the Army moved. This is an important counterfactual anchor: when Sunni commentators accused the Army of acting without civilian authorization, they were making a claim that the contemporaneous diplomatic record contradicts. Solh’s silence in the face of this false charge — noted in paragraph 5 — was a political choice, not a factual concession.

Parallel negotiations: The pattern of a senior Lebanese minister (Khalaf) conducting back-channel talks with the insurgents while another arm of the state (the Army) prepares a forced entry on a set deadline is a characteristic Lebanese governmental mode. Each track acts as leverage for the other; each creates deniability for the other. In this case the tracks failed to coordinate: Khalaf did not deliver a negotiated dismantling of the barricades before the deadline, the Army moved, and the result was the March 1–2 battle. Khalaf’s subsequent frustration (he reportedly wanted to resign and was blocked from doing so only by Jumblatt) reflects the position of a negotiator whose process was short-circuited by his own government.

PFLP identification: The first public attribution by an Embassy cable to a specific fedayeen faction in the Sidon fighting. The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, founded by George Habash in 1967, was the largest of the “rejectionist” factions — those opposed to any diplomatic settlement with Israel. By 1975 the PFLP was a core component of the Rejectionist Front (formed October 1974) and had a major presence in Ain al-Hilweh camp just outside Sidon. The attribution here confirms the Embassy’s February 26 hypothesis that Sidon was being used as a staging ground by factions specifically opposed to the PLO-Fatah mainstream’s diplomatic opening. The insurgent arsenal listed — RPGs, Katyushas, recoilless rifles, 23mm heavy machine-guns — is not that of a neighborhood self-defense group; it is a light infantry brigade’s worth of weapons, pre-positioned.

Civilian-clothed traffic control: The most precise single image of the sovereignty question in these cables. The Lebanese state’s formal arm — the Army — has been withdrawn. The gendarmerie is positioned on the outskirts. The coastal road is open. But traffic inside Sidon is being directed by men in civilian clothes: fedayeen or fedayeen-aligned leftists, functioning as the de facto municipal authority. This is a precise documentary record of the transfer of practical sovereignty from the state to the armed groups on Lebanese territory — not by proclamation but by the small administrative fact of who stands at the intersection and waves the cars through.

Malik Salam resignation: Salam’s resignation as Minister of Water and Electricity on March 3 was the first cabinet-level defection from the Solh government produced by the Sidon crisis. A Sunni politician from Beirut’s Salam clan (a leading Sunni family; Saeb Salam had been Prime Minister multiple times), Malik Salam framed his resignation as specifically tied to the failure to dismiss General Ghanem. It was a political act aimed at creating momentum for precisely the army-command reform that Frangieh had refused to consider. Within ten weeks Solh himself would resign on the same ground.

The Army-acted-alone myth: An important example of how political narratives are constructed in real time from material that the record shows to be false. The Sunni street’s belief — or convenient claim — that the Army had moved without civilian authorization allowed Sunni political leaders to demand General Ghanem’s dismissal without having to demand Prime Minister Solh’s dismissal, and allowed Prime Minister Solh to avoid having to defend the decision he had actually concurred in. The Embassy’s notation that Solh “has done nothing to deny” the false charge is the key point: Solh chose silence because correcting the record would have forced him to defend a policy he could not politically defend. The fiction was load-bearing for everyone.

Solh’s denial, restated: The same denial the Embassy flagged as implausible in cable 1975BEIRUT02682 is now flagged again. Eight days after the fighting began, after PFLP involvement has been confirmed by Army G-2 and the PLO has sent its senior security official (Abu Za’im) to negotiate with the insurgents, the Prime Minister is still publicly insisting that “no rpt no fedayeen” have been involved. The use of the teletype convention “rpt” (repeat, used to emphasize an unusual or key word so it is not read as a typo) is the Embassy’s wry signal that it is flagging this claim as diplomatic fiction.

The Embassy’s structural diagnosis of Sunni political leadership: The Sunni political leader — Solh here, but the structure applies to his predecessors and successors — is caught between formal responsibility for a state apparatus he does not fully control (the Army command is Maronite) and an electoral base whose sympathies lie substantially with non-Lebanese causes (the Palestinian struggle) that produce exactly the confrontations he is then expected to manage. The Embassy treats this not as a personal failing of Solh but as a structural feature of the Lebanese political system. In the long view it is a prediction: no Sunni Prime Minister will be able to deliver on the Maronite half of his brief, and the office will therefore periodically collapse into resignation crises. Solh’s own May 15 resignation confirms the diagnosis.

The Chamoun fishing-company bombing: A detail that retrospectively reads as a miniature template for everything that followed in 1975–76. A political-economic grievance in Sidon (the Protéine concession) produces mass protest, which produces an Army shooting, which produces fedayeen-Army confrontation, which produces a retaliatory bombing of a Maronite commercial target in Beirut, which deepens Maronite conviction that the left is waging an undeclared war on Christian commerce and persons. The Embassy notes that the bombing was attributed to fishermen but clearly was the work of “radical leftists” — a distinction that in practice did not matter: the perception on the Christian side was of Sunni-leftist violence against Christians, and that perception was mobilizable into militia recruitment.

The Kissinger timing: Secretary of State Henry Kissinger was in the midst of his ongoing shuttle diplomacy between Israel and the Arab states in early 1975, attempting to broker a second Egyptian-Israeli disengagement agreement (which would be signed September 4, 1975). The Embassy’s hypothesis — that rejectionist fedayeen timed the Sidon provocation to coincide with Kissinger’s expected return to the region — places the Sidon crisis in the context of the broader Palestinian factional struggle. The PLO mainstream under Arafat was inclining cautiously toward political engagement (the Ten-Point Program of June 1974); the rejectionists wanted to foreclose that path. A Lebanese Army “massacre” of fedayeen-aligned protesters during Kissinger’s shuttle would have been devastating for Arafat’s diplomatic legitimacy. The Embassy notes with restrained relief that this particular objective “has not been attained.”

Rockets from the citadel: The March 3 ambush was qualitatively different from the February 26 or March 1 fighting. It was not an urban melee; it was a pre-planned ambush of a military convoy on the main coastal artery, using heavy weapons (rockets, machine guns) from fortified positions inside Sidon’s Crusader-era citadel itself. The choice of firing position is pointed: the citadel is the most recognizable historical landmark in Sidon, and using it as a heavy-weapons platform against the Lebanese Army was a deliberate political statement about who controlled the town. It also repurposed a building identified in cable 1975BEIRUT02611 as a fedayeen ammunition dump — including SAM-7 surface-to-air missiles — into an active firing position.

The Army’s aborted clean-up operation: The most important single operational fact in these cables. After the March 3 ambush, the Lebanese Army command seriously considered and then shelved a plan for an all-out clearing operation in Sidon. The decision not to proceed was not taken because the operation was considered militarily infeasible — the Army had the force to clear Sidon at cost — but because the political aftermath of an Army-fedayeen pitched battle with high civilian casualties in a Sunni city was judged unsurvivable by the Solh government. This is the moment at which the Lebanese state formally conceded to itself that the Sidon problem would not be resolved by military action. Every subsequent decision in the crisis flows from this concession.

Abu Za’im’s arrest: The Embassy’s unspoken question in this paragraph — “how did the PLO’s own security chief manage to produce the instigator of an attack on a Lebanese Army convoy so quickly?” — is a polite way of observing that the PLO was acting as the functional police authority in Sidon. Either Abu Za’im knew who the attackers were because the PLO had been in communication with them, or the PLO had its own intelligence penetration of the insurgent networks deep enough to produce a suspect on demand. Either way, the answer is that the PLO and not the Lebanese state was the authority with the operational capacity to act inside Sidon — the Lebanese state had to ask the PLO for the arrest, and the arrest was delivered as a political favor to avert the feared Army clean-up operation.

The March 3 funeral: Eight of the insurgent/civilian dead from the March 1–2 fighting were buried together on March 3. That the funeral — a gathering of leftist and fedayeen mourners in a town still held by armed insurgents — proceeded “without incident” is a signal of the effective ceasefire then prevailing. It also established a template: the larger, more politically charged funeral for Maarouf Saad himself, whose own death was then three days away, would take place on March 7 amid countrywide strikes and demonstrations (see cable 1975BEIRUT03064).

readerNarrative.headline: The Army Tries to Take Sidon Back, and Fails
readerNarrative.subheadline: Two cables filed March 3 and March 4, 1975 document the second round of the Sidon crisis: the Lebanese Army tries to reopen the coastal road, is ambushed by 1,000+ fedayeen armed with rockets and recoilless rifles, is forced to withdraw, and then sees one of its trucks hit by rockets fired from the medieval citadel itself. Army casualties pass 9 dead, 43 wounded. An all-out clean-up operation is planned for March 4, then scotched. The PLO is running the town.
readerNarrative.summary: After the February 27 Army withdrawal to the outskirts of Sidon, the town remained closed to Lebanese state authority. Fedayeen-manned barricades held the coastal road shut. The Sidon garrison was penned in its barracks; all Lebanese Army units in South Lebanon were cut off from resupply. On March 1 President Frangieh, in consultation with Prime Minister Solh, ordered the Army to force the coastal road open. The resulting 48-hour battle produced five Army dead and ten wounded and ended in a second Army withdrawal. Two days later, on March 3, an Army resupply truck was ambushed with rockets fired from inside Sidon’s Crusader-era citadel; one soldier was killed and 29 wounded. Army leadership seriously considered an all-out clean-up operation before shelving it in exchange for the PLO arresting — with conspicuous speed — the alleged instigator of the attack. By the morning of March 4 Sidon remained quiet but under insurgent control; traffic inside the town was being directed by men in civilian clothes; the first cabinet resignation (Malik Salam) had landed; and the Lebanese state had demonstrated, in practice, that it could not impose its will on the town.
keyRevelations: The March 1 Army re-entry was a logistical imperative, not aggression. All Lebanese Army units in South Lebanon were cut off: the Sidon garrison was penned in its barracks, the coastal road was blocked, and the mountain passes to the Bekaa were blocked by snow. The Army had to reopen the coast road or lose control of an entire region. It could not.

Frangieh ordered the operation with Solh’s concurrence. The Sunni narrative that the Army acted unilaterally — which became the basis of the demand to sack General Ghanem — is contradicted by Army G-2’s reporting to the Embassy. Solh knew. He simply chose not to defend the decision publicly.

The insurgents had heavy weapons in military quantities. RPGs, Katyusha rockets, recoilless rifles, 23mm Soviet heavy machine-guns. The Army came with tanks and APCs; the fedayeen put “several armored vehicles out of commission by rocket fire.” This was a pitched battle between two light-mechanized forces, not a crowd-control operation.

PFLP is named. The first direct Embassy attribution to a specific fedayeen faction comes from Army G-2: the insurgents were “leftist Sidonian civilians and fedayeen (primarily PFLP).” The rejectionist hypothesis of cable 1975BEIRUT02611 is confirmed.

The March 4 all-out clean-up operation was scotched. After the March 3 citadel ambush, the Army seriously planned a full clearing operation in Sidon. It was cancelled — not because the Army could not execute it, but because the Solh government could not survive ordering it. This is the moment at which the Lebanese state implicitly conceded that Sidon would not be taken back by military means.

Abu Za’im produces the instigator. The PLO security chief arrests the alleged attack organizer and hands him to the GOL with startling speed. The Embassy notes, drily, that no explanation has been offered for how Abu Za’im managed this — implying the obvious answer: the PLO, not the Lebanese state, was the functional security authority in Sidon.

keyFigures.name: Rashid Solh
keyFigures.role: Prime Minister of Lebanon — trapped between street and palace
keyFigures.desc: Sunni Prime Minister, October 1974 to May 15, 1975. Across this cable he is seen making impossible choices: concurring in the Army re-entry on March 1, allowing the false ‘Army acted alone’ charge to circulate unrefuted, holding his cabinet together against Sunni pressure to dissolve it, and still insisting in public — eight days into a battle in which PFLP has been named by name — that ‘no rpt no fedayeen’ have been involved. He would resign ten weeks later on exactly the ground of army-command reform.

keyFigures.name: Suleiman Frangieh
keyFigures.role: President of Lebanon — ordered the re-entry
keyFigures.desc: Maronite Christian President (1970–1976). It was Frangieh, in consultation with Solh and the Army high command, who gave the March 1 order to force the coastal road open. His refusal throughout the crisis to consider Sunni demands for army-command reform — specifically the dismissal of General Ghanem — was the political brick wall against which the Solh government would eventually break.

keyFigures.name: Kamal Jumblatt
keyFigures.role: Druze paramount chief — still holding the cabinet together
keyFigures.desc: Founder of the Progressive Socialist Party and paramount leader of Lebanon’s Druze community. In this cable he is seen preventing his own Minister of Economy, Abbas Khalaf, from resigning — continuing the ‘ticklish position’ diagnosed in cable 1975BEIRUT02682. He is cooperating with Frangieh to restore order while privately sympathetic to the leftist-fedayeen position. The contradiction was about to crack open entirely.

keyFigures.name: Yasser Arafat
keyFigures.desc: Chairman of the Palestine Liberation Organization and leader of its largest faction, Fatah. Not named directly in these cables but present in the form of his security chief Abu Za’im, whose ability to arrest the March 3 attack instigator at speed demonstrated that the PLO under Arafat — not the Lebanese state — was the functional security authority in Sidon. The rejectionist provocation aimed at embarrassing Arafat’s mainstream had, by this point, forced him to act as the de facto policing arm of the Lebanese state.

keyFigures.name: Abu Za’im (Atallah Atallah)
keyFigures.role: Fatah security chief — PLO interlocutor with the GOL
keyFigures.desc: Senior Fatah intelligence officer and head of PLO security in Lebanon during the Sidon crisis. Arafat’s principal lieutenant for managing the Lebanese-PLO relationship. His arrest of the March 3 attack instigator, and the speed with which he produced the suspect, demonstrated the depth of PLO operational control inside Sidon. He later defected to a pro-Jordanian dissident faction and died in 2008.

keyFigures.name: Zuhayr Muhsen
keyFigures.role: Sa’iqa leader — the Syrian Palestinian seat at the table
keyFigures.desc: Leader of Sa’iqa, the Syrian Ba’ath-sponsored Palestinian faction, and senior PLO Executive Committee member. His presence on the GOL-PLO mediation team alongside Abu Za’im signals the direct involvement of Syrian-backed Palestinian leadership in the Sidon negotiations — a reminder that the rejectionist/mainstream dichotomy did not map cleanly onto Palestinian factional lines. Assassinated in Cannes in July 1979.

readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
The logistical trap

To understand why the Lebanese Army re-entered Sidon on March 1, 1975, and why the operation ended the way it did, it is necessary to see the Army’s position not as a political choice but as a logistical emergency.

On February 27 the Army had withdrawn to the outskirts of Sidon in return for unconfirmed PLO assurances that the PLO would restore order inside the town. Over the next 48 hours, the PLO did not do so. Fedayeen-manned barricades stayed up. The coastal road stayed closed. The Sidon garrison — a regular Army unit in its own barracks inside the town — found itself effectively besieged, unable to receive ammunition, rations, or rotation. Much more seriously, every Lebanese Army unit in the entire south of the country depended on the coastal road for resupply, because the alternative routes — the mountain passes to the Bekaa Valley in the east — were blocked by unusually heavy late-February snow.

The Lebanese Army therefore faced a binary choice within 48 hours: reopen the coastal road or progressively lose its capacity to operate in South Lebanon. President Frangieh, in consultation with Prime Minister Solh and the Army high command, chose to reopen the road. A 1700 local deadline was set for the voluntary dismantling of the barricades. When the deadline passed without compliance, the Army moved.

One detachment was ambushed on its approach to the town. That first engagement was, in retrospect, the warning. The Army proceeded into Sidon with tanks, armored cars, and APCs. Over the next 48 hours it fought a running urban battle against a force of insurgents armed with RPGs, Katyusha rockets, recoilless rifles, and 23mm Soviet heavy machine-guns, firing from rooftops, windows, and alleyways. Several armored vehicles were put out of commission by rocket fire. By 1600 local on March 2 a second truce had been negotiated and the Army had, again, withdrawn.

PFLP named

Cable 02837 is the first Embassy cable to name a specific fedayeen faction as responsible for the Sidon insurgency. Army G-2 — the intelligence section of the Lebanese Armed Forces — identifies the insurgents as “a combination of leftist Sidonian civilians and fedayeen (primarily PFLP).”

The attribution is significant. The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, founded by George Habash in 1967, was the largest and most militarily capable of the Palestinian “rejectionist” factions — those opposed to any negotiated settlement with Israel. The Rejectionist Front, formed in October 1974 in response to the PLO’s Ten-Point Program, had brought together the PFLP, the PFLP-General Command, the Arab Liberation Front, and dissident Sa’iqa elements in a common position against Arafat’s diplomatic opening. By 1975 the PFLP was headquartered in Beirut and had a major armed presence in Ain al-Hilweh camp, just outside Sidon.

The February 26 Embassy hypothesis — that the fishermen’s demonstration was a ruse engineered by rejectionist fedayeen to draw the Lebanese Army into a confrontation that would embarrass the PLO mainstream — is now confirmed by the Army’s own intelligence. The force the Lebanese Army had been fighting was not a crowd of angry townspeople; it was a pre-positioned light-infantry battalion of a specific political faction, with weapons it had been stockpiling for exactly this kind of engagement.

The weapons themselves tell the story. RPGs, Katyushas, recoilless rifles, 23mm heavy machine-guns — these are not the arms of a neighborhood self-defense committee. They are the arms of a unit that expected an armored assault and had prepared for it. The fedayeen did not merely defeat the Army’s re-entry; they defeated it efficiently, putting tanks and APCs out of action in hours of street fighting.

Civilian clothes and traffic control

One of the most quietly devastating sentences in cable 02837 appears in paragraph 4. The Army, after its second withdrawal, has left the outer perimeter to the gendarmerie. The coastal road is open again. But inside Sidon, “traffic on it and elsewhere in Sidon was being directed by persons wearing civilian clothes.”

This is the practical face of sovereignty lost. Not a declaration, not a speech, not a formal transfer — just the small administrative fact of who stands at the intersection and waves the cars through. In Sidon in early March 1975, that person was no longer a Lebanese policeman or Lebanese gendarme. It was a fedayeen or a fedayeen-aligned leftist, functioning as the de facto municipal authority in a Lebanese city. The Lebanese state had withdrawn not just its Army but its capacity to perform even the most routine administrative functions. The town was being governed by the people who had defeated the Army.

The Sunni political cascade

Paragraph 5 of cable 02837 documents the political fallout as it unfolded inside the Solh government. Governor Henri Lahoud of South Lebanon had already been placed on 20 days “administrative leave” — a euphemism for sacrificial suspension. On March 3, Malik Salam, Minister of Water and Electricity and a member of the prominent Salam clan of Beirut, resigned in protest at the failure to dismiss General Ghanem. Abbas Khalaf, Minister of Economy and a member of Kamal Jumblatt’s Progressive Socialist Party bloc, reportedly wanted to resign but was blocked by Jumblatt himself, who was still trying to hold the cabinet together from his “ticklish position.”

The specific Sunni demand is important. It was not for Prime Minister Solh to be replaced; it was for General Ghanem, the Army Commander, to be dismissed. The demand rested on a false premise — the claim that the Army had acted unilaterally on March 1, without civilian authorization. The Embassy’s reporting, drawing on Army G-2, directly contradicts this: the March 1 operation was ordered by Frangieh “in consultation with Primin Solh and Army high command.” But Solh chose not to defend the decision publicly. His silence was a political calculation: to admit that he had concurred in the Army re-entry would have meant defending the resulting Army operation, and defending the Army operation was exactly what his Sunni base would not accept.

The structural problem visible here is one the Embassy has diagnosed repeatedly across the Sidon file. A Sunni Prime Minister of Lebanon is responsible for a state apparatus — the Army command — whose confessional composition he cannot change. He cannot deliver army-command reform without Frangieh’s agreement, and Frangieh will not agree. His electoral base demands the reform. When a crisis comes that requires the Army to be either mobilized (against the fedayeen) or constrained (in deference to Sunni sentiment), he cannot do either with full authority, and so he does both partially and ends up defending neither. The Sidon crisis is this structural trap activated. Solh will resign from it on May 15.

The Kissinger timing

The Embassy’s closing Comment in cable 02837 returns to the hypothesis of February 26 and strengthens it. The Sidon clashes, the cable argues, can now be read more confidently as “a deliberate attempt by fedayeen ‘rejectionist’ elements and their local leftist allies to cause commotion on the eve of Secretary Kissinger’s return to the Middle East and to embroil fedayeen leadership with the Lebanese Army and GOL.”

The political logic is precise. Henry Kissinger was in the middle of shuttle diplomacy between Israel and Egypt; the second Sinai disengagement agreement was six months away. Arafat’s PLO mainstream, under the Ten-Point Program of June 1974, was cautiously inclining toward accepting political engagement. The rejectionists wanted to destroy that opening. A Lebanese Army “massacre” of fedayeen-aligned protestors during Kissinger’s visit would have been a gift to them: it would have forced Arafat to respond with force or lose all legitimacy with his own base, it would have tipped Lebanon into open Palestinian-state confrontation, and it would have made the diplomatic opening impossible.

The Embassy observes — with what is clearly relief — that this particular objective has not been achieved. The GOL has not broken with the PLO mainstream; indeed, the PLO through Abu Za’im has been drawn in as a partner in crisis management. But this success was narrow. The Embassy closes with the observation that preventing a general PLO-GOL rupture is “probably the only plus to emerge out of this whole sad affair.”

The citadel ambush

Cable 02894, filed the next afternoon, reports an incident whose theatrical quality is impossible to miss. At 1815 on March 3, an Army truck carrying soldiers to their units in South Lebanon was ambushed on the main coastal road by “armed elements firing rockets and machine guns from positions in the town’s citadel.”

The firing position matters. Sidon’s citadel — the Castle of St. Louis on its landward side, the Sea Castle on the water — is the most visible historical monument in the city. It is also, as cable 1975BEIRUT02611 had established a week earlier, the location where fedayeen munitions (including SAM-7 surface-to-air missiles) were being stockpiled. To convert the citadel into a heavy-weapons firing position and then use it against a Lebanese Army convoy was not merely a military act. It was a deliberate political statement about who held Sidon.

The official casualty toll — one dead and 29 wounded — brought the Army’s cumulative losses to 9 dead and 43 wounded. Nine dead soldiers in ten days. In a Lebanese Army of the size and cohesion of the mid-1970s, these were not losses that could be absorbed without a response.

The clean-up operation that wasn’t

Paragraph 2 of cable 02894 contains the single most operationally revealing sentence in the entire Sidon file: “We understand that it also caused Army leadership to consider launching an all-out clean-up operation in Sidon March 4, but this idea apparently was scotched.”

The Army command, after the citadel ambush, seriously planned a full clearing operation in Sidon. The plan was abandoned. The reason it was abandoned was not that the operation was militarily impossible — the Lebanese Army had the forces to clear Sidon at cost — but that the political aftermath of an Army assault producing high civilian casualties in a predominantly Sunni city, coming on top of the February 26 shooting of Maarouf Saad, was judged unsurvivable by the Solh government.

This is the moment at which the Lebanese state formally conceded to itself that the Sidon problem would not be resolved by military action. Every decision after this point — the negotiations, the cabinet committee for army-command “study,” the transfer of the southern district commander to “other posts” — flows from this decision. The state chose accommodation over escalation because the escalation would have destroyed the state before it destroyed the armed groups.

In exchange, the state received a gesture: Abu Za’im’s arrest of the alleged attack organizer. The speed of the arrest is the Embassy’s most eloquent observation. The PLO’s security chief produced the suspect “so handily” that the cable cannot resist noting the implication. Either Abu Za’im knew who the attackers were because the PLO had been in communication with them, or the PLO had its own security penetration of the insurgent networks deep enough to produce a suspect on demand. Either way, the arrest demonstrated that the operational security authority in Sidon was the PLO, not the Lebanese state. The Lebanese state had to ask the PLO to make the arrest; the PLO did so as a political favor, in exchange for the cancellation of the clean-up operation.

A town held and a death approaching

By the morning of March 4, Sidon was “again quiet but still under insurgent control.” The coastal road was open; traffic was moving; the negotiations between the GOL-PLO team and the leftist Sidonian elements were continuing. The eight fighters killed in the weekend battle were buried together on March 3 in a funeral that passed, the Embassy notes, “without incident.”

The larger funeral was two days away. On March 6 Maarouf Saad would die of his wounds at American University Hospital in Beirut — the Embassy’s February 27 prediction validated to the day. On March 7 the funeral of Maarouf Saad himself would take place in Sidon, paralyzing Beirut through a countrywide general strike, filling every Sunni city with mourning processions, and producing the fourth cable in this series: 1975BEIRUT03064, “SECURITY SITUATION IN LEBANON.”

But already the pattern was set. The Army had tried to take Sidon back and had failed, twice, in eight days. The clean-up operation had been considered and scotched. The PLO was the functional security authority inside the town. The Sunni street was mobilizing. The cabinet had its first resignation. And the Embassy was reporting all of it to Washington, precisely, in time. None of it was stopped.

cables.excerpt: Saad dies at mid-day March 6 at AUB Hospital. The Embassy’s Feb 27 prediction is validated within hours. Compounded by fears of Israeli reprisal for the previous night’s Savoy Hotel attack in Tel Aviv: PLO offices in Beirut evacuated; fedayeen on full alert; fedayeen fire on overflying Lebanese Air Force planes mistaking them for Israeli. The Higher Islamic Council demands the Solh cabinet resign, naming Frangieh, the Army leadership, and Solh personally. By the afternoon of March 7, Beirut is under general strike; Corniche Mazraa is paralyzed by armed fedayeen from nearby camps; Israeli aircraft sonic-boom overhead; the Embassy sends non-essential American staff home at 1030 local.
cables.annotatedBody:
Originally classified CONFIDENTIAL · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State · Now UNCLASSIFIED

Archival Note — Merged Entry

This is a merged archival entry combining two companion cables filed on consecutive days, March 6 and March 7, 1975, documenting the cascade that followed Maarouf Saad’s death. Cable 1975BEIRUT03028 (061547Z) is the same-day report: Saad has died at AUB Hospital at mid-day March 6; PLO offices in Beirut have been evacuated; fedayeen are on full alert; fedayeen fire on overflying Lebanese Air Force planes thinking they are Israeli; Beirut streets are blocked by leftist-Sunni demonstrations. Cable 1975BEIRUT03064 (071050Z) is the next morning’s report: general strike across Lebanon, Beirut paralyzed, Corniche Mazraa in the hands of armed fedayeen from nearby camps, Israeli sonic booms overhead, the Higher Islamic Council has demanded the Solh cabinet resign, and the Embassy has sent its non-essential staff home. The two cables together document the precise 24-hour period in which the crisis shifted from a South Lebanon incident to a nationwide confessional rupture.

Cable 1 of 2 — 1975BEIRUT03028 — 061547Z Mar 75

Subject: Renewal of Tension in Sidon and Elsewhere in Lebanon · CONFIDENTIAL · Ref: BEIRUT 2894 and previous

1.
Tensions generated throughout Lebanon over the past week by clashes between the Lebanese Army and “armed elements” in Sidon had begun to lessen perceptibly late on March 5, following country-wide manifestations by citizens[1] (mostly Christians but some Shi’a) demonstrating in support of the Army and GOL. Demonstrations went off more or less peacefully, with only one person reported killed (accidentally by stray bullet). The Council of Ministers meeting the evening of March 5 resulted in a decision by the Solh cabinet (backed by Pres Frangie) to continue in office, although Min of Water and Electricity Malik Salam carried out his threat to resign and walked out of the meeting. The stage thus seemed set for further diminution of tensions and a progressive return to normality on March 6, thanks to a typically Lebanese solution in which no problems were really solved but were merely to be brushed under the rug for the time being.[2]

2.
Unfortunately, widespread apprehension re possible Israeli retaliation against Lebanon for last night’s terrorist operation in Tel Aviv,[3] followed by news at mid-day March 6 of the death in AUB Hospital of ex-deputy Maarouf Saad[4] (who had been wounded in the Feb 26 clashes in Sidon (see Beirut 2611)), have changed all this. PLO offices in Beirut apparently have been evacuated, and fedayeen are reportedly on full alert in and around the country’s 15 refugee camps, including those north of Tripoli where trigger-happy elements this morning actually opened fire on overflying Lebanese Air Force planes, probably on the assumption they were Israeli.[5] As news of Saad’s death spread during the afternoon, other disruptive incidents began occurring at various points in Beirut, where groups of his leftist and Sunni Moslem sympathizers (accompanied in some places by fedayeen) have taken to blocking roads, burning tires, shooting in air, etc. Sidon reportedly is again gripped by tension, with large numbers of “armed elements” (i.e., fedayeen and their leftist allies) having reoccupied street barricades and positions on rooftops. Lebanese Army and internal security forces have cancelled all leaves and units are currently engaged in trying to clear crowds and barricades from several arteries in Beirut, including the road to the airport. Most shops and businesses closed earlier than usual, and late-afternoon rush-hour traffic appears less than normal.

3.
Conditions described above have created a palpable atmosphere of public nervousness and foreboding. The general feeling seems to be that further trouble — generated internally or by the Israelis, or both — is still to come. I have taken the precaution of advising the Embassy’s American staff to avoid unnecessary movement at least during the night of March 6-7.[6]

HOUGHTON

Cable 2 of 2 — 1975BEIRUT03064 — 071050Z Mar 75

Subject: Security Situation in Lebanon · CONFIDENTIAL · Ref: BEIRUT 3028

1.
As of mid-day March 7, the tense security situation in Beirut and other major urban areas remains much as outlined reftel. The funeral of leftist leader Maarouf Saad is scheduled to take place at noon in Sidon and will be accompanied by services at mosques in Beirut and other towns having large Sunni Moslem populations.[7] Large mourning processions and demonstrations staged by leftist and Sunni elements are expected to follow this afternoon in Beirut, Sidon and Tripoli. Although Lebanese security authorities hope these will occur without major disturbances, they are not optimistic.

2.
Right now Beirut is generally quiet as the result of a general strike,[8] but groups of men (some of them armed) can be observed at roadblocks scattered throughout the city, and scattered small-arms fire (probably in air) plus several loud explosions (apparently sonic booms caused by overflying Israeli aircraft)[9] were heard during the late morning hours. The Corniche Mazraa area is paralyzed, with armed fedayeen from nearby camps much in evidence, and several main roads — including that leading to the airport — in outlying areas are blocked by milling demonstrators. The road leading from the Embassy to the main hotel district is also blocked.[10] Lebanese security authorities have taken the unusual precaution of publicly urging all foreigners to stay off the streets.

3. Comment
Although we hope that the day will pass without further trouble, the possibility of ugly incidents and violence occurring is still with us. The situation is compounded by the fact that events over the past nine days have tended increasingly to assume confessional overtones,[11] with Sunni Muslims displaying growing and open dissatisfaction over what they regard as Christian monopolization of power within the GOL and the country at large. (The Higher Islamic Council on March 6 issued a strong demand for the Solh cabinet to resign, blaming the current state of affairs entirely on Pres Frangie, the Army leadership and Primin Solh.)[12] Christians, in return, have tended more and more to react hostilely to these pressures, attributing them to leftist and Palestinian “subversion” and manipulation of the Sunni population.[13] Although many leaders on both sides are still counseling moderation, there is no telling where events of the next 12-24 hours may lead. We expect to have a better picture of the situation when the Saad funeral and its aftermath are over.

4.
In view of the foregoing, I have sent non-essential employees home at 1030 local[14] and instructed them to remain there for the remainder of March 7. The British Embassy has done the same.

HOUGHTON

REF: BEIRUT 3028

footnotes: The March 5 Christian demonstrations: In the days before Saad’s death, pro-Army demonstrations took place in Christian areas of Beirut and the mountain, organized principally by the Kataeb (Phalange) Party of Pierre Gemayel and the National Liberal Party of Camille Chamoun. The demonstrations were framed as support for the state and the rule of law against “armed elements.” In confessional terms, however, they represented the first mass public mobilization of Christian street forces in response to the Sunni-leftist agitation of the previous week. The Embassy’s careful phrase — “mostly Christians but some Shi’a’ — acknowledges the confessional character while noting the limited Shi’a participation (consistent with Musa Sadr’s cautious silence during the first phase of the crisis, which would end a week later with his open agitation against the GOL).

The Embassy’s “brushed under the rug” diagnosis: The March 5 cabinet meeting had resolved nothing structural. The Solh government continued in office. General Ghanem was not dismissed. The army command was not reformed. Salam’s resignation was absorbed. The Sidon insurgency remained unresolved. But the immediate political crisis had been contained by the formula of continuing consultations, a ‘study commission’ on army reform, and a promise to satisfy the fishermen — a formula that the Embassy characterizes with characteristic dryness as the “typically Lebanese solution” in which nothing is decided but everyone can go home. The phrase is diagnostic of the entire political system: compromises that defer problems rather than resolve them, producing an accumulation of unresolved issues that would collapse the system in April 1975.

The Tel Aviv Savoy Hotel attack (March 5, 1975): On the night of March 5, 1975, eight Fatah fighters from the Force 17 / Black September Organization landed by rubber dinghy on the Tel Aviv seafront, stormed the Savoy Hotel on HaYarkon Street, and took 11 hostages. In the 10-hour siege that followed, Israeli special forces (Sayeret Matkal) assaulted the hotel; seven attackers, eight hostages, and three Israeli soldiers were killed. The attack was planned and executed by the mainstream Fatah wing, not by a rejectionist faction — which complicates the picture of which faction wanted what. The operation came immediately after the Sidon ambushes and was presumed by the Embassy to be likely to produce an Israeli reprisal against Lebanon. As cable 1975BEIRUT03203 would document a week later, that Israeli reprisal — if it came while the Sidon crisis was unresolved — would force the Lebanese Army to respond or lose all public credibility, potentially tipping Lebanon into open conflict with Israel at a moment when it could not afford one.

Maarouf Saad’s death, March 6, 1975: Eight days after he was shot by Lebanese Army fire during the fishermen’s demonstration of February 26, Maarouf Saad died of his wounds at American University Hospital in Beirut. The prediction the Embassy had filed on February 27 — “If Saad should actually die, these manifestations could assume serious proportions” — was validated to the day. Historians including Kamal Salibi, Fawwaz Traboulsi, and Walid Khalidi identify Saad’s death as the specific political event that tipped a regional unrest into a national confessional crisis. The Ain al-Rummaneh bus attack of April 13, widely named as the start of the civil war, was five weeks and one day away.

Fedayeen fire on Lebanese Air Force planes: One of the most politically charged incidents of the cable. Palestinian fighters at refugee camps north of Tripoli opened fire on aircraft overflying the camps, mistaking them for Israeli. The aircraft were in fact Lebanese Air Force. The incident is a miniature portrait of the crisis: the armed groups were in a posture of expecting immediate Israeli attack, the population inside the camps was operating with nerves stretched taut, and the confusion of who was shooting at whom — and on what assumption — was itself a symptom of the breakdown in coordination between the state and the armed groups it could not control. That fedayeen in Tripoli were prepared to open fire without confirming the target nationality is a signal of the level of tension; that they would assume Israel was already attacking, hours after Saad’s death and the Savoy attack, is a signal of what everyone expected to happen next.

Houghton’s staff-safety advisory: The specific direction to Embassy American staff to avoid unnecessary movement was the first formal staff-safety measure of the crisis. The next cable (1975BEIRUT03064) would escalate this to sending non-essential employees home at 1030 local. The measured escalation of Embassy security posture is a useful indicator of the Embassy’s own threat assessment in real time. In diplomatic practice, sending non-essential staff home is a serious measure; coordination with the British Embassy to do the same indicates that the concern was being communicated across the allied diplomatic community.

The Saad funeral, March 7, 1975: The funeral of Maarouf Saad in Sidon at noon on March 7 was the largest public assembly of the Sunni-leftist-Palestinian coalition since the crisis began. Secondary sources describe the funeral as producing the image of Sidon under Palestinian armed control in a specifically political form: PLO and Sa’iqa units marched in uniform in the procession, fedayeen flags flew alongside Lebanese flags, and speeches called for the replacement of General Ghanem, the dismissal of the Solh cabinet, and army reform. Simultaneous mosque services in Beirut, Tripoli, and other Sunni cities created a coordinated national moment in which the Sunni political and religious establishment publicly aligned with the fedayeen-leftist coalition. The synchronous mosque-and-funeral structure — using the religious infrastructure of the Sunni community as the coordinating mechanism for a political mobilization — was unprecedented in the scale and coordination of its execution.

The general strike of March 7: A country-wide general strike declared by the Sunni-leftist political bloc, observed substantially across Sunni commercial districts, mixed districts, and — critically — by the Palestinian camps. Christian commercial districts largely did not observe the strike, which produced its own confessional geography in real time: the commercial sectors that did and did not close on March 7 became a map of the political coalition that was forming. The explicit observation that “Beirut is generally quiet as the result of a general strike” is a careful diplomatic construction: the city is quiet in the sense that commerce has stopped, but it is not peaceful, because the cessation of commerce is itself a political act.

Israeli overflights, March 7: Sonic booms from overflying Israeli aircraft over Beirut on the morning of March 7 were the Israeli political signal of the day. The overflights were not attacks; they were a demonstration of Israeli air capability over Lebanese urban territory, timed to coincide with the Saad funeral and the general strike. In Israeli operational logic this was standard pre-reprisal signaling — establishing that Israel was watching, that Israeli strike capability was present, and that a decision could be taken at any moment. The Embassy’s notation that the booms were “apparently sonic booms caused by overflying Israeli aircraft” registers both the event and its political meaning. Together with the fedayeen shooting at Lebanese planes the previous day in the mistaken belief they were Israeli, the overflights produced a saturated airspace in which the question was not whether Israel would attack but when.

The blocked road from the Embassy to the hotel district: The U.S. Embassy in Beirut in March 1975 was at the corner of Rue de la France and Avenue de Paris in Ain el-Mreisseh — the building that would be destroyed by a suicide truck bomb on April 18, 1983. The “main hotel district” refers to the Phoenicia-St. George-Holiday Inn cluster in Ras Beirut. The road between these two points — which the Embassy used for routine business — passed through an area now blocked by demonstrators. The practical consequence was that the Embassy’s American staff could not circulate in their routine business areas, and that Beirut’s commercial and hotel infrastructure had been paralyzed. The observation is small but important: the Embassy itself was now constrained by the crisis, not simply observing it.

The confessional turn: The single most consequential political observation in cable 03064 is that “events over the past nine days have tended increasingly to assume confessional overtones.” The Sidon crisis had begun, on February 26, as an economic grievance about fishermen and a fishing concession. By March 7, the Embassy was describing it as a Sunni-Christian confrontation with the Sunni community in religious-political mobilization against a Christian-dominated state apparatus. This reframing is not the Embassy’s invention; it is a description of the way the political actors themselves were now framing the crisis. The movement from economic grievance to confessional war over nine days is the accelerated version of a decades-long drift in Lebanese political alignment. The confessional framing, once established, was very difficult to reverse.

The Higher Islamic Council demand: The Higher Islamic Council’s March 6 demand that the Solh cabinet resign, explicitly blaming President Frangieh, the Army leadership, and Prime Minister Solh himself, was a specifically religious intervention in a political crisis. The Council is the supreme body of the Sunni religious establishment in Lebanon, headed by the Grand Mufti; its political pronouncements carry the weight of Sunni religious authority. For the Council to demand the resignation of a Sunni Prime Minister and to name him personally was unprecedented. It meant that Solh had lost the Sunni religious establishment — the final confessional constituency that might have sheltered him politically. His eventual May 15 resignation was, in essence, already written on March 6.

The Christian counter-narrative: Parallel to the Sunni religious-political mobilization, Christian political leaders were constructing a counter-narrative in which the Sunni agitation was not a grass-roots response to a genuine confessional grievance but a product of “leftist and Palestinian subversion and manipulation of the Sunni population.” On this reading, the Sidon crisis was a Palestinian-engineered provocation (consistent with the Embassy’s own ‘ruse’ hypothesis of February 26, though deployed differently), and the Sunni response was evidence of how deeply the Sunni community had been penetrated by Palestinian-leftist agitation. The narrative did not need to be entirely accurate to be politically effective; it provided the Christian right with a framework in which the proper response was not conciliation but defense. The Kataeb and NLP militias would organize accordingly.

The 1030 Embassy closure: The U.S. Embassy in Beirut sent its non-essential employees home at 10:30 local time on March 7, 1975, with instructions to remain at home for the remainder of the day. The British Embassy did the same. In diplomatic practice, a daytime staff drawdown of this kind is initiated only when the Chief of Mission judges the streets unsafe for routine Embassy circulation. The measure was calibrated: it was not an evacuation, not a closure, not an emergency action reporting requirement — it was a protective daytime drawdown pending the outcome of a specific event (the Saad funeral). The fact that the Embassy judged this measure necessary is a useful indicator of the actual threat level at street level in Beirut on the afternoon of March 7, 1975 — days before the April 13 bus attack would begin the civil war.

readerNarrative.headline: The Day Maarouf Saad Died
readerNarrative.subheadline: Two cables filed March 6 and March 7, 1975 document the 24 hours in which the Sidon crisis became a national confessional rupture: Saad dies at mid-day March 6 at AUB Hospital; the Savoy Hotel attack in Tel Aviv saturates Lebanon with fear of Israeli reprisal; fedayeen fire on Lebanese planes thinking they are Israeli; Beirut is under general strike on March 7; the Higher Islamic Council has demanded the cabinet’s resignation; Israeli aircraft sonic-boom over Beirut during the funeral; the U.S. Embassy sends non-essential staff home at 1030 local.
readerNarrative.summary: On the evening of March 5, 1975, the Solh government had survived a cabinet confidence vote. The Sidon crisis — though unresolved in substance — appeared to be stabilizing. One cabinet minister (Malik Salam) had resigned, Christian counter-demonstrations had boosted the regime’s confidence, and the Embassy believed a “typically Lebanese” solution of deferring decisions indefinitely was taking hold. Two events on March 5–6 destroyed that equilibrium within 24 hours. First, on the night of March 5, eight Fatah fighters landed on the Tel Aviv waterfront and attacked the Savoy Hotel, killing eleven Israelis. Second, at mid-day on March 6, Maarouf Saad died at AUB Hospital of the wounds he had received on February 26. The Embassy’s February 27 prediction — “If Saad should actually die, these manifestations could assume serious proportions” — was validated precisely. PLO offices in Beirut were evacuated. Fedayeen in the Tripoli camps, believing Israeli retaliation was imminent, opened fire on overflying Lebanese Air Force planes. By mid-day March 7, Beirut was under a general strike. The Corniche Mazraa area was paralyzed by armed fedayeen from the nearby camps. Israeli aircraft were creating sonic booms over the city. The Higher Islamic Council had formally demanded the Solh cabinet’s resignation, naming the President, the Army leadership, and the Prime Minister by name. The Embassy sent its non-essential American staff home at 1030 local.
keyRevelations: Saad died at AUB Hospital at mid-day on March 6, 1975. The Embassy’s February 27 prediction that his death would produce manifestations of serious proportions was validated within hours. The cable logged “palpable atmosphere of public nervousness and foreboding” before the sun had set on the day of his death.

PLO offices in Beirut were evacuated within hours of Saad’s death. The response was not to the death itself but to the anticipated Israeli reprisal for the Savoy Hotel attack of the previous night. The simultaneity of the two events — Fatah raid in Tel Aviv, Saad death in Beirut — created a political shockwave that no single mechanism could have produced.

Fedayeen fired on Lebanese Air Force planes north of Tripoli, mistaking them for Israeli. An inadvertent but consequential incident: Palestinian fighters were operating in a posture of expecting Israeli attack hours after Saad’s death. The confusion of nationality of aircraft is a miniature portrait of the breakdown in state-fedayeen coordination.

The Higher Islamic Council demanded the Solh cabinet resign on March 6, naming Frangieh, the Army leadership, and Solh himself. For the supreme body of the Sunni religious establishment to publicly call for the resignation of a Sunni Prime Minister was a confessional rupture. Solh had lost the constituency that might have sheltered him.

Beirut was under a general strike on March 7; Corniche Mazraa was in the hands of armed fedayeen. The road from the Embassy to the main hotel district was blocked. Israeli aircraft were sonic-booming overhead. Lebanese security authorities publicly urged all foreigners to stay indoors. The sovereignty collapse seen in Sidon on February 27 was now visible in Beirut.

The Embassy sent non-essential American staff home at 1030 local. The British Embassy did the same. In diplomatic practice this is a calibrated protective drawdown initiated only when streets are judged unsafe for routine circulation. The Embassy’s own security posture confirms the actual threat level — five weeks before Ain al-Rummaneh.
