keyFigures.name: Maarouf Saad
keyFigures.desc: Leader of the Popular Nasserist Organization, shot by Lebanese Army fire on February 26, 1975 during the fishermen’s demonstration in Sidon. Died at mid-day March 6 at AUB Hospital. His funeral on March 7 produced the countrywide general strike, the Palestinian-Sunni political alignment, and the confessional framing that the Embassy now describes as the dominant political mode. Historians identify his death as the precipitating event of the chain of incidents that produced the Lebanese Civil War on April 13.

keyFigures.name: Rashid Solh
keyFigures.role: Prime Minister of Lebanon — publicly named by Higher Islamic Council
keyFigures.desc: Sunni Prime Minister, October 1974 to May 15, 1975. On March 6 the Higher Islamic Council publicly demanded his resignation, naming him personally alongside Frangieh and the Army leadership. For the Sunni religious establishment to withdraw its confidence from a sitting Sunni Prime Minister was unprecedented and politically terminal; his May 15 resignation was, in substance, written on March 6.

keyFigures.name: Suleiman Frangieh
keyFigures.role: President of Lebanon — publicly blamed by Higher Islamic Council
keyFigures.desc: Maronite Christian President. The Higher Islamic Council’s March 6 declaration named him first, blaming him for “the current state of affairs.” His refusal to consider army-command reform throughout the crisis was the specific grievance. His presidency would end in 1976 amid the civil war that began six weeks later.

keyFigures.name: Kamal Jumblatt
keyFigures.role: Druze paramount chief — the coalition was now his
keyFigures.desc: Founder of the Progressive Socialist Party and leading figure of the Lebanese left. The Sunni-leftist-Palestinian mobilization of March 6–7 — the general strike, the funeral procession, the Corniche Mazraa barricades — was the coalition Jumblatt would formally lead within weeks as head of the Lebanese National Movement. The ‘ticklish position’ of late February had resolved itself: he was now on the other side.

keyFigures.name: Yasser Arafat
keyFigures.role: PLO Chairman — evacuating offices under fear of Israeli reprisal
keyFigures.desc: Chairman of the PLO and head of Fatah. The Savoy Hotel attack of March 5 was executed by his own Fatah faction; his Beirut offices were evacuated within hours in anticipation of the expected Israeli reprisal. The simultaneity of the Savoy attack and Saad’s death produced exactly the political earthquake the rejectionists had sought to create a week earlier — except that the rejectionists had no hand in either event. The political consequences would shape the rest of the civil war.

keyFigures.name: Dwight J. Houghton
keyFigures.role: Deputy Chief of Mission, U.S. Embassy Beirut — signing these cables
keyFigures.desc: Career Arabist serving as DCM in Beirut through the 1973–1975 period. His name is on these cables, on the 1973 Melkart Protocol cables, and on the first Sidon-crisis reports. On March 7 he made the operational decision to send non-essential American Embassy staff home at 1030 local and to coordinate the same action with the British Embassy. Cables filed from March 12 onward in this series bear the signature of Ambassador G. McMurtrie Godley.

readerNarrative.bodyHtml:
The equilibrium of March 5

To understand what happened on March 6, 1975, it is necessary to understand what the Embassy believed was happening on March 5. Cable 03028’s opening paragraph describes a situation that had, after nine days of escalation, begun to stabilize.

The country-wide demonstrations in support of the Army and government on March 5 had gone off without serious violence. Christian political parties — principally the Kataeb and the NLP — had mobilized their street constituencies in defense of the state. The cabinet meeting that evening had produced the decision that the Solh government would continue in office. Malik Salam’s resignation had been absorbed; the first cabinet-level casualty of the crisis had not brought down the government. An agreement had been reached to refer Sunni-leftist demands for army-command reform to a cabinet study committee, to satisfy the Sidon fishermen economically, and to transfer the army’s southern district commander to “other posts” — a formula that addressed the Sunni complaint without conceding the structural issue of army command.

The Embassy’s characterization is precise: “thanks to a typically Lebanese solution in which no problems were really solved but were merely to be brushed under the rug for the time being.” The crisis had been managed, not resolved. The arrangement depended on nothing external disturbing it.

Two external disturbances arrived within fourteen hours.

The Savoy Hotel attack

On the night of March 5, 1975, eight Fatah fighters from the Black September Organization — operating under Fatah’s internal designation Force 17 — landed by rubber dinghy on the Tel Aviv seafront. They were led by Mohammed Yousef al-Najjar’s deputy and were briefed, according to Israeli reconstruction, to take as many civilian hostages as possible and exchange them for imprisoned Palestinian fighters.

They came ashore at the Savoy Hotel on HaYarkon Street, a beachfront tourist hotel in central Tel Aviv, and stormed the building. Eleven guests were taken hostage. Over the next ten hours, Israeli special forces from Sayeret Matkal assaulted the hotel; all but one of the attackers were killed, along with eight Israeli civilians and three Israeli soldiers. The attack was among the deadliest inside Israel in the history of the Palestinian armed struggle to that point.

The political problem the attack created for Lebanon was not the attack itself but the geography of its origins. The fighters had launched from Lebanese territory — standard practice by this point — and the probability that Israel would retaliate against Lebanon was approximately certain. The Lebanese state could calculate, as it had calculated after every Palestinian attack from Lebanese soil since 1968, that an Israeli reprisal would come; the question was scale and target. At a moment when the Sidon crisis had been contained but not resolved, an Israeli reprisal that required the Lebanese Army to respond would convert the containment into a regional war.

Saad’s death

At mid-day on March 6, 1975, Maarouf Saad died at American University Hospital in Beirut, eight days after he had been shot by Lebanese Army fire in the fishermen’s demonstration. The Embassy’s prediction of February 27 was validated.

The cable is precise in its wording: “News at mid-day March 6 of the death in AUB Hospital of ex-deputy Maarouf Saad (who had been wounded in Feb 26 clashes in Sidon).” The death is placed on a specific cable and a specific paragraph, connected to the Feb 26 cause by a direct reference. The cable does not need to editorialize: the connection between cause and effect is in the diplomatic record across the nine days.

The immediate operational response was swift. PLO offices in Beirut — the Fatah headquarters in Fakhani, the PFLP offices in Hamra, the DFLP offices, the Sa’iqa offices — were evacuated. Personnel and materials were moved from known political addresses into the refugee camps and distributed safe houses. This was the standard PLO response to an expected Israeli air or commando operation. Fedayeen went on full alert at the fifteen refugee camps. The country was posturing for an Israeli attack that it believed was coming within hours.

The cascade that the February 27 cable had predicted — mass demonstrations, general strike, paralysis of urban life — began within hours of the death being announced. Leftist and Sunni Muslim sympathizers, accompanied in many places by fedayeen, blocked roads, burned tires, fired weapons in the air. The barricades that had been dismantled in Sidon after the March 2 truce reappeared. In Beirut, the army’s internal security forces found themselves attempting to clear crowds from arteries they had never expected to be blocked — including the road to the airport.

Fire on the Lebanese planes

In the cascade of events on the morning of March 6, one small incident stands out as a miniature portrait of the crisis. Palestinian fighters at refugee camps north of Tripoli — the Beddawi and Nahr al-Bared camps, though the cable does not specify — opened fire on aircraft overflying their positions. The aircraft were in fact Lebanese Air Force, on routine operations. The fedayeen had assumed they were Israeli.

The incident reveals the posture of expectation. Palestinian fighters were operating, hours after Saad’s death and the news of the Savoy attack, in a state of readiness for immediate Israeli assault. The confusion of nationality — Lebanese aircraft assumed to be Israeli — is a symptom of the conditions under which people take cover first and identify later. It is also a signal of how far the operational coordination between the Lebanese state and the armed groups it nominally hosted had broken down. Lebanese Air Force aircraft could not fly over Lebanese territory without being mistaken for enemy aircraft by armed groups on that territory.

What the incident would have looked like if the fedayeen had been equipped with the SAM-7s reported in Sidon’s citadel is an exercise the reader may perform. No Lebanese pilot was hit; no Lebanese aircraft went down. But the underlying fact — that Palestinian fighters in Lebanese territory had the armament and the disposition to shoot down aircraft without identifying them — was one the Lebanese state could not ignore.

The Higher Islamic Council

On March 6, the Higher Islamic Council of the Lebanese Republic — the supreme body of the Sunni religious-political establishment, headed by the Grand Mufti — issued a public declaration demanding that the Solh cabinet resign. The declaration named three men as responsible for “the current state of affairs”: President Frangieh, the Army leadership, and Prime Minister Rashid Solh himself.

In Lebanese confessional politics, the Prime Minister’s office is reserved for a Sunni Muslim. Any Sunni Prime Minister governs with the consent — or at least the non-opposition — of the Sunni religious establishment. For the Higher Islamic Council to publicly demand the resignation of a sitting Sunni Prime Minister, and to name him by name, was an act of confessional abandonment. It meant that Solh’s own religious community had formally withdrawn its political confidence from him. No Sunni Prime Minister could govern without the Council behind him. The Council had moved.

Solh survived in office for another ten weeks. But his May 15 resignation was not a new event when it arrived; it was the formal acknowledgment of a political reality that had already taken shape on March 6. The Council’s declaration was the turning point at which the confessional framing of the Sidon crisis became institutional. From this point forward, the crisis was not about a fishing concession or an army operation; it was about the balance of confessional power in the Lebanese state.

March 7: a city under general strike

Cable 03064 is the Embassy’s late-morning report from March 7, filed from a city under general strike. “Right now Beirut is generally quiet as the result of a general strike,” the cable opens — but the sentence ends in its own qualification: “groups of men (some of them armed) can be observed at roadblocks scattered throughout the city.”

The strike was effective in the Sunni and mixed commercial districts. It was not observed in Christian commercial districts. The resulting geography was itself politically eloquent: the districts that closed and the districts that stayed open constituted, in real time, a map of the political coalition forming in response to Saad’s death. What the cable describes as “Beirut generally quiet” is a city in which half of commercial life has stopped and the other half has not, with the line between the two corresponding to the confessional fault lines of the country.

In the Corniche Mazraa area — adjacent to the Sabra and Shatila refugee camps and to the Fakhani PLO headquarters district — “armed fedayeen from nearby camps much in evidence.” This was not a discrete political demonstration; it was the practical deployment of fedayeen forces to hold a major Beirut artery against Lebanese state authority. The road to the airport was blocked by “milling demonstrators.” The road from the U.S. Embassy in Ain el-Mreisseh to the main hotel district in Ras Beirut was blocked. The Lebanese security authorities publicly urged all foreigners to stay off the streets — a measure that concedes, in the language of public-order announcements, that the authorities could not guarantee the safety of foreigners on the streets of the capital.

The Israeli sonic booms

The cable notes, in passing, that “several loud explosions (apparently sonic booms caused by overflying Israeli aircraft) were heard during the late morning hours.” In the spectrum of Israeli pressure signals, the sonic boom is a deliberate low-end demonstration: the aircraft are there, they are visible and audible, but they are not striking. The boom is political, not military.

The timing of the overflights was precise. They coincided with the morning of the Saad funeral and the general strike. They were Israeli signaling to the Lebanese government and to the Palestinian leadership simultaneously: Israel was watching, Israel had strike capability in the airspace, a decision could be taken at any moment. Together with the fedayeen firing on Lebanese planes the previous day in the mistaken belief that they were Israeli, the overflights produced a saturated airspace in which every party was calibrating to the same imminent possibility.

No Israeli attack on Lebanon came in those 24 hours. When Israeli retaliation for the Savoy Hotel attack finally materialized — in the form of Operation Marvad / the Mount Moussa raid on December 2, 1975 — it was nine months later, the civil war had been under way for six months, and the Lebanese state had already lost the capacity to respond that the Embassy feared would be forced on it. But on March 7, 1975, the possibility of immediate Israeli reprisal was part of the air over Beirut.

The Embassy closes

The final paragraph of cable 03064 is short and operationally specific. At 1030 local on March 7, the U.S. Embassy sent its non-essential American employees home with instructions to remain there for the remainder of the day. The British Embassy did the same. In diplomatic practice, a daytime protective drawdown of this kind is initiated only when the Chief of Mission judges the streets unsafe for routine Embassy circulation.

The measure was not an evacuation. It was not an emergency action. It was a calibrated protective response: keep the people we do not need out of the streets until the event (the Saad funeral and its aftermath) has passed. But the fact that the measure was judged necessary, and the fact that it was taken in coordination with the British, is the cleanest indicator in these cables of the Embassy’s actual real-time assessment of the threat level on the streets of Beirut on March 7, 1975.

The cable closes with the Embassy’s acknowledgment that the confessional turn had set in: “Events over the past nine days have tended increasingly to assume confessional overtones, with Sunni Muslims displaying growing and open dissatisfaction over what they regard as Christian monopolization of power within the GOL and the country at large.” And: “Christians, in return, have tended more and more to react hostilely to these pressures, attributing them to leftist and Palestinian ‘subversion’ and manipulation of the Sunni population.”

The framing was now in place. The civil war would begin five weeks and one day later, on April 13, 1975, when Phalange gunmen attacked a bus of Palestinian workers on their way home to the Tel al-Zaatar refugee camp in Ain al-Rummaneh. The fuse lit on February 26 in Sidon, confirmed by Saad’s death on March 6, institutionalized by the Higher Islamic Council’s declaration of the same day, and deployed on the streets of Beirut on March 7, had five weeks and one day left to burn.

cables.excerpt: Ambassador Godley’s SECRET/LIMDIS/NOFORN strategic assessment: Brigadier Kanaan reveals the Lebanese Army was 8:1 outnumbered in Sidon (100–150 troops vs over 1,000 fedayeen); identifies Abu Saleh (recently returned from East Berlin exile) as the fedayeen commander; alleges the PLO is playing a ‘double game’; names Soviet Ambassador Soldatov as the source of ‘scare stories’ fed to Arafat; warns that Israeli retaliation for the March 5 Savoy Hotel attack would force the Lebanese Army to respond or lose all credibility. Forwarded same-day to Kissinger’s Jerusalem shuttle via cable STATE 057899 (TOSEC 523). The March 12 cabinet compromise preserves the Solh government; the civil war begins four weeks later.

cables.annotatedBody:
Originally classified SECRET / LIMDIS / NOFORN · Declassified and released by U.S. Department of State · Now UNCLASSIFIED

Archival Note — Merged Entry

This is a merged archival entry combining the two companion SECRET/LIMDIS strategic-assessment cables that close the Sidon crisis diplomatic record, plus the State Department cable that forwarded the first of them to Secretary Kissinger during his Jerusalem shuttle. Cable 1975BEIRUT03203 (121845Z Mar 75) is Ambassador Godley’s retrospective assessment filed on the eve of the March 12 cabinet meeting, documenting for the first time Brigadier Kanaan’s intelligence briefing on the scale of the fedayeen deployment in Sidon (over 1,000 fighters versus 100–150 Army troops) and the identity of its commander (Abu Saleh, recently returned from East Berlin exile). Cable 1975BEIRUT03256 (140715Z Mar 75) is Godley’s follow-up two days later: the compromise has been achieved, Solh’s cabinet survives, and Kanaan has provided further revelations about the PLO’s “double game,” Soviet Ambassador Soldatov’s alleged role in feeding Arafat “scare stories,” and Sa’iqa’s participation despite Syrian denials. Cable 1975STATE057899 (14 Mar 75 2047Z, signed INGERSOLL) is the Department’s forwarding cable transmitting the full text of BEIRUT 3203 to Secretary Kissinger’s traveling party in Jerusalem — establishing as an administrative matter that Godley’s warning about Israeli retaliation was placed in front of the Secretary at the decision point regarding the Savoy Hotel reprisal.

Cable 1 of 3 — 1975BEIRUT03203 — 121845Z Mar 75

Subject: Recent Clashes in Sidon and Their Political Repercussions · SECRET / LIMDIS / NOFORN · Dept pass Secretary’s Party

Summary.
Political repercussions resulting from recent clashes between the Lebanese Army and “armed elements” (mostly fedayeen) in Sidon have dangerously aroused confessional feelings in Lebanon. While wiser heads among the country’s traditional political leaders are working hard to compose feelings among extremist elements in Moslem and Christian communities, the GOL has become further discredited in the eyes of a substantial portion of the Moslem population,[1] and the Lebanese Army’s ability to control the fedayeen — much less to act with the confidence and approval of most Lebanese — has been reduced significantly. In our view, any Israeli retaliation in the near future for the Mar 5 terrorist raid on Tel Aviv in light of the recent Army/civilian clashes would force the Lebanese Army to respond or lose all credibility with the Lebanese public.[2] End summary.

1.
The security situation in Beirut continues to improve in most visible respects since last weekend. Demonstrations and other street disturbances have largely ceased and the city has more or less resumed normal activity. In Sidon, however, the general strike enforced by leftist and fedayeen elements continues to prevail, and the town — while outwardly quiet — remains entirely under control of “armed elements” (mostly fedayeen) who seized key positions in and around Sidon Feb 26.[3]

2.
The local political scene however remains tense and unsettled, as Lebanon’s Sunni Moslem community, including virtually all its political leaders, continues to agitate strongly against the GOL and the Lebanese Army over what Sunnis insist was the latter’s unwarranted intervention in the troubles in Sidon. (This anti-GOL agitation has lately been joined by Shi’ite Imam Musa Sadr, who had remained curiously silent throughout most of last week’s troubles.)[4] Sunnis are also holding the GOL responsible for the death of Maarouf Saad (whom the Army believes was NOT repeat NOT killed by Army bullets)[5] and are decrying what they regard as generally anti-Moslem attitudes displayed at the highest levels of the Frangie regime. Sunni and leftist leaders have joined in demanding inter alia (A) that Army leadership be controlled by a “Command Council” that would ostensibly give non-Christians greater voice in determining military policies, (B) that the concession granted by the GOL to Chamoun’s “Protein” fishing company be revoked,[6] and (C) that the Army commander in Sidon (who is a Moslem) be replaced. Primin Solh has lost heavily in the crisis and would probably be forced to resign were it not that most responsible political leaders do not want a cabinet crisis under present conditions. Primin Solh, in response to above pressures, has evidently decided to adopt many Sunni-leftist demands as his own and to press for their fulfillment as the price of his continuance in office.[7]

3.
With the Council of Ministers meeting scheduled for this evening (Mar 12) and confessional feeling still running high, there has been considerable speculation that a cabinet split (along Christian-Moslem lines) over the above demands would cause the Solh govt to fall, leading to prolonged aggravation of the crisis and a Moslem “boycott” (i.e., by passive and perhaps not-so-passive resistance) of the Frangie regime altogether. Fortunately, however, moderate leaders on both sides have remained in close touch with one another throughout the crisis, attempting to resolve matters by traditional Lebanese means of compromise and conciliation and to restrain their more extreme associates and followers from exacerbating tensions further. Over the past 24 hours, these efforts seem to have borne fruit. The prospect at this writing is that Christian cabinet ministers and Pres Frangie will agree to accept Sunni-leftist demands for “study” by a special ministerial commission[8] and that Primin Solh, together with his Jumblattist and Sunni colleagues in the cabinet, will hold on to their portfolios at least for the time being.

4. Comment.
The confused and emotion-ridden situation described above represents probably one of the more serious surges of confessional feeling in recent years.[9] A contributing factor, of course, can be found in widespread uncertainty and uneasiness experienced by Lebanese and Palestinians alike over the future course of the ME settlement effort and what it spells for them. Another source of current instability, however, doubtless stems from growing Moslem disgruntlement over the Frangie regime’s increasing insensitivity to Moslem interests and aspirations in the conduct of governmental affairs. Events of the past two weeks in Sidon and Beirut have given leftist (especially communist and Baathist) elements an unusually golden opportunity to play on latent Sunni feelings in this regard, supplementing their ongoing efforts to derive advantage from general popular discontent stemming from the GOL’s abysmal neglect of pressing economic and social problems.[10] Given the present highly-charged state of Sunni feelings and the ugly Christian backlash which Sunni agitation has evoked, they appear to have made the most of this opportunity.

5.
Even more mischievous role has been played by the fedayeen. Fedayeen participation in the Sidon clashes and in the widespread anti-GOL demonstrations that followed certainly equalled, and probably surpassed, the leftist role in polarizing confessional feeling over the past week. A reliable Lebanese Army source (Deputy COS for Operations Brig Kanaan)[11] confirms our initial suspicion (Beirut 2611) that “leftist” fedayeen elements (not only from “rejectionist” groups but also elements from Sa’iqa and Fatah as well) at least took advantage of the Sidon affair from the very start, although he claims that other fedayeen units — and not just “militia” from nearby camps — quickly joined in, with overall command being assumed by Fatah’s “leftist” military leader Abu Saleh (recently returned from exile in East Berlin).[12] The result was that the Lebanese Army, when it attempted with only 100-150 troops to force open the main coastal road at Sidon on the evening of Mar 1 (Beirut 2837), found itself opposed by over 1,000 fedayeen firing machine-guns, RPG rockets and recoilless rifles from rooftops and other fortified positions in and around Sidon’s Old City.[13] (Kanaan says that the Army killed some 25-30 fedayeen during this fighting and that the Army’s own losses would have been heavier had its troops not been using armored personnel carriers).

6.
Given deep concern among responsible members of the Moslem and Christian communities that the crisis might degenerate into serious confessional strife, the chances are that the government will contain the crisis and the Solh cabinet will remain in office for the time being. The Army, however, has unfortunately become the subject of confessional controversy, has been hurt by the crisis, and its ability (already limited) to control the fedayeen sorely weakened.[14] Many Lebanese of both faiths, probably correctly, consider the crisis might have been avoided but for the entry of the Army into Sidon. Some, unfairly, blame the Army for action ordered by the civilian GOL leadership. Given these special circumstances, Israeli retaliation against Lebanon in the near future for the Mar 5 terrorist raid on Tel Aviv would place the GOL in an impossible position vis-à-vis many of its own citizens, as well as the fedayeen, if it does not order the Army to respond.

7.
Although we can well understand and sympathize with the depth of Israeli feeling against the fedayeen which has resulted from the Mar 5 raid and may be prompting the GOI to reply in kind, we hope Israeli leadership will think long and hard before undertaking action which could threaten the integrity of the present Lebanese regime and would almost certainly force the Lebanese Army (against its will but of necessity — i.e., to avoid being classed as traitors in Sunni, leftist and fedayeen eyes after “having killed brother Arabs” in Sidon) to respond energetically to any Israeli action.[15]

GODLEY

Note by OC/T: Not passed Secretary’s party.

Cable 2 of 3 — 1975BEIRUT03256 — 140715Z Mar 75

Subject: Security Situation in Lebanon · SECRET / LIMDIS / NOFORN · Ref: BEIRUT 3203

Summary.
The compromise solution foreseen reftel between the GOL and Sunni-leftist leaders who have been agitating fiercely over recent events in Sidon was agreed upon in the Council of Ministers meeting Mar 12. We expect this will help confessional animosities to subside and enable the Solh cabinet to continue in office, at least for the time being. End summary.

1.
As foreseen reftel, the Lebanese Council of Ministers Mar 12 agreed to refer the Sunni-leftist demands for reorganization of the Army command to a special cabinet committee for study.[16] At the same time, the cabinet charged Economy Min Abbas Khalaf with satisfying the demands of Sidon’s fishermen, and Pres Frangie and Primin Solh reportedly have decided to transfer the commander of the Army’s Southern District and his intelligence officer to “other posts”.[17] As a result of these steps, the Solh cabinet will continue in office, confessional tensions will probably be eased somewhat, and there is speculation that the general strike still in progress in Sidon will soon be called off by the “armed elements” who control that city.

2.
Re the situation in Sidon, further details provided by the Lebanese Army (Brig Kanaan) on the role played by the fedayeen during the past two weeks are particularly revealing. Kanaan states that although PLO’s Abu Za’im and Abu Hassan — acting on orders from ’Arafat and Fatah’s Abu Jihad — attempted to assist GOL officials in “negotiating” with Abu Saleh and other “armed elements” in Sidon, their efforts have not been particularly successful.[18] (Kanaan tends to believe, despite the fact that the Army picked up Fatah radio communications urging Abu Saleh and his associates to cooperate with GOL, that PLO leadership has been playing a double game — i.e., pretending to cooperate with GOL while privately doing little or nothing to reduce fedayeen occupation of Sidon.[19] He thinks that ’Arafat, having been filled full of scare stories re an impending Lebanese Army attempt to “liquidate” the fedayeen presence by Soviet officials — including Amb Soldatov — in recent weeks, was anxious to see the Army’s ability to confront the fedayeen further circumscribed by the Sidon clashes and the confessional/political turmoil that he expected would ensue from them.)[20]

3.
According to Kanaan, the GOL and Army leadership never entertained any intention of “smashing” the fedayeen in Sidon, since they knew full well that such a move would provoke an all-out confrontation with the fedayeen and their Lebanese sympathizers throughout the country. Nevertheless, the latter were quick to portray the Army’s Mar 1 action as an initial GOL step to provoke just such a confrontation, thereby successfully polarizing and inflaming Sunni-Christian passions further — so successfully, in fact, that many Sunnis in Sidon have been openly referring to the fedayeen as “our Army”, while Christian groups have been demonstrating in support of “our (Lebanese) Army”.[21]

4.
One murky aspect in all the foregoing is the role played by Syria.[22] We note reports in other channels that SARG had counselled Sa’iqa forces in Lebanon to withdraw from the Sidon area and avoid trouble with the Lebanese Army. We note other reports in the same channels, however, that Sa’iqa leaders Zohayr and Majid Muhsen were not overly careful to comply with these instructions,[23] and Kanaan categorically insists that Sa’iqa elements took part in the clashes in and occupation of Sidon. (Both PLO and Sa’iqa units played a highly visible role in the Mar 7 funeral procession for Maarouf Saad in Sidon.) Kanaan suspects, but cannot prove or figure out precisely why, the SARG may also have encouraged the Sidon clashes in order to foment wider disturbances in Lebanon.[24]

5. Comment.
Although some degree of normal life may return to Sidon as Lebanese confessional and political tensions subside, the fedayeen from reports appear to be showing some reluctance to allow that city to revert to full GOL control.[25] As noted reftel, the Lebanese Army’s ability to correct this situation has been significantly diminished by the events of the past two weeks.

GODLEY

Cable 3 of 3 — 1975STATE057899 — 14 Mar 75 2047Z (forwarding cable)

From Acting Secretary Ingersoll to Kissinger’s shuttle party via Jerusalem · SECRET / LIMDIS / TOSEC 523 · Repeat of BEIRUT 3203

Editorial note — forwarding cable

Cable STATE 057899, signed by Acting Secretary Robert S. Ingersoll, is an administrative repeat: it transmits the full verbatim text of BEIRUT 3203 — Godley’s strategic assessment with the warning about Israeli retaliation — to Secretary Kissinger’s traveling party via the U.S. Consulate in Jerusalem. The reference line “TOSEC 523” is the administrative indicator that the cable is being delivered to the Secretary’s party (sequence number 523 in the series of cables sent to the Secretary during his travels). Kissinger was in Israel March 12–14 conducting shuttle diplomacy on what would become the collapsed second Sinai interim agreement; his shuttle collapsed on March 22 over Israeli refusal to accept partial withdrawal from the Mitla and Giddi passes. The forwarding establishes as an administrative matter that Godley’s Sidon assessment — including its operative conclusion that an Israeli reprisal for the Savoy Hotel attack would collapse the Lebanese regime — was placed before the Secretary at the active decision point regarding the Savoy Hotel reprisal. No Israeli reprisal materialized in the March window; the eventual Israeli response (Operation Marvad / Mount Moussa raid) came on December 2, 1975, by which point the Lebanese civil war had been under way for eight months and the concerns Godley had raised had largely been overtaken by events.[26]

[The verbatim text inside the quotation marks of STATE 057899 is identical to the text of BEIRUT 3203 above and is not repeated here to avoid duplication.]

INGERSOLL

CABLE 1 OF 3: 1975BEIRUT03203 — 121845Z MAR 75
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

S E C R E T BEIRUT 3203 LIMDIS/NOFORN

FM AMEMBASSY BEIRUT
TO SECSTATE WASHDC PRIORITY 3334, DIA WASHDC PRIORITY
INFO AMEMBASSY AMMAN, AMEMBASSY CAIRO, AMEMBASSY DAMASCUS,
     AMCONSUL JERUSALEM, AMEMBASSY JIDDA, AMEMBASSY KUWAIT,
     AMEMBASSY TEL AVIV, USINT BAGHDAD, USCINCEUR

DEPT PASS SECRETARY'S PARTY
E.O. 11652: GDS
TAGS: PINS PGOV LE
SUBJECT: RECENT CLASHES IN SIDON AND THEIR POLITICAL REPERCUSSIONS

SUMMARY: POLITICAL REPERCUSSIONS RESULTING FROM RECENT CLASHES BETWEEN
LEBANESE ARMY AND "ARMED ELEMENTS" (MOSTLY FEDAYEEN) IN SIDON HAVE
DANGEROUSLY AROUSED CONFESSIONAL FEELINGS IN LEBANON. WHILE WISER HEADS
AMONG COUNTRY'S TRADITIONAL POLITICAL LEADERS ARE WORKING HARD TO COMPOSE
FEELINGS AMONG EXTREMIST ELEMENTS IN MOSLEM AND CHRISTIAN COMMUNITIES,
GOL HAS BECOME FURTHER DISCREDITED IN EYES OF SUBSTANTIAL PORTION OF
MOSLEM POPULATION, AND LEBANESE ARMY'S ABILITY TO CONTROL FEDAYEEN --
MUCH LESS TO ACT WITH CONFIDENCE AND APPROVAL OF MOST LEBANESE -- HAS
BEEN REDUCED SIGNIFICANTLY. IN OUR VIEW, ANY ISRAELI RETALIATION IN NEAR
FUTURE FOR MAR 5 TERRORIST RAID ON TEL AVIV IN LIGHT RECENT ARMY/CIVILIAN
CLASHES WOULD FORCE LEBANESE ARMY TO RESPOND OR LOSE ALL CREDIBILITY WITH
LEBANESE PUBLIC. END SUMMARY

1. SECURITY SITUATION IN BEIRUT CONTINUES TO IMPROVE IN MOST VISIBLE
RESPECTS SINCE LAST WEEKEND. DEMONSTRATIONS AND OTHER STREET DISTURBANCES
HAVE LARGELY CEASED AND CITY HAS MORE OR LESS RESUMED NORMAL ACTIVITY.
IN SIDON, HOWEVER, GENERAL STRIKE ENFORCED BY LEFTIST AND FEDAYEEN
ELEMENTS CONTINUES TO PREVAIL, AND TOWN -- WHILE OUTWARDLY QUIET --
REMAINS ENTIRELY UNDER CONTROL OF "ARMED ELEMENTS" (MOSTLY FEDAYEEN) WHO
SEIZED KEY POSITIONS IN AND AROUND SIDON FEB 26.

2. LOCAL POLITICAL SCENE HOWEVER REMAINS TENSE AND UNSETTLED, AS
LEBANON'S SUNNI MOSLEM COMMUNITY, INCLUDING VIRTUALLY ALL ITS POLITICAL
LEADERS, CONTINUES TO AGITATE STRONGLY AGAINST GOL AND LEBANESE ARMY OVER
WHAT SUNNIS INSIST WAS LATTER'S UNWARRANTED INTERVENTION IN TROUBLES IN
SIDON. (THIS ANTI-GOL AGITATION HAS LATELY BEEN JOINED BY SHI'ITE IMAM
MUSA SADR, WHO HAD REMAINED CURIOUSLY SILENT THROUGHOUT MOST OF LAST
WEEK'S TROUBLES.) SUNNIS ARE ALSO HOLDING GOL RESPONSIBLE FOR DEATH OF
MAAROUF SAAD (WHOM ARMY BELIEVES WAS NOT RPT NOT KILLED BY ARMY BULLETS)
AND ARE DECRYING WHAT THEY REGARD AS GENERALLY ANTI-MOSLEM ATTITUDES
DISPLAYED AT HIGHEST LEVELS OF FRANGIE REGIME. SUNNI AND LEFTIST LEADERS
HAVE JOINED IN DEMANDING INTER ALIA (A) THAT ARMY LEADERSHIP BE
CONTROLLED BY "COMMAND COUNCIL" THAT WOULD OSTENSIBLY GIVE NON-CHRISTIANS
GREATER VOICE IN DETERMINING MILITARY POLICIES, (B) THAT CONCESSION
GRANTED BY GOL TO CHAMOUN'S "PROTEIN" FISHING COMPANY BE REVOKED, AND (C)
THAT ARMY COMMANDER IN SIDON (WHO IS A MOSLEM) BE REPLACED. PRIMIN SOLH
HAS LOST HEAVILY IN CRISIS AND WOULD PROBABLY BE FORCED RESIGN WERE IT
NOT THAT MOST RESPONSIBLE POLITICAL LEADERS DO NOT WANT CABINET CRISIS
UNDER PRESENT CONDITIONS. PRIMIN SOLH, IN RESPONSE TO ABOVE PRESSURES,
HAS EVIDENTLY DECIDED TO ADOPT MANY SUNNI-LEFTIST DEMANDS AS HIS OWN AND
TO PRESS FOR THEIR FULFILLMENT AS PRICE OF HIS CONTINUANCE IN OFFICE.

3. WITH COUNCIL OF MINISTERS MEETING SCHEDULED FOR THIS EVENING (MAR 12)
AND CONFESSIONAL FEELING STILL RUNNING HIGH, THERE HAS BEEN CONSIDERABLE
SPECULATION THAT CABINET SPLIT (ALONG CHRISTIAN-MOSLEM LINES) OVER ABOVE
DEMANDS WOULD CAUSE SOLH GOVT TO FALL, LEADING TO PROLONGED AGGRAVATION
OF CRISIS AND MOSLEM "BOYCOTT" (I.E., BY PASSIVE AND PERHAPS
NOT-SO-PASSIVE RESISTANCE) OF FRANGIE REGIME ALTOGETHER. FORTUNATELY,
HOWEVER, MODERATE LEADERS ON BOTH SIDES HAVE REMAINED IN CLOSE TOUCH WITH
ONE ANOTHER THROUGHOUT CRISIS, ATTEMPTING TO RESOLVE MATTERS BY
TRADITIONAL LEBANESE MEANS OF COMPROMISE AND CONCILIATION AND TO RESTRAIN
THEIR MORE EXTREME ASSOCIATES AND FOLLOWERS FROM EXACERBATING TENSIONS
FURTHER. OVER PAST 24 HOURS, THESE EFFORTS SEEM TO HAVE BORNE FRUIT.
PROSPECT AT THIS WRITING IS THAT CHRISTIAN CABINET MINISTERS AND PRES
FRANGIE WILL AGREE TO ACCEPT SUNNI-LEFTIST DEMANDS FOR "STUDY" BY SPECIAL
MINISTERIAL COMMISSION AND THAT PRIMIN SOLH, TOGETHER WITH HIS
JUMBLATTIST AND SUNNI COLLEAGUES IN CABINET, WILL HOLD ON TO THEIR
PORTFOLIOS AT LEAST FOR TIME BEING.

4. COMMENT: CONFUSED AND EMOTION-RIDDEN SITUATION DESCRIBED ABOVE
REPRESENTS PROBABLY ONE OF MORE SERIOUS SURGES OF CONFESSIONAL FEELING
IN RECENT YEARS. CONTRIBUTING FACTOR, OF COURSE, CAN BE FOUND IN
WIDESPREAD UNCERTAINTY AND UNEASINESS EXPERIENCED BY LEBANESE AND
PALESTINIANS ALIKE OVER FUTURE COURSE OF ME SETTLEMENT EFFORT AND WHAT
IT SPELLS FOR THEM. ANOTHER SOURCE OF CURRENT INSTABILITY, HOWEVER,
DOUBTLESS STEMS FROM GROWING MOSLEM DISGRUNTLEMENT OVER FRANGIE REGIME'S
INCREASING INSENSITIVITY TO MOSLEM INTERESTS AND ASPIRATIONS IN CONDUCT
OF GOVERNMENTAL AFFAIRS. EVENTS OF PAST TWO WEEKS IN SIDON AND BEIRUT
HAVE GIVEN LEFTIST (ESPECIALLY COMMUNIST AND BAATHIST) ELEMENTS AN
UNUSUALLY GOLDEN OPPORTUNITY TO PLAY ON LATENT SUNNI FEELINGS IN THIS
REGARD, SUPPLEMENTING THEIR ONGOING EFFORTS TO DERIVE ADVANTAGE FROM
GENERAL POPULAR DISCONTENT STEMMING FROM GOL'S ABYSMAL NEGLECT OF
PRESSING ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL PROBLEMS. GIVEN PRESENT HIGHLY-CHARGED
STATE OF SUNNI FEELINGS AND UGLY CHRISTIAN BACKLASH, WHICH SUNNI
AGITATION HAS EVOKED, THEY APPEAR TO HAVE MADE THE MOST OF THIS
OPPORTUNITY.

5. EVEN MORE MISCHIEVOUS ROLE HAS BEEN PLAYED BY FEDAYEEN. FEDAYEEN
PARTICIPATION IN SIDON CLASHES AND IN WIDESPREAD ANTI-GOL DEMONSTRATIONS
THAT FOLLOWED WAS FACTOR WHICH CERTAINLY EQUALLED, AND PROBABLY
SURPASSED, LEFTIST ROLE IN POLARIZING CONFESSIONAL FEELING OVER PAST
WEEK. RELIABLE LEBANESE ARMY SOURCE (DEPUTY COS FOR OPERATIONS BRIG
KANAAN) CONFIRMS OUR INITIAL SUSPICION (BEIRUT 2611) THAT "LEFTIST"
FEDAYEEN ELEMENTS (NOT ONLY FROM "REJECTIONIST" GROUPS BUT ALSO ELEMENTS
FROM SA'IQA AND FATAH AS WELL) AT LEAST TOOK ADVANTAGE OF SIDON AFFAIR
FROM VERY START, ALTHOUGH HE CLAIMS THAT OTHER FEDAYEEN UNITS -- AND NOT
JUST "MILITIA" FROM NEARBY CAMPS -- QUICKLY JOINED IN, WITH OVERALL
COMMAND BEING ASSUMED BY FATAH'S "LEFTIST" MILITARY LEADER ABU SALEH
(RECENTLY RETURNED FROM EXILE IN EAST BERLIN). RESULT WAS THAT LEBANESE
ARMY, WHEN IT ATTEMPTED WITH ONLY 100-150 TROOPS TO FORCE OPEN MAIN
COASTAL ROAD AT SIDON ON EVENING MAR 1 (BEIRUT 2837), FOUND ITSELF
OPPOSED BY OVER 1,000 FEDAYEEN FIRING MACHINE-GUNS, RPG ROCKETS AND
RECOILLESS RIFLES FROM ROOFTOPS AND OTHER FORTIFIED POSITIONS IN AND
AROUND SIDON'S OLD CITY. (KANAAN SAYS THAT ARMY KILLED SOME 25-30
FEDAYEEN DURING THIS FIGHTING AND THAT ARMY'S OWN LOSSES WOULD HAVE BEEN
HEAVIER HAD ITS TROOPS NOT BEEN USING ARMORED PERSONNEL CARRIERS).

6. GIVEN DEEP CONCERN AMONG RESPONSIBLE MEMBERS MOSLEM AND CHRISTIAN
COMMUNITIES THAT CRISIS MIGHT DEGENERATE INTO SERIOUS CONFESSIONAL
STRIFE, CHANCES ARE GOVERNMENT WILL CONTAIN CRISIS AND SOLH CABINET WILL
REMAIN IN OFFICE FOR TIME BEING. ARMY, HOWEVER, HAS UNFORTUNATELY BECOME
SUBJECT OF CONFESSIONAL CONTROVERSY, HAS BEEN HURT BY CRISIS AND ITS
ABILITY (ALREADY LIMITED) TO CONTROL FEDAYEEN SORELY WEAKENED. MANY
LEBANESE OF BOTH FAITHS, PROBABLY CORRECTLY, CONSIDER CRISIS MIGHT HAVE
BEEN AVOIDED BUT FOR ENTRY OF ARMY INTO SIDON. SOME, UNFAIRLY, BLAME
ARMY FOR ACTION ORDERED BY CIVILIAN GOL LEADERSHIP. GIVEN THESE SPECIAL
CIRCUMSTANCES, ISRAELI RETALIATION AGAINST LEBANON IN NEAR FUTURE FOR
MAR 5 TERRORIST RAID ON TEL AVIV WOULD PLACE GOL IN IMPOSSIBLE POSITION
VIS-A-VIS MANY OF ITS OWN CITIZENS, AS WELL AS FEDAYEEN, IF IT DOES NOT
ORDER ARMY TO RESPOND.

7. ALTHOUGH WE CAN WELL UNDERSTAND AND SYMPATHIZE WITH DEPTH ISRAELI
FEELING AGAINST FEDAYEEN WHICH HAS RESULTED FROM MAR 5 RAID AND MAY BE
PROMPTING GOI TO REPLY IN KIND, WE HOPE ISRAELI LEADERSHIP WILL THINK
LONG AND HARD BEFORE UNDERTAKING ACTION WHICH COULD THREATEN INTEGRITY
PRESENT LEBANESE REGIME AND WOULD ALMOST CERTAINLY FORCE LEBANESE ARMY
(AGAINST ITS WILL BUT OF NECESSITY -- I.E., TO AVOID BEING CLASSED AS
TRAITORS IN SUNNI, LEFTIST AND FEDAYEEN EYES AFTER "HAVING KILLED
BROTHER ARABS" IN SIDON) TO RESPOND ENERGETICALLY TO ANY ISRAELI ACTION.

GODLEY

NOTE BY OC/T: NOT PASSED SECRETARY'S PARTY.

S E C R E T BEIRUT 3256 LIMDIS NOFORN

FM AMEMBASSY BEIRUT
TO SECSTATE WASHDC 3358, DIA
INFO AMEMBASSY AMMAN, AMEMBASSY CAIRO, AMEMBASSY DAMASCUS,
     AMCONSUL JERUSALEM, AMEMBASSY JIDDA, AMEMBASSY KUWAIT,
     AMEMBASSY TEL AVIV, USCINCEUR, USINT BAGHDAD

E.O. 11652: GDS
TAGS: PINS PGOV LE
SUBJECT: SECURITY SITUATION IN LEBANON
REF: BEIRUT 3203

SUMMARY: COMPROMISE SOLUTION FORESEEN REFTEL BETWEEN GOL AND
SUNNI-LEFTIST LEADERS WHO HAVE BEEN AGITATING FIERCELY OVER RECENT
EVENTS IN SIDON WAS AGREED UPON IN COUNCIL OF MINISTERS MEETING MAR 12.
WE EXPECT THIS WILL HELP CONFESSIONAL ANIMOSITIES TO SUBSIDE AND ENABLE
SOLH CABINET TO CONTINUE IN OFFICE, AT LEAST FOR TIME BEING. END
SUMMARY.

1. AS FORESEEN REFTEL, LEBANESE COUNCIL OF MINISTERS MAR 12 AGREED TO
REFER SUNNI-LEFTIST DEMANDS FOR REORGANIZATION OF ARMY COMMAND TO
SPECIAL CABINET COMMITTEE FOR STUDY. AT SAME TIME, CABINET CHARGED
ECONOMY MIN ABBAS KHALAF WITH SATISFYING DEMANDS OF SIDON'S FISHERMEN,
AND PRES FRANGIE AND PRIMIN SOLH REPORTEDLY HAVE DECIDED TO TRANSFER
COMMANDER OF ARMY'S SOUTHERN DISTRICT AND HIS INTELLIGENCE OFFICER TO
"OTHER POSTS". AS RESULT OF THESE STEPS, SOLH CABINET WILL CONTINUE IN
OFFICE, CONFESSIONAL TENSIONS WILL PROBABLY BE EASED SOMEWHAT, AND THERE
IS SPECULATION THAT GENERAL STRIKE STILL IN PROGRESS IN SIDON WILL SOON
BE CALLED OFF BY "ARMED ELEMENTS" WHO CONTROL THAT CITY.

2. RE SITUATION IN SIDON, FURTHER DETAILS PROVIDED BY LEBANESE ARMY
(BRIG KANAAN) ON ROLE PLAYED BY FEDAYEEN DURING PAST TWO WEEKS ARE
PARTICULARLY REVEALING. KANAAN STATES THAT ALTHOUGH PLO'S ABU ZA'IM AND
ABU HASSAN -- ACTING ON ORDERS FROM 'ARAFAT AND FATAH'S ABU JIHAD --
ATTEMPTED TO ASSIST GOL OFFICIALS IN "NEGOTIATING" WITH ABU SALEH AND
OTHER "ARMED ELEMENTS" IN SIDON, THEIR EFFORTS HAVE NOT BEEN
PARTICULARLY SUCCESSFUL. (KANAAN TENDS BELIEVE, DESPITE FACT THAT ARMY
PICKED UP FATAH RADIO COMMUNICATIONS URGING ABU SALEH AND HIS
ASSOCIATES TO COOPERATE WITH GOL, THAT PLO LEADERSHIP HAS BEEN PLAYING
DOUBLE GAME -- I.E., PRETENDING TO COOPERATE WITH GOL WHILE PRIVATELY
DOING LITTLE OR NOTHING TO REDUCE FEDAYEEN OCCUPATION OF SIDON. HE
THINKS THAT 'ARAFAT, HAVING BEEN FILLED FULL OF SCARE STORIES RE AN
IMPENDING LEBANESE ARMY ATTEMPT TO "LIQUIDATE" FEDAYEEN PRESENCE BY
SOVIET OFFICIALS -- INCLUDING AMB SOLDATOV -- IN RECENT WEEKS, WAS
ANXIOUS TO SEE ARMY'S ABILITY TO CONFRONT FEDAYEEN FURTHER CIRCUMSCRIBED
BY SIDON CLASHES AND CONFESSIONAL/POLITICAL TURMOIL THAT HE EXPECTED
WOULD ENSUE FROM THEM.

3. ACCORDING TO KANAAN, GOL AND ARMY LEADERSHIP NEVER ENTERTAINED ANY
INTENTION OF "SMASHING" FEDAYEEN IN SIDON, SINCE THEY KNEW FULL WELL
THAT SUCH MOVE WOULD PROVOKE ALL-OUT CONFRONTATION WITH FEDAYEEN AND
THEIR LEBANESE SYMPATHIZERS THROUGHOUT THE COUNTRY. NEVERTHELESS, LATTER
WERE QUICK TO PORTRAY ARMY'S MAR 1 ACTION AS INITIAL GOL STEP TO PROVOKE
JUST SUCH A CONFRONTATION, THEREBY SUCCESSFULLY POLARIZING AND INFLAMING
SUNNI-CHRISTIAN PASSIONS FURTHER -- SO SUCCESSFULLY, IN FACT, THAT MANY
SUNNIS IN SIDON HAVE BEEN OPENLY REFERRING TO FEDAYEEN AS "OUR ARMY",
WHILE CHRISTIAN GROUPS HAVE BEEN DEMONSTRATING IN SUPPORT OF "OUR
(LEBANESE) ARMY".

4. ONE MURKY ASPECT IN ALL THE FOREGOING IS ROLE PLAYED BY SYRIA. WE
NOTE REPORTS IN OTHER CHANNELS THAT SARG HAD COUNSELLED SA'IQA FORCES IN
LEBANON TO WITHDRAW FROM SIDON AREA AND AVOID TROUBLE WITH LEBANESE
ARMY. WE NOTE OTHER REPORTS IN SAME CHANNELS, HOWEVER, THAT SA'IQA
LEADERS ZOHAYR AND MAJID MUHSEN WERE NOT OVERLY CAREFUL TO COMPLY WITH
THESE INSTRUCTIONS, AND KANAAN CATEGORICALLY INSISTS THAT SA'IQA
ELEMENTS TOOK PART IN CLASHES IN AND OCCUPATION OF SIDON. (BOTH PLO AND
SA'IQA UNITS PLAYED HIGHLY VISIBLE ROLE IN MAR 7 FUNERAL PROCESSION FOR
MAAROUF SAAD IN SIDON.) KANAAN SUSPECTS, BUT CANNOT PROVE OR FIGURE OUT
PRECISELY WHY, SARG MAY ALSO HAVE ENCOURAGED SIDON CLASHES IN ORDER TO
FOMENT WIDER DISTURBANCES IN LEBANON.

5. COMMENT: ALTHOUGH SOME DEGREE OF NORMAL LIFE MAY RETURN TO SIDON AS
LEBANESE CONFESSIONAL AND POLITICAL TENSIONS SUBSIDE, FEDAYEEN FROM
REPORTS APPEAR TO BE SHOWING SOME RELUCTANCE TO ALLOW THAT CITY TO
REVERT TO FULL GOL CONTROL. AS NOTED REFTEL, LEBANESE ARMY'S ABILITY TO
CORRECT THIS SITUATION HAS BEEN SIGNIFICANTLY DIMINISHED BY EVENTS OF
PAST TWO WEEKS.

GODLEY

CABLE 3 OF 3: 1975STATE057899 — 14 MAR 75 2047Z (forwarding cable)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

S E C R E T STATE 057899 LIMDIS; TOSEC 523

FM SECSTATE WASHDC
TO SECRETARY'S PARTY (via AMCONSUL JERUSALEM)

DRAFTED BY NEA/ARN:PKBULLEN:GCB
APPROVED BY NEA/ARN:PKBULLEN
DISTRIBUTION: NSC/E; S/S

FOL REPEAT BEIRUT 3203
SENT ACTION SECSTATE DIA
INFO AMMAN CAIRO DAMASCUS JERUSALEM JIDDA KUWAIT TEL AVIV BAGHDAD USCINCEUR
MAR 12 QTE

[NOTE BY OC/T: the body of this cable is the verbatim text of BEIRUT 3203 above, being relayed by the Department to Secretary Kissinger's traveling party. Kissinger was in Israel March 12–14 conducting shuttle negotiations on what would become the collapsed second Sinai interim agreement. The forwarding of a SECRET/LIMDIS assessment of the Sidon crisis to the Secretary's active shuttle in Jerusalem is the administrative record that Godley's Sidon assessment — including its operative conclusion that Israeli retaliation would collapse the Lebanese regime — was placed in front of the Secretary at the active decision point regarding Israeli retaliation for the Savoy Hotel attack.]

UNQUOTE

INGERSOLL

[Note: Robert S. Ingersoll, Acting Secretary of State during Kissinger's travel absence, signs the forwarding cable.]
footnotes: The Embassy’s judgment of “further discredited”: By March 12, Ambassador Godley had concluded that the Sidon crisis had produced a measurable decline in the Frangieh regime’s political standing within the Sunni community. The word “further” is diagnostic: the regime had not started from a strong baseline. The Higher Islamic Council’s March 6 demand for the cabinet’s resignation (cable 1975BEIRUT03064) had formalized the Sunni religious establishment’s withdrawal of confidence from Prime Minister Solh. Six days later, Godley is stating the political fact: the Sunni community’s political alienation from the Frangieh government had become structural.

The core warning of cable 03203: The operational finding of the cable is that any Israeli retaliation against Lebanon in the near future would force the Lebanese Army to respond. Godley’s logic: if the Army did not respond to an Israeli reprisal, it would be branded as traitors in Sunni, leftist, and fedayeen eyes after “having killed brother Arabs” in Sidon. The Army, already confessionally polarized by Sidon, could not afford further politically-fatal inaction. An Israeli reprisal would therefore drag Lebanon into direct conflict with Israel at a moment when the state lacked the political consensus to sustain such a conflict. The cable was forwarded to Kissinger’s shuttle in Jerusalem the same day by State cable 057899, establishing that the warning reached the Secretary at the active decision window on Israeli reprisal for the Savoy Hotel attack.

Sidon remained under fedayeen control March 12: Two weeks after February 26, Sidon was still occupied by the armed elements that had taken position on February 26. The Lebanese Army had tried to re-enter on March 1, had been ambushed (cable 1975BEIRUT02837), and had not returned. The March 2 truce had given the armed groups effective possession of the city. The general strike continued. The town was quiet only in the sense that no fighting was in progress; it was not under state authority. This is the starting fact of the cable: a Lebanese provincial capital had been outside state control for two weeks, and the state had not yet found a way to reassert itself.

Musa Sadr joins the agitation: Imam Musa al-Sadr — founder of the Movement of the Deprived (1974), Iranian-born Shia cleric, and the principal political organizer of Lebanon’s Shia community — had been conspicuously silent during the first two weeks of the Sidon crisis. The Embassy registers his silence in the parenthetical “curiously silent”. His public alignment with the Sunni-leftist agitation around March 10–11 marked the entry of the organized Shia community into the anti-Frangieh opposition. The political significance is considerable: the Shia had been broadly absent from the Sunni-Palestinian alignment until Sadr moved them. The Amal Movement would be publicly named four months later, in July 1975. In the chronology of Lebanese Shia political mobilization, Sadr’s March 1975 entry into the Sidon agitation is a step along the path from the Movement of the Deprived to Amal to the armed Shia political power of the later civil war.

The Army’s denial that it killed Saad: The parenthetical “whom the Army believes was NOT repeat NOT killed by Army bullets” is the Lebanese Army’s formal counter-narrative to what had by March 12 become a national Sunni political charge. The Army’s position was that Saad was shot by a fedayeen bullet, possibly deliberately, in order to produce exactly the political escalation that had followed. The position had political utility but had not persuaded Sunni opinion; the Sunni community continued to treat Saad’s death as an Army killing. The “repeat NOT” emphasis in the cable is diplomatic craft: repeating “NOT” in all-caps is how cables signaled that the reader should not misread a negative under the visual confusion of all-caps transmission.

The Protein Company SAL concession: The commercial enterprise headed by Camille Chamoun — former President, patriarch of the National Liberal Party, pillar of the Maronite right — that had received an exclusive Mediterranean fishing concession. The concession threatened the livelihoods of approximately 1,000 small-boat fishermen at Sidon and Tripoli. The fishermen’s February 26 demonstration at which Saad was shot was a protest against this concession. For the revocation of the Protein concession to be listed as a Sunni-leftist demand at the Council of Ministers on March 12 was the closing of a circle: the economic grievance that had sparked the crisis was now a formal political demand.

Solh adopts the Sunni-leftist demands: Prime Minister Rashid Solh’s political calculation was that his political survival now depended on adopting the Sunni-leftist agenda as his own. His Sunni base had been mobilized against him by the Higher Islamic Council; his only path to political viability ran through becoming the internal GOL champion of the demands that had been formulated against his government. Solh survived in office for another ten weeks on this basis, but the adoption deepened the cabinet fracture rather than closing it. His May 15 resignation came when the strategy ran out of political road.

Refer to “study” by special ministerial commission: The Lebanese parliamentary tradition of deferring a demand by referring it to a study commission was a well-established technique. The practical effect was to remove the demand from the immediate political agenda, allow tempers to cool, and — if possible — let the demand die in committee. The Embassy understood exactly what was happening and said so in the March 6 cable: “a typically Lebanese solution in which no problems were really solved but were merely to be brushed under the rug.” The Command Council demand — if pursued — would have required constitutional amendment and a reopening of the National Pact; referring it to study was the political equivalent of killing it without saying so.

The Embassy’s comparative judgment: “Probably one of the more serious surges of confessional feeling in recent years” is an explicit comparative statement. Godley is comparing Sidon-March-1975 to the previous benchmarks of confessional crisis in Lebanon — the 1958 civil war, the May 1973 Army-PLO clashes, and the confessional tensions of 1969 that produced the Cairo Agreement. To say that Sidon had produced confessional feelings comparable to these earlier crises was to say that a threshold had been crossed. The benchmark for civil war was closer than the Ambassador was prepared to state outright in a cable that would be distributed across the Washington bureaucracy.

The economic-and-social-problems paragraph: Godley’s Paragraph 4 comment on the “abysmal neglect of pressing economic and social problems” is the Embassy’s acknowledgment that the confessional crisis was not purely a product of fedayeen opportunism or communist agitation but had a real structural base. Lebanese economic stagnation, the government’s neglect of South Lebanon, the concentration of wealth in the Maronite commercial elite, the absence of rural development investment — these were the conditions that allowed the leftist parties to mobilize Sunni popular feeling. The cable is unusual in State Department reporting from this period for the candor of its judgment that the GOL’s structural neglect of social and economic problems was a direct contributor to the confessional polarization.

Brigadier Kanaan as source: Deputy Chief of Staff for Operations of the Lebanese Armed Forces, Brigadier Kanaan is the Lebanese Army’s operational intelligence chief. His briefing to the U.S. Defense Attaché’s Office (DAO) is the single most important documentary source in the Sidon diplomatic record. He is the source for: (a) the figure of over 1,000 fedayeen in Sidon, (b) the identification of Abu Saleh as the commander, (c) the Army’s estimate of 25–30 fedayeen killed, (d) the allegation that Arafat was fed ‘scare stories’ by Soviet Ambassador Soldatov, and (e) the insistence that Sa’iqa participated despite Syrian denials. Kanaan’s briefings would continue through the civil war; his professional judgments appear repeatedly in Embassy cables as “reliable Lebanese Army source”.

Abu Saleh (Nimr Saleh): A senior Fatah military commander of the leftist/Fatah-Uprising tendency within the PLO. Founding Fatah member. The identification of Abu Saleh as the commander of the Sidon fedayeen operation is the Lebanese Army’s professional judgment that Sidon was not a spontaneous camp-militia response to the fishermen’s demonstration but a professionally-commanded Fatah leftist operation, executed under the direction of a senior commander. His East Berlin exile (late 1974 / early 1975) is itself diagnostic: East Germany in the 1970s hosted the Fatah left, provided security-service training to Palestinian commanders, and maintained direct political relations with the faction. Abu Saleh would later break publicly with Arafat and lead Fatah al-Intifada against him in 1983; his leftist posture in Sidon in March 1975 was an early marker of that eventual rupture. He died in 2013.

100-150 Army vs over 1,000 fedayeen: Kanaan’s numerical disclosure is the most important operational fact in the cable. The Lebanese Army had attempted, on the evening of March 1, to reopen the main coastal road at Sidon with 100 to 150 troops. They met over 1,000 fedayeen firing machine guns, RPGs, and recoilless rifles from fortified rooftop positions in and around the Old City. This is an 8:1 numerical disadvantage, with the defender holding the terrain and the firepower. The Army’s decision to commit only 100–150 troops suggests it had not accurately assessed the opposing strength before the engagement; the defeat of the engagement produced exactly the political-military embarrassment the cable is now describing. The use of APCs was decisive: without armored protection, Army losses “would have been heavier”, in Kanaan’s phrasing.

The Army sorely weakened: The Embassy’s judgment that the Army’s ability to control the fedayeen — already limited — had been sorely weakened by the Sidon crisis is the operative conclusion about the state’s capacity to enforce sovereignty within its borders. From this point onward, the Lebanese Army faced a deteriorating political condition: every confessional-political crisis would make action against armed groups harder, because Army action would immediately reopen the confessional wound of Sidon. The Ain al-Rummaneh bus attack on April 13, five weeks later, would find the Army in precisely this paralysis: incapable of imposing state authority on either the Phalange militia or the PLO, because moving against either would be framed as taking the other’s side in the confessional war.

The closing appeal to Israeli leadership: Paragraph 7 of the cable is an explicit appeal to Israeli decision-makers to refrain from near-term retaliation. Godley states directly that he understands and sympathizes with Israeli feeling after the Savoy attack and acknowledges that Israel “may be prompted to reply in kind”. He then requests that Israeli leadership “think long and hard” before acting. In Embassy Beirut’s voice, this is an implicit request that the State Department transmit this concern to Israeli channels — which State did, same day, via cable 057899 to Kissinger in Jerusalem. The eventual Israeli reprisal (Operation Marvad on December 2, 1975) came nine months later, after the civil war had already destroyed the political structure Godley was trying to protect.

Referral of Command Council to study committee: The March 12 Council of Ministers decision was the specific political compromise that allowed the Solh cabinet to survive. The Sunni-leftist demand for a Command Council reorganizing the Army’s Maronite-monopolized command structure was referred to a special cabinet study committee. In Lebanese parliamentary practice, this was a deferral rather than a concession; but it was a deferral that did not require the Christian cabinet ministers to publicly oppose the demand, and it did not require Frangieh to oppose it either. The compromise held the cabinet together. It did not close the issue; the Command Council question would return in 1976.

Transfer of Southern District commander and intelligence officer: The specific operational concession. The Army commander of the Southern District — who had ordered the March 1 intervention at Sidon, and who was himself a Muslim — was to be transferred to “other posts”, along with his intelligence officer. This was the tactical concession to the Sunni-leftist demand for his replacement. In Lebanese political practice, such a transfer was not a demotion but a lateral reassignment that allowed both sides to claim outcomes: the Sunni-leftist coalition could claim that they had secured the commander’s removal, while the Army command could claim that the officer had merely been rotated in the normal course of assignments.

Abu Za’im and Abu Hassan as Arafat’s emissaries: The intra-PLO politics of the negotiation are revealing. Abu Za’im (Atallah Atallah, a senior Fatah intelligence officer) had been arrested by the Lebanese Army on March 2 (cable 1975BEIRUT02894) during the Sidon clashes; his subsequent deployment by Arafat as negotiator-to-Abu-Saleh three days later is one of the sharper illustrations of the PLO-state relationship in the period. Abu Hassan is Ali Hassan Salameh, Arafat’s senior intelligence operative and Western contact man, who would be assassinated by Mossad in Beirut in January 1979. Their operation was to be conducted under the direction of ‘Arafat and Abu Jihad (Khalil al-Wazir); the combined authority is the Fatah political-military command in Beirut. That the negotiations “had not been particularly successful” is the Embassy’s polite formula for the assessment that the Fatah leadership had either lacked the ability to control Abu Saleh’s leftist faction or had not really tried.

Kanaan’s “double game” charge: The most politically consequential allegation in the cable. Kanaan’s judgment is that the PLO leadership — Arafat and the Fatah central command — was publicly pretending to cooperate with the GOL while privately doing nothing to reduce the fedayeen occupation of Sidon. The Army had intercepted Fatah radio communications urging cooperation; the radio communications themselves were part of the double game, giving Arafat a paper trail of apparent cooperation while the underlying operational posture remained unchanged. The allegation is serious because it fingers the political strategy of the PLO leadership: to use the Sidon crisis as a lever to weaken the Lebanese state’s capacity to confront the fedayeen, while maintaining a surface posture of cooperation that protected the PLO from direct GOL retaliation.

Soviet Ambassador Soldatov’s role in Arafat’s calculations: Kanaan’s charge — that Soldatov and other Soviet officials had been feeding Arafat scare stories about an impending Lebanese Army liquidation operation — is the Lebanese Army’s reading of the political mechanism by which Arafat had been induced into his pre-Sidon posture. The charge is routed through Lebanese Army G-2 intelligence; the Embassy does not independently confirm it but passes it forward as the professional judgment of the Army’s operations chief. Soldatov’s name appearing by name, signed by a U.S. Ambassador, in a SECRET/LIMDIS/NOFORN cable forwarded to Kissinger’s shuttle, is a significant diplomatic marker: the U.S. is now registering Soviet political-intelligence activity as a specific factor in the chain of events that produced the Sidon crisis.

“Our Army” — fedayeen or Lebanese: The confessional fracture made literal. The cable records that by mid-March 1975 Sunni residents of Sidon were openly referring to the fedayeen as “our army”, while Christian groups in Beirut and the mountain were demonstrating in support of “our (Lebanese) army”. The phrase “our army” was now being claimed by two different populations to mean two different armed formations. The state monopoly on armed force, already fictive, had been verbally surrendered in Sidon. This is the phrase the Embassy chooses to preserve in the cable because it captures the diagnostic condition of the pre-civil-war political order: two armies, each publicly claimed by a different confessional community, operating in the same country.

The murky Syrian role: Cable 03256 is unusual in Embassy reporting of this period for its direct engagement with the question of Syrian intentions. The Embassy identifies contradictory evidence: Syria had counselled Sa’iqa to withdraw from Sidon; but Sa’iqa leaders Zohayr and Majid Muhsen had not obeyed; and Kanaan categorically insists Sa’iqa elements participated. The Embassy’s comment that Kanaan “suspects, but cannot prove or figure out precisely why, the SARG may also have encouraged the Sidon clashes in order to foment wider disturbances in Lebanon” is the diplomatic register of the Lebanese Army’s suspicion that Syria was playing a double game of its own — publicly restraining Sa’iqa while privately encouraging the operation as a way to destabilize a Lebanese government whose Maronite Christian orientation ran counter to Syrian strategic interests.

Zuhayr Muhsen: Leader of the Sa’iqa Palestinian faction, directly controlled by the Syrian Ba’th Party. Muhsen was famously quoted in 1977 (to the Dutch newspaper Trouw) stating that there was no Palestinian people, only Jordanians and Syrians — a statement reflecting his pan-Arabist and Syrian-nationalist political position. He was assassinated in Cannes in 1979. His brother Majid Muhsen held the second-rank command in Sa’iqa. Their non-compliance with Syrian government counsel to withdraw from Sidon suggests either that they were operating with a different set of orders from Syrian intelligence, or that Sa’iqa’s operational discipline in this period was looser than the SARG publicly claimed.

Syrian strategic calculation: The Embassy’s hypothesis, via Kanaan, is that the SARG may have had an interest in fomenting wider disturbances in Lebanon. The Syrian strategic reasons would have been several: to weaken the Frangieh regime, which was perceived as aligned with Saudi Arabia and the West; to create political leverage for eventual Syrian intervention in Lebanon; to discipline the PLO by producing a crisis the PLO could not control; and, more diffusely, to produce a Lebanese instability that would block Lebanese movement toward any bilateral peace initiative with Israel. In hindsight, the Syrian intervention in Lebanon would begin in April 1976 under cover of the civil war; the Sidon crisis of March 1975 may be read as an early marker of Syrian willingness to accept Lebanese destabilization as a strategic good.

Fedayeen reluctance to cede Sidon back to the state: The closing comment of cable 03256 is Godley’s judgment that the fedayeen were showing “some reluctance to allow that city to revert to full GOL control”. What the Embassy was observing was the beginning of the dual-sovereignty condition that would characterize Sidon for the rest of the pre-war period and through much of the civil war. The Lebanese state was formally sovereign; the fedayeen held operational control of key urban positions. The fishermen’s grievance had been resolved and the general strike would be called off, but the fedayeen occupation of the Old City had simply become the new normal. The Lebanese Army would not return to the city in force until after the Syrian intervention of 1976.

Cable STATE 057899 — the forwarding to Kissinger’s shuttle: The State Department cable of March 14, 1975 transmitted the verbatim text of BEIRUT 3203 to Secretary Kissinger’s traveling party, routed through the U.S. Consulate in Jerusalem. The reference “TOSEC 523” identifies the cable as number 523 in the series sent to the Secretary during this particular travel. The cable was drafted by NEA/ARN’s P.K. Bullen and approved by Bullen himself; distribution was limited to NSC/Executive Secretariat and S/S (the Secretary’s immediate staff). The cable was signed by Robert S. Ingersoll, Acting Secretary during Kissinger’s absence. The administrative significance: Godley’s warning that Israeli retaliation for the Savoy attack would collapse the Lebanese regime was placed before the Secretary at the active decision point for U.S. policy on Israeli reprisal. Kissinger’s shuttle negotiations collapsed on March 22, 1975; no U.S.-sanctioned Israeli reprisal for the Savoy attack occurred in the immediate window. The eventual Israeli response (Operation Marvad / Mount Moussa raid, December 2, 1975) came nine months later, by which point the Lebanese civil war had been under way for eight months.

readerNarrative.headline: The Strategic Assessment of the Sidon Crisis
readerNarrative.subheadline: Ambassador Godley’s SECRET/LIMDIS warning of March 12, 1975: the Lebanese Army is 8:1 outnumbered in Sidon, the commander of the fedayeen force is Abu Saleh (recently returned from East Berlin), the PLO is playing a ‘double game’, Soviet Ambassador Soldatov has been feeding Arafat ‘scare stories’, Syria may have encouraged the clashes, Musa Sadr has publicly joined the agitation, and an Israeli reprisal for the Savoy Hotel attack would collapse the regime. The cable was forwarded same-day to Kissinger’s Jerusalem shuttle.
readerNarrative.summary: Fourteen days after the Sidon clashes began, Ambassador G. McMurtrie Godley filed the Embassy’s strategic assessment of the crisis in two companion SECRET/LIMDIS/NOFORN cables. The first (1975BEIRUT03203, filed the evening before the decisive Council of Ministers meeting) was the retrospective analysis: the crisis had dangerously aroused confessional feelings, the GOL had been further discredited in Muslim eyes, the Lebanese Army’s ability to control the fedayeen had been sorely weakened. Brigadier Kanaan, Deputy Chief of Staff for Operations, had briefed the Embassy: on March 1, the Army had tried to reopen the coastal road with 100–150 troops and had been opposed by over 1,000 fedayeen firing machine-guns, RPGs, and recoilless rifles from fortified positions; the Army killed 25–30 fedayeen; the commander of the fedayeen force was Fatah’s “leftist” military leader Abu Saleh, recently returned from exile in East Berlin. The Shia cleric Musa Sadr, whose silence during the first two weeks of the crisis had been conspicuous, had now publicly joined the Sunni-leftist agitation. The Embassy’s operational warning was delivered in explicit terms: any Israeli retaliation for the March 5 Savoy Hotel attack in Tel Aviv would force the Lebanese Army to respond or lose all credibility with the Lebanese public. The cable was forwarded the same day by State Department cable 057899 to Secretary Kissinger’s traveling party in Jerusalem, where Kissinger was conducting the shuttle negotiations on what would become the collapsed second Sinai interim agreement. The second Embassy cable (1975BEIRUT03256, filed 48 hours later) recorded the compromise outcome: the Council of Ministers had referred the demand for Army-command reform to a special cabinet committee for study, had tasked the Economy Minister with satisfying the fishermen, and had quietly transferred the Army’s Southern District commander to ‘other posts’. The Solh cabinet survived. But Kanaan’s further briefing recorded in the second cable delivered three additional revelations: (1) the PLO leadership was playing a ‘double game’, publicly negotiating while privately doing nothing to reduce the fedayeen occupation; (2) Soviet Ambassador Soldatov and other Soviet officials had filled Arafat full of ‘scare stories’ about an impending Lebanese Army ‘liquidation’ operation, inducing Arafat to welcome exactly the confessional turmoil that was now destabilizing Lebanon; (3) Sa’iqa had participated in the Sidon operation despite Syrian government instructions to withdraw — and Kanaan suspected Syria had encouraged the clashes in order to foment wider disturbances. The cables close the Sidon crisis diplomatic record. The civil war would begin four weeks later.
keyRevelations: The Lebanese Army was 8:1 outnumbered in Sidon on March 1. Brigadier Kanaan’s briefing to the Embassy: 100–150 Army troops faced over 1,000 fedayeen firing machine-guns, RPGs, and recoilless rifles from fortified rooftop positions in and around the Old City. The Army killed 25–30 fedayeen. The 8:1 disadvantage is the operational truth about why the Army had not returned to Sidon.

The commander of the fedayeen force was Abu Saleh, recently returned from East Berlin exile. The Lebanese Army’s professional intelligence judgment was that Sidon was not a spontaneous camp-militia response but a professionally-commanded Fatah leftist operation, directed by a senior commander with direct East German / Stasi intelligence connections.

The PLO leadership was playing a ‘double game’, according to Lebanese Army intelligence. Arafat and the Fatah central command publicly deployed Abu Za’im and Abu Hassan to negotiate with Abu Saleh; the Army intercepted Fatah radio traffic urging cooperation; but Kanaan judged the cooperation performative and the underlying operational posture of the PLO unchanged.

Soviet Ambassador Soldatov had been feeding Arafat ‘scare stories’ about an impending Lebanese Army ‘liquidation’ of the fedayeen. A U.S. Ambassador’s signature on a cable naming the Soviet Ambassador to Lebanon as an active manipulator of Arafat’s political calculations is a significant diplomatic marker, forwarded to Kissinger’s shuttle the same day.

The Embassy warned that any Israeli reprisal for the Savoy Hotel attack would collapse the Lebanese regime. Godley’s operational conclusion: an Israeli reprisal would force the Lebanese Army to respond or be branded as traitors after ‘having killed brother Arabs’ in Sidon. The warning was forwarded same-day to Kissinger in Jerusalem via cable STATE 057899.

Imam Musa Sadr, whose silence had been conspicuous, publicly joined the agitation. The Shia community’s most organized political figure entered the Sunni-leftist opposition to the Frangieh regime around March 10–11. Four months later, the Amal Movement would be publicly named.

Syria may have encouraged the Sidon clashes, while publicly telling Sa’iqa to withdraw. Kanaan categorically insists Sa’iqa participated; Syrian leaders Zohayr and Majid Muhsen did not obey withdrawal instructions; Kanaan suspects the SARG had a strategic interest in foment wider disturbances. One year later, Syrian troops would enter Lebanon under cover of the civil war.
